definition: Events, experiences or material viewed as opportunities for creating posts, videos or other creative work.
example: The creator visited the festival for the content, hoping to find stories to film.
distinctions: For the content can describe seeking material to create work; it need not refer to a video or post that already exists.
usage: Internet colloquial use, with first-syllable stress. The example explains the creator’s stated purpose.

originalSense.definition: The potential of creative work for a content creator.

definition: A period of work undertaken under a temporary contract.
example: She completed a six-month contract at the research centre.
distinctions: This contract names a period or stint of work; the contract document records the agreement’s terms.
usage: Noun with first-syllable stress. The period is temporary; the agreement determines its actual terms.

originalSense.definition: A period of work agreed to under a temporary contract.

definition: Existing or happening now; current.
example: The present timetable will remain in use until Friday.
distinctions: Present before a noun can mean current; present after a noun can identify people who are here. Compare the present members and the members present.

originalSense.definition: Relating to now, for the time being; current.
originalSense.example: The barbaric practice continues to the present day.

distinctionTask.prompt: The present timetable means the _____ timetable.
distinctionTask.explanation: The adjective present can mean current or existing now.

definition: Here or at the place being discussed.
example: All the students present signed the attendance sheet.
distinctions: The members present means the members who are here; the present members can mean the current membership. Absent expresses the opposite attendance state.
usage: Adjective with first-syllable stress. Often after the noun when it means attending.

originalSense.definition: Located in the immediate vicinity.
originalSense.example: Only half of all present members were present at the meeting.

distinctionTask.prompt: The members present means the members who _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Present after the noun commonly describes attendance.

definition: Fast-acting or producing an immediate effect.
example: In the older phrase “a more present remedy”, present means more immediately effective.
distinctions: This obsolete adjective concerns speed of effect; a present-day remedy concerns the current period.
usage: Obsolete medical or related use. This reading note explains Burton’s phrase and does not endorse the historical treatment described in its source.

originalSense.definition: Having an immediate effect (of a medicine, poison etc.); fast-acting.
originalSense.example: Amongſt this number of Cordials and Alteratiues, J doe not find a more preſent remedy, then a cup of wine, or ſtrong drinke, and if it be ſoberly and opportunely vſed.

definition: Immediate or without delay.
example: In the older request “a present pardon”, present means an immediate pardon.
distinctions: This obsolete present means without delay; the current-time adjective can instead describe what exists now.
usage: Obsolete. The example explains the recorded phrase.

originalSense.definition: Not delayed; immediate; instant.
originalSense.example: Sign me a present pardon for my brother,

definition: Ready or quick to respond, especially in an emergency.
example: In the dated phrase “a present wit”, present describes a mind ready to respond quickly.
distinctions: This dated adjective concerns readiness; presence of mind is a related modern expression for calm, effective thinking in a difficult situation.
usage: Dated. This is an explanation of the source phrase.

originalSense.definition: Ready; quick in emergency.
originalSense.example: a present wit

definition: Favourably attentive or willing to respond.
example: In the older phrase “a god so present to my prayer”, present means favourably attentive to the prayer.
collocations: present to my prayer (obsolete source wording)
distinctions: This obsolete present concerns favourable attention; present at a meeting concerns attendance.
usage: Obsolete. The reading note explains the source wording without making a religious claim.

originalSense.definition: Favorably attentive; propitious.
originalSense.example: to find a god so present to my prayer

definition: Being referred to in the current text or situation, in a use similar to this.
example: The present chapter explains how the experiment was designed.
distinctions: The present chapter means this chapter in the current context; a chapter written in the present tense concerns a separate grammatical meaning.
usage: Adjective with first-syllable stress; common in formal writing.

originalSense.definition: Relating to something a person is referring to in the very context, with a deictic use similar to the demonstrative adjective this.
originalSense.example: Near-synonyms: this (determiner), this (pronoun), current

definition: Attentive and mentally engaged with the current situation.
example: She put away her phone so she could be fully present during the conversation.
distinctions: Being present physically does not necessarily mean being attentive; this sense concerns mental engagement.

originalSense.definition: Attentive; alert; focused.
originalSense.example: Sorry, I was distracted just now, I'll try to be more present from now on.

definition: Indicating neither support nor opposition in a voting procedure that permits that response.
example: Under the committee’s rules, a member could vote present rather than yes or no.
distinctions: A present vote can express abstention under the applicable rules; it is not automatically a yes vote. Its effect on attendance or quorum depends on the procedure.
usage: Political or procedural use. Voting rules vary.

originalSense.definition: Neither for or against (used in voting to express abstention)

distinctionTask.prompt: Under rules allowing a present vote as abstention, voting present is _____ a yes vote.
distinctionTask.explanation: The rules determine the effects of abstention; present does not automatically express support.

definition: The current moment or period of time.
example: The exhibition traces changes from the 1950s to the present.
distinctions: At present means now; for the present means for now or temporarily. A present meaning a gift is a separate noun.

originalSense.definition: The current moment or period of time.

definition: The present tense in grammar.
example: The verb form walks is in the simple present.
distinctions: Grammatical present tense does not always refer to this exact moment: habits and some scheduled future events can also use present forms.

originalSense.definition: The present tense.

distinctionTask.prompt: In “She walks to work every day”, the simple present describes _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Present-tense forms can describe habits as well as current situations.

definition: A gift given to someone, often on a special occasion.
example: They gave her a book as a birthday present.
distinctions: A present is a gift; the present is the current time. Context and the article help distinguish the noun senses.

originalSense.definition: A gift, especially one given for birthdays, Christmas, anniversaries, graduations, weddings, or any other special occasions.
originalSense.example: wedding present

definition: The position of a soldier when presenting arms.
example: In the drill sentence “The platoon stands at present”, present names a military position.
distinctions: At present ordinarily means now; this specialised noun instead names the presenting-arms position in drill.
usage: Military terminology. The example explains the source sentence, without providing drill instructions.

originalSense.definition: The position of a soldier in presenting arms.
originalSense.example: The platoon stands at present.

definition: Faeces, referred to humorously or euphemistically as a gift.
example: The cat had left an unwelcome present beside the litter tray.
distinctions: Present is a humorous euphemism in this context; it does not describe an intended gift.
usage: Colloquial and euphemistic; the reference should be clear from context.

originalSense.definition: Poo; feces.
originalSense.example: I think our toddler's just left us a little present in his diaper...

definition: To introduce someone formally to another person.
example: The host presented the visiting researcher to the audience.
distinctions: Present someone to an audience introduces the person; present someone with an award gives them something.

originalSense.definition: To bring (someone) into the presence of (a person); to introduce formally.
originalSense.example: to present an envoy to the king

distinctionTask.prompt: Presenting a visitor to an audience means _____ the visitor.
distinctionTask.explanation: Present someone to introduces; present someone with can express giving.

definition: To appear or come across outwardly in a particular way.
example: The candidate presented well during the interview.
distinctions: Present well describes the impression someone makes; be present describes attendance or attention.

originalSense.definition: To appear or represent oneself outwardly.
originalSense.example: With your shabby attire, you do not present well as a prospective investment banking associate!

definition: To nominate a member of the clergy for appointment to a benefice.
example: The patron presented a candidate to the bishop for the vacant benefice.
collocations: present a candidate to the bishop
distinctions: Presentation nominates a candidate; it is not itself every subsequent step of appointment. The rules depend on the church and jurisdiction.

originalSense.definition: To nominate (a member of the clergy) for an ecclesiastical benefice; to offer to the bishop or ordinary as a candidate for institution.

definition: To submit a complaint, problem or other matter to a court or authority for consideration.
example: The residents presented their complaint to the council.
distinctions: Presenting a complaint submits it for consideration; it does not establish that its allegations are true or that the authority has upheld it.

originalSense.definition: To offer (a problem, complaint) to a court or other authority for consideration.

definition: To bring a person before an authority on a charge or accusation.
example: In the historical account of people being “presented for saying” something, presented means formally accused or reported to an authority.
distinctions: This rare legal or ecclesiastical use concerns an accusation; present a visitor to an audience means introduce them. An accusation is not a finding of guilt.
usage: Now rare. The reading note explains the source construction.

originalSense.definition: To charge (a person) with a crime or accusation; to bring before court.
originalSense.example: In the diocese of Gloucester in 1548 two inhabitants of Slimbridge were presented for saying that holy oil was ‘of no virtue but meet to grease sheep’.

definition: To appear or come forward in person, especially formally.
example: Applicants must present themselves at reception on arrival.
distinctions: Present oneself concerns appearing in person; present itself of an idea concerns something becoming available to the mind.
usage: Reflexive verb: use the appropriate form of oneself.

originalSense.definition: To come forward, appear in a particular place or before a particular person, especially formally.
originalSense.example: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the lord.

definition: To show or display something so that it can be seen.
example: The guide presented the model to the group.
distinctions: Present shows or puts something forward; hide or withhold prevents it from being seen or made available. The object and context determine the more specific use.

originalSense.definition: To put (something) forward in order for it to be seen; to show, exhibit.
originalSense.example: So ladies in romance assist their knight, / Present the spear, and arm him for the fight.

definition: To put information or an idea forward for understanding or consideration.
example: The report presents the results in a clear table.
distinctions: Presenting results concerns how they are communicated; producing results concerns obtaining them. Presentation alone does not verify a claim.
usage: Transitive verb, often used in academic writing.

originalSense.definition: To make clear to one's mind or intelligence; to put forward for consideration.
originalSense.example: I do begin to realize that the matter must be presented in such a way as may interest the reader.

distinctionTask.prompt: Presenting results concerns how they are _____; producing results concerns obtaining them.
distinctionTask.explanation: Presentation communicates information without itself proving it true.

definition: To stage or put on a performance or production.
example: The college will present a new play next month.
distinctions: Present a play means put it on for an audience; compose or write a play concerns creating the text.

originalSense.definition: To put on, stage (a play etc.).
originalSense.example: The theater is proud to present the Fearless Fliers.

definition: To point or hold a firearm in a position ready for use.
example: In the historical scene, the sentry presented his musket towards the gate.
distinctions: This military verb concerns the weapon’s position; presenting arms in a ceremonial drill is a related but context-specific use.
usage: Military or historical terminology. The example is a fictional illustration, not a weapon-handling instruction.

originalSense.definition: To point (a firearm) at something, to hold (a weapon) in a position ready to fire.

definition: To occur to the mind or become available for consideration.
example: A simpler solution presented itself during the discussion.
distinctions: A solution presenting itself becomes apparent; a person presenting themselves appears in person.
usage: Reflexive verb, usually with itself when the subject is an idea, solution or opportunity.

originalSense.definition: To offer oneself for mental consideration; to occur to the mind.
originalSense.example: Well, one idea does present itself.

definition: To come to medical attention, often with particular symptoms.
example: The patient presented with a persistent cough.
distinctions: Present with a symptom describes how someone comes to medical attention; diagnose identifies a condition. The symptom alone does not establish a diagnosis.

originalSense.definition: To come to the attention of medical staff, especially with a specific symptom.
originalSense.example: The patient presented with insomnia.

distinctionTask.prompt: A patient presenting with a cough has come to medical attention with a _____.
options: confirmed diagnosis established by that phrase alone
distinctionTask.explanation: Presenting symptoms do not by themselves establish a diagnosis.

definition: To be positioned so that a particular fetal part is directed towards the birth canal for delivery.
example: During delivery, the baby presented head first.
distinctions: Fetal presentation describes which part comes towards the birth canal; it is a specialised medical sense of present.
usage: Obstetrics; intransitive verb. The sentence illustrates terminology rather than offering clinical guidance.

originalSense.definition: To appear (in a specific way) for delivery (of a fetus); to appear first at the mouth of the uterus during childbirth.

definition: To express or represent oneself outwardly as having a particular gender.
example: The character presents as a woman in public.
distinctions: Presentation concerns outward expression; it does not by itself establish a person’s gender identity.
usage: Intransitive verb with as. The example describes a fictional character.

originalSense.definition: To appear or represent oneself (as having a certain gender).
originalSense.example: At that time, Elbe was presenting as a man.

definition: To act as the host or presenter of a broadcast programme.
example: She presents a weekly radio programme about science.
distinctions: Presenting a programme is hosting it; producing it concerns arranging or creating the production. The roles can overlap.
usage: Broadcasting; transitive verb, especially British English.

originalSense.definition: To act as presenter on (a radio, television programme etc.).
originalSense.example: Anne Robinson presents "The Weakest Link".

definition: To give someone a gift, award or other presentation.
example: The college presented her with an award for community service.
distinctions: Present someone with an award and present an award to someone both express giving; present someone to an audience expresses introduction.

originalSense.definition: To give a gift or presentation to (someone).
originalSense.example: She was presented with an honorary degree for her services to entertainment.

distinctionTask.prompt: The college gave her an award: it presented her _____ the award.
distinctionTask.explanation: Present someone with an award and present an award to someone are both valid giving constructions.

definition: To offer or convey something abstract, such as thanks or compliments.
example: Please present my compliments to the hosts.
distinctions: Present compliments means convey them; a physical present is a gift. This construction is more formal than give someone my thanks.

originalSense.definition: To deliver (something abstract) as though as a gift; to offer.
originalSense.example: I presented my compliments to Lady Featherstoneshaw.

definition: To hand over a bill or similar document for payment.
example: The server presented the bill at the end of the meal.
distinctions: Presenting a bill requests or initiates payment; it does not mean the bill has already been paid.
usage: Business or payment terminology; transitive verb.

originalSense.definition: To hand over (a bill etc.) to be paid.

distinctionTask.prompt: Presenting a bill for payment means the bill has _____ paid.
distinctionTask.explanation: Presenting a bill requests or initiates payment; payment is a separate event.

definition: In some animals, to adopt a sexually receptive posture displaying the genital region.
example: During courtship, the female presents to the male by adopting a receptive posture.
distinctions: This zoological use concerns reproductive signalling in particular species; it is separate from presenting an award or introducing someone.
usage: Zoology; intransitive verb. The example is a neutral description of animal behaviour.

originalSense.definition: To display one's female genitalia in a way that signals to others that one is ready for copulation. Also referred to as lordosis behaviour.

definition: In omegaverse fiction, to have a fictional secondary designation such as alpha or omega become apparent.
example: In the source discussion, “presenting as an omega” means the character’s fictional designation becoming apparent.
distinctions: These designations belong to a fictional setting; they are not biological categories for real people. This present is also separate from gender presentation in ordinary English.
usage: Fandom terminology. This reading note explains the cited phrase without reproducing its surrounding narrative.

originalSense.definition: In omegaverse fiction, to have one's secondary sex (alpha, omega, or beta) become apparent, typically at puberty.
originalSense.example: Sherlock’s gender performance itself remains unchanged, with the exception of the hormonal changes he goes through after presenting as an omega.

definition: Source grouping: uses involving direction, communication and location.

usage: Source meaning group. The grouped meanings remain separately available.

originalSense.definition: Direction.

distinctions: Preparation is the source heading; the quotation about “no small degree of address” specifically illustrates skill or resourcefulness, not every preparation use.
usage: Source meaning group. Choose the relevant child meaning for study.

definition: To prepare oneself or get ready.

originalSense.definition: To prepare oneself.

definition: To direct speech to someone, without an expressed direct object.

originalSense.definition: To direct speech.

definition: To direct or aim something towards a destination.
example: In the older phrase “his way with me addrest”, addrest means directed his course.
distinctions: This obsolete address concerns directing a course or object; address a problem concerns attending to it.
usage: Obsolete. The reading note explains the recorded construction.

originalSense.definition: To aim; to direct.
originalSense.example: And this good knight his way with me addrest.

definition: To prepare or make someone or something ready.

originalSense.definition: To prepare or make ready.
originalSense.example: His foe was soone addrest.

definition: To apply one’s attention, skill or effort to a task.

usage: Formal reflexive construction, with to followed by the task or object of attention.

originalSense.definition: To prepare oneself; to apply one's skill or energies (to some object); to betake.
originalSense.example: These men addressed themselves to the task.

definition: To direct one’s remarks to a person or audience.
example: The speaker addressed herself to the audience.
distinctions: Address oneself to an audience concerns speaking to it; address oneself to a task concerns applying effort to it.
usage: Reflexive construction. Context distinguishes speaking from preparing for a task.

originalSense.definition: To direct one’s remarks (to someone).

1701, Thomas Brown, Laconics, or New Maxims of State and Conversation, London: Thomas Hodgson, section 76, p. 103,
In the Reign of King Charles the Second, a certain Worthy Divine at Whitehall, thus Address’d himself to the Auditory at the conclusion of his Sermon.

definition: To dress, clothe or array someone.
example: In the older phrase “addressed herself in … apparel”, addressed means dressed.
distinctions: This archaic address means clothe or dress; the modern address a person normally means speak to them.
usage: Archaic. The reading note explains the recorded construction.

originalSense.definition: To clothe or array; to dress.

example: She addressed her remarks to the committee.
distinctions: Address remarks to the committee makes the remarks the direct object; address the committee makes the audience the direct object.
usage: Transitive construction with to introducing the recipient.

originalSense.definition: To direct, as words (to anyone or anything); to make, as a speech, petition, etc. (to any audience).

definition: To speak or write to a person or group.

originalSense.definition: To direct speech to; to make a communication to, whether spoken or written; to apply to by words, as by a speech, petition, etc., to speak to.

definition: To put a recipient’s name and delivery details on correspondence.

originalSense.definition: To direct in writing, as a letter; to superscribe, or to direct and transmit.
originalSense.example: He addressed a letter.

distinctionTask.prompt: To identify the recipient on an envelope, address it _____ the admissions office.
distinctionTask.explanation: Addressing identifies delivery details; delivery happens separately.

definition: To court someone or make a romantic approach.

distinctions: This older courtship sense differs from the ordinary modern meaning speak to someone. A romantic approach does not imply acceptance.
usage: Older or literary. The example explains the specialised use rather than quoting a historical sentence.

originalSense.definition: To make suit to as a lover; to court; to woo.

definition: To consign or entrust something to an agent or another person’s care.
example: In the shipping example “The ship was addressed to a merchant”, addressed means consigned to the merchant’s care.
collocations: a ship addressed to a merchant (older)
distinctions: This consignment sense concerns entrusting care or agency; addressing a letter concerns its delivery details.
usage: Older commercial usage. The note explains the source example.

originalSense.definition: To consign or entrust to the care of another, as agent or factor.
originalSense.example: The ship was addressed to a merchant in Baltimore.

definition: To turn one’s attention or efforts to something.
example: She addressed the task with patience and care.
distinctions: Addressing a task means applying attention or effort; it does not by itself mean the task is complete.
usage: Transitive use. The more specific address a problem emphasises an attempt to resolve it.

originalSense.definition: To address oneself to; to prepare oneself for; to apply oneself to; to direct one's speech, discourse or efforts to.
originalSense.example: He stepped away from the sink, put up the toilet ring (Vi complained bitterly if he forgot to put it down when he was through, but never seemed to feel any pressing need to put it back up when she was), and addressed the John.

definition: To give attention to a problem in an attempt to deal with it.
example: The new plan addresses the shortage of study space.
distinctions: Address a problem means attend to or try to deal with it; solve means successfully find a solution. Address does not guarantee success.
usage: Formal transitive verb; useful in academic and professional writing.

originalSense.definition: To direct attention towards a problem or obstacle, in an attempt to resolve it.

"This remains a big issue for us and without some form of censorship purely focusing on [violent videos], I'm not sure how we can address it."

definition: To refer to or select a location in computer memory.

originalSense.definition: To refer to a location in computer memory.

distinctionTask.prompt: Addressing a memory location identifies or selects it; reading describes _____ there.
options: the spelling of a postal street name
distinctionTask.explanation: The address identifies a location and the memory operation determines what happens there.

definition: To take up the position from which to strike a golf ball.
example: The golfer addressed the ball before beginning the swing.
distinctions: Addressing the ball prepares for the stroke; it is not the act of striking it. The word is not limited to a ball on a tee.
usage: Golf; the source records Scottish usage. This is a vocabulary illustration rather than coaching advice.

originalSense.definition: To get ready to hit (the ball on the tee).

definition: A planned undertaking with a goal, often completed through several stages.
example: The students completed a project on local water use.

originalSense.definition: An urban, low-income housing building.

example: In the dated phrase “a man given to projects”, projects means impractical schemes.
distinctions: This dated project evaluates a scheme as impractical; modern a research project does not carry that judgement automatically.

originalSense.definition: An idle scheme; an impracticable design.
originalSense.example: a man given to projects

definition: An inexperienced recruit expected to improve substantially with coaching.

definition: To stick out beyond a surface or edge.

originalSense.definition: To extend beyond a surface.

definition: To cast an image, shadow or other visible form onto a surface.
example: The device projected the diagram onto the screen.
distinctions: Projecting an image displays it on a surface; projecting a future total estimates it.
usage: Transitive verb, with onto often introducing the receiving surface.

originalSense.definition: To cast (an image or shadow) upon a surface; to throw or cast forward; to shoot forth.

definition: To extend a part or appendage outwards.
example: The snail projected its tentacles beyond the shell.
distinctions: This transitive project states the part extended as its object; the balcony projects uses the intransitive construction.

originalSense.definition: To extend (a protrusion or appendage) outward.

definition: To plan for or estimate a future state or result.

usage: Transitive verb with second-syllable stress. State the assumptions when they matter.

originalSense.definition: To make plans for; to forecast.
originalSense.example: The CEO is projecting the completion of the acquisition by April 2007.

distinctionTask.prompt: A projected change from 100 to 120 is a _____ increase, assuming the projection occurs.
distinctionTask.explanation: The increase is 20 relative to the starting 100, giving 20%. A projection is conditional on its assumptions.

definition: To convey a particular impression or image of oneself.
example: She projected confidence during the presentation.
distinctions: Project confidence concerns the impression conveyed; it does not establish how confident someone feels internally.
usage: Transitive or reflexive use; second-syllable stress.

originalSense.definition: To present (oneself), to convey a certain impression, usually in a good way.
originalSense.example: It is difficult to gauge the exact point at which women stop trying to fool men and really begin to deceive themselves, but an objective analyst cannot escape the conclusion (1) that partly from a natural device inherent in the species, women deliberately project upon actual or potential suitors an impression of themselves that is not an accurate picture of their total nature, and (2) that few women ever are privileged to see themselves as they really are.

distinctionTask.prompt: Projecting confidence describes the _____ someone conveys.
distinctionTask.explanation: The impression conveyed need not match the person’s internal feeling.

definition: To attribute one’s own feelings or attitudes to someone else.
example: In the fictional example, he projects his own anxiety onto his colleague.
distinctions: Projection attributes one’s own state to someone else; it is not evidence of that other person’s feelings. A single action does not establish a clinical diagnosis.
usage: Psychology or psychoanalytic terminology; the example explains the concept.

originalSense.definition: To assume qualities or mindsets in others based on one's own personality.

definition: To transform spatial coordinates into another map projection or coordinate reference system.
example: The analyst projected the data from geographic coordinates into a suitable local projected coordinate system.
distinctions: Reprojection changes coordinate values to represent locations in another system; assigning a coordinate system labels how existing numbers are interpreted. A change of datum may require an additional transformation.
usage: Cartography and GIS. Projection can change scale, shape, area or other map properties.

originalSense.definition: To change the projection (or coordinate system) of spatial data with another projection.

distinctionTask.prompt: Reprojecting spatial data changes coordinates; assigning a CRS mainly changes their _____.
options: measured location by physically moving the feature
distinctionTask.explanation: Assigning a CRS labels how existing values are interpreted. Reprojection calculates values in another CRS.

definition: To form a new geometric figure by drawing rays from a fixed point through the original figure to a receiving surface.
example: In the construction, points A and B are projected from centre P onto the target line.
distinctions: This central projection uses rays through a fixed centre; parallel projection instead uses parallel projecting lines.
usage: Geometry. The diagram is a two-dimensional cross-section of the construction.

originalSense.definition: To draw straight lines from a fixed point through every point of any body or figure, and let these fall upon a surface so as to form the points of a new figure.

distinctionTask.prompt: Central projection uses rays through _____; parallel projection uses parallel lines.
distinctionTask.explanation: The illustrated central construction uses the same finite centre P for each ray.

definition: For neurons, to extend axons to another region.
example: Neurons in this region project to the spinal cord.
distinctions: A neural projection describes anatomical connections; it does not alone specify every effect or the direction of all information flow through a circuit.
usage: Neuroanatomy; the example illustrates a connection without describing a particular clinical condition.

originalSense.definition: (of a neuron or group of neurons) to have axon(s) extending to and therefore able to influence a remote location

definition: To make one’s voice or words carry to listeners at a distance.
example: The actor projected her voice to the back of the hall.
collocations: project to the back of a room
distinctions: Projecting a voice concerns making it carry clearly; it need not mean shouting.
usage: Transitive verb, common in performance contexts.

originalSense.definition: To cause (one's voice or words) to be heard at a great distance.

definition: To speak or sing so that one can be heard at a distance.
example: Even without a microphone, the speaker could project well.
distinctions: This intransitive project has no direct object; project one’s voice names the voice as its object.

originalSense.definition: To speak or sing in such a way that one can be heard at a great distance.
originalSense.example: You would think that topic coulda put me to sleep, but HE can really project when HE wants to.

definition: To extend an idea, inference or interpretation to another point or context.
example: The historian warned against projecting modern assumptions back into the past.
distinctions: Projecting an assumption into another period extends an interpretation; it does not establish that people in that period held the assumption.

originalSense.definition: To extend to reach a point.
originalSense.example: When a word occurs only in Indo-European languages of northern or western Europe, for instance, projecting that word back to Proto-Indo-European is considered dubious.

definition: To make or yield something, without stating it as a direct object.
example: The factory continued to produce throughout the year.
distinctions: This intransitive construction leaves the product unstated; produce containers gives the transitive verb a direct object.

originalSense.definition: To make or yield something.
originalSense.example: Now it is also my understanding, I believe I am correct in this, that either one or two other manufacturers did not produce this year, which also created a certain shortage.

definition: To bring forward or make something available for inspection or use.
example: She produced her ticket when the inspector asked to see it.
distinctions: Produce a ticket makes an existing ticket available; it does not normally mean manufacture the ticket in that context.

originalSense.definition: To make (a thing) available to a person, an authority, etc.; to provide for inspection.
originalSense.example: It was necessary for the prisoner to produce a witness to prove his innocency.

definition: To organise, finance or oversee the making of a film, programme or other production.

originalSense.definition: To sponsor and present (a motion picture, etc) to an audience or to the public.

definition: To extend a line segment or side beyond an endpoint along the same straight line.
example: Produce side AB beyond B to a new point C.

distinctions: Produce AB beyond B extends the line through B; it does not create a second parallel segment.
usage: Geometry; formal instruction wording. The diagram uses collinear points A, B and C.

originalSense.definition: To extend an area, or lengthen a line.

distinctionTask.prompt: Produce AB beyond B to C means A, B and C lie on _____ line.

definition: To prolong or extend something in time or extent.

distinctions: This obsolete produce means prolong; modern produce a result normally means cause or generate it.

definition: To shape a musical recording using production techniques or technology.

originalSense.definition: That which is produced.

distinctionTask.prompt: The ordinary construction is “He refused _____ the form”.
distinctionTask.explanation: Refuse takes a to-infinitive for the declined action.

definition: To make something finer, purer or clearer.
example: The process fines the liquid by removing suspended matter.
distinctions: This verb concerns refinement or clarification; refine is the more general modern word. It is separate from fine meaning impose a penalty.

originalSense.definition: To make finer, purer, or cleaner; to purify or clarify.
originalSense.example: to fine gold

definition: To become finer, purer or clearer.
example: In the intransitive process sense, a liquid fines when it becomes clearer.
distinctions: This intransitive verb describes the material changing; fine a liquid names the material as a direct object.
usage: Technical or older use; reading recognition.

originalSense.definition: To become finer, purer, or cleaner.

definition: To reduce the coarseness of a material or texture.
example: In the recorded material sense, to fine something is to make it less coarse.
distinctions: This verb concerns texture or particle size; the adjective fine meaning excellent concerns a judgment of quality.
usage: Technical or older use; reading recognition.

originalSense.definition: To make finer, or less coarse, as in bulk, texture, etc.
originalSense.example: The tools to be used for this surface tillage are those that comminute or fine the soil most completely without compacting it or leaving it in ridges or in furrows

definition: To change something through small gradations.
example: In the recorded gradation sense, fine means change by small degrees.
distinctions: This rare verb concerns gradual change; fine-tune is the familiar modern verb for small adjustments.

originalSense.definition: To change by fine gradations.
originalSense.example: to fine down a ship's lines, i.e. to diminish her lines gradually

definition: To clarify wine or beer by removing suspended particles.
example: The producer fined the wine before bottling.
distinctions: Fining commonly uses agents that bind particles for removal, often by settling. Filtration is a distinct clarification method and is not required in every fining process.

originalSense.definition: To clarify (wine and beer) by filtration.

definition: To diminish or dwindle gradually, often with away, down or off.
example: In the dated verb sense, fine away means gradually diminish.
distinctions: This dated diminishing sense is separate from a modern fine meaning a monetary penalty.

originalSense.definition: To become gradually fine; to diminish; to dwindle (with away, down, or off).
originalSense.example: I watched her [the ship] […] gradually fining down in the westward until I lost sight of her hull.

definition: Money imposed as a penalty for breaking a law or rule.
example: The driver received a fine for illegal parking.
distinctions: A fine is a penalty; a fee is a charge for a service, permission or transaction. The two are not interchangeable.

originalSense.definition: A fee levied as punishment for breaking the law.
originalSense.example: The fine for jay-walking has gone from two dollars to thirty in the last fifteen years.

distinctionTask.prompt: A monetary penalty for an offence is a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A fine is punitive; a fee can be a charge for a service.

definition: An initial tenancy payment made in exchange for a low or nominal rent.
example: In the obsolete tenancy sense, a fine is an upfront payment associated with reduced rent.
distinctions: This historical payment is not necessarily a punishment; modern legal meaning depends on the document and jurisdiction.

originalSense.definition: Money paid by a tenant on the commencement of a tenancy so that their rent may be small or nominal.

definition: A drink imposed as a penalty in a Cambridge student drinking custom.
example: In the recorded Cambridge slang, a fine names the penalty drink in a social drinking game.
collocations: a fine at a student meal
distinctions: The drink penalty is a local social usage, separate from a legal monetary fine. This note explains the term without treating participation as compulsory.

originalSense.definition: A drink that must be taken during a meal or as part of a drinking game, following an announcement that anyone who has done some (usually outrageous) deed is to be fined; similar to I have never; commonly associated with swaps; very similar to a sconce at Oxford University, though a fine is the penalty itself rather than the act of issuing it.
originalSense.example: Fine if you've…

definition: To impose a monetary penalty on someone.
example: The council fined the company for breaching the regulations.
distinctions: Fine someone for doing something identifies the breach; charge someone a fee can concern an ordinary service instead.

originalSense.definition: To issue a fine as punishment to (someone).
originalSense.example: She was fined a thousand dollars for littering, but she appealed.

distinctionTask.prompt: The usual construction is “They fined the company _____ breaching the rule”.
distinctionTask.explanation: Fine someone for an offence or for doing something identifies the reason.

definition: To pay a fine, in the recorded intransitive use.
example: The source also records fine as an intransitive verb meaning pay a fine.
distinctions: Modern learners normally say pay a fine. The common transitive fine someone means impose the penalty, not pay it.

originalSense.definition: To pay a fine.
originalSense.example: Men fined for the king's good will; or that he would remit his anger; women fined for leave to marry.

definition: The end of a musical composition.
example: In the recorded musical sense, fine names the end of a composition.
distinctions: The musical term fine means end and is commonly pronounced /ˈfiːneɪ/; fine meaning satisfactory is /faɪn/.

originalSense.definition: The end of a musical composition.
wordFamily: da capo al fine=D.C. al fine

definition: A score marking showing where to end the piece, including after a return.
example: After the instruction D.C. al Fine, the player returned to the beginning and stopped at Fine.
distinctions: Fine marks the stopping place under the relevant instruction. It does not always mean stop on the first encounter before a required return.
usage: Music; commonly /ˈfiːneɪ/. D.C. returns to the beginning; D.S. returns to the sign.

originalSense.definition: The location in a musical score that indicates the end of the piece, particularly when the piece ends somewhere in the middle of the score due to a section of the music being repeated.
wordFamily: da capo al fine=D.C. al fine

distinctionTask.prompt: The musical marking Fine commonly has the pronunciation _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The Italian musical end marking has a different pronunciation from ordinary fine.

definition: To finish or come to an end.
example: In the obsolete intransitive verb sense, fine means finish or cease.
distinctions: This obsolete ending verb is distinct from the modern penalty verb fine.

originalSense.definition: To finish; to cease.
wordFamily: da capo al fine=D.C. al fine

definition: To bring something to an end or cause it to stop.
example: In the obsolete transitive verb sense, fine means cause something to cease.
distinctions: This obsolete transitive sense takes what is stopped as its object; the related intransitive sense describes something ending.

originalSense.definition: To cause to cease; to stop.
wordFamily: da capo al fine=D.C. al fine

definition: An end, conclusion or termination.
example: In the obsolete noun sense, fine means an ending or conclusion.
distinctions: This obsolete noun differs from a financial fine and from the specialised Italian musical marking.

originalSense.definition: End; conclusion; termination; extinction.
originalSense.example: And secret feare, to see their fatall fine
wordFamily: da capo al fine=D.C. al fine

definition: A final agreement concerning land or rents in feudal law.
example: In the recorded feudal-law sense, a fine is a final agreement about land or rents.
distinctions: This historical legal agreement is distinct from a monetary punishment. Its effect depends on the period and legal system.

originalSense.definition: A final agreement concerning lands or rents between persons, as the lord and his vassal.
originalSense.example: To cause them to pay more rent or a gretter fyne than they haue ben acustomed to do in tyme past.
wordFamily: da capo al fine=D.C. al fine

definition: A payment for a legal benefit or privilege, such as admission to copyhold or renewal of a lease.
example: In a historical English property record, a fine may be a payment for admission or lease renewal.
distinctions: This property payment is not automatically a penalty for an offence. Read the specific legal document and period.
usage: British historical property law; reading recognition.

originalSense.definition: A sum of money or price paid for obtaining a benefit, favor, or privilege, as for admission to a copyhold, or for obtaining or renewing a lease.
wordFamily: da capo al fine=D.C. al fine

definition: Fine, a family name.
example: Capitalised Fine can be a surname.
distinctions: A surname identifies a family or person; it does not describe the person as satisfactory or impose a penalty.
usage: Proper name; pronunciation is person-specific and is not inferred here.

originalSense.definition: A surname.
wordFamily: da capo al fine=D.C. al fine

definition: Of very good or excellent quality.
example: The gallery has a fine collection of landscape paintings.
distinctions: Fine can mean excellent; I’m fine can instead mean satisfactory or well. Context determines the strength of praise.

originalSense.definition: Of superior quality.

definition: Bad or inappropriate, when used ironically.
example: That is a fine way to welcome a guest—locking them outside!
distinctions: Irony reverses the literal praise. Context and tone are needed; fine is not automatically negative.

originalSense.definition: Impressively bad, inappropriate, or unsatisfactory.

distinctionTask.prompt: In “a fine mess”, fine can be _____ rather than praise.
distinctionTask.explanation: Context can reverse literal positive praise.

definition: Acceptable or satisfactory; well enough to cause no concern.
example: Tuesday is fine for me.
distinctions: Fine often means satisfactory or acceptable, which is weaker than excellent. A statement of well-being does not identify a medical condition.

originalSense.definition: Being acceptable, adequate, passable, or satisfactory; having one's well-being be no cause for concern.

distinctionTask.prompt: In “Tuesday is fine for me”, fine means _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The scheduling context expresses acceptability.

definition: Good-looking or attractive.
example: She thought the actor looked fine in the new portrait.
distinctions: In the appearance sense, fine expresses attraction or admiration; it is not an objective assessment of someone’s worth.

originalSense.definition: Good-looking, attractive.

definition: Subtle or delicately balanced, especially in a distinction.
example: There is a fine distinction between the two legal terms.
distinctions: A fine distinction is subtle; a clear distinction can be easy to notice. Fine does not mean morally better here.

originalSense.definition: Subtle, delicately balanced or discriminated.

distinctionTask.prompt: A fine distinction is a _____ difference.
distinctionTask.explanation: Fine describes a small or delicately discriminated distinction.

definition: Showy or excessively decorated.
example: In the obsolete sense, fine can describe something showy or overdecorated.
distinctions: This obsolete use differs from ordinary modern praise such as fine craftsmanship.

originalSense.definition: Showy; overdecorated.

definition: Delicate, exquisite or skilfully executed.
example: The carving shows fine craftsmanship in every small detail.
distinctions: This fine emphasises delicacy or skill; fine powder emphasises small particles.

originalSense.definition: Delicate; subtle; exquisite; artful; dexterous.

definition: Used in a response about well-being that may avoid further discussion.
example: “I’m fine” can be a sincere reassurance or a way to avoid explaining more. The words alone do not establish how the speaker feels.
distinctions: Listen to context and what the person chooses to share; do not treat this expression as proof that someone is upset or concealing a problem.
usage: Pragmatic usage note /faɪn/; interpretation depends on context.

originalSense.definition: An answer often used to cover an unnecessary explanation, rather to avoid conflict or an argument. Saying "I'm fine" can be used to avoid inquiry when the speaker is not really okay.

definition: A named condition grade for a collectible, below higher grades such as very fine or mint in relevant systems.
example: The dealer graded the coin as fine under the stated grading standard.
distinctions: Fine as a technical grade is a position in a particular scale, not simply general praise. Grade definitions vary by collectible and system.

originalSense.definition: Of a particular grade of quality, usually between very good and very fine, and below mint.

definition: Sunny and not raining, when describing weather.
example: We hope for fine weather during the weekend.
distinctions: Fine weather concerns fair conditions, not necessarily high temperature.

originalSense.definition: Sunny and not raining.

definition: Made up of very small particles or pieces.
example: Sieve the flour to remove lumps and leave a fine powder.
distinctions: Fine particles are small; coarse particles are larger. Fine does not automatically mean better for every application.

originalSense.definition: Consisting of especially minute particulates; made up of particularly small pieces.

distinctionTask.prompt: The opposite of fine in a particle-size comparison is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Fine describes smaller particles; coarse describes larger particles.

definition: Very thin, narrow or slender.
example: A fine crack ran across the glaze.
distinctions: Fine here describes small thickness or width; tiny can describe small overall size.

originalSense.definition: Particularly slender; especially thin, narrow, or of small girth.

definition: Made from thin filaments or fibres.
example: The scarf was woven from fine wool.
distinctions: Fine fibres have small diameter; a fine-quality textile is a judgment of quality that may involve other properties.

originalSense.definition: Made of slender or thin filaments.

definition: Containing a specified proportion of pure metal.
example: A mark of 999 fine indicates 999 parts of the specified metal per thousand.
distinctions: Fineness describes purity. A millesimal value of 999 means 99.9%, not 999%, and does not specify the object’s total mass.

originalSense.definition: Having a (specified) proportion of pure metal in its composition.

distinctionTask.prompt: 999 parts of pure metal per thousand is _____ purity.

definition: A contest or trial of strength or skill.
example: The two debaters prepared for their match.
distinctions: A match is a contest; a match meaning a suitable pairing concerns correspondence instead. Sporting events are a specific child meaning.

originalSense.definition: Any contest or trial of strength or skill, or to determine superiority.
originalSense.example: Ferrer his Taberd vvith rich Verry ſpred, / VVell knovvne in many a vvarlike match before; […]

definition: Equality or balance of conditions in a contest.
example: The handicap was intended to make an even match.
distinctions: An even match describes balanced competition; a drawn match describes an equal final score.

originalSense.definition: Equality of conditions in contest or competition.
originalSense.example: It were no match, your nail against his horn.

definition: A pair of things or people with suitable or corresponding characteristics.
example: The curtains are a good match for the carpet.
distinctions: A good match means suitable correspondence; an exact match means the compared features agree exactly. Suitability need not require identity.

originalSense.definition: A pair of items or entities with mutually suitable characteristics.
originalSense.example: The carpet and curtains are a match.

distinctionTask.prompt: A good match for a role means _____ for that role.
distinctionTask.explanation: Suitability depends on relevant needs and features, not complete identity.

definition: Suitability for a purpose, person or situation.
example: Her experience makes her a strong match for the role.
distinctions: This match concerns fit for a purpose; equal numbers alone do not establish suitability.

originalSense.definition: Suitability.

definition: A support or formed block that holds a mould pattern and shapes the parting surfaces of a mould.
example: In mould-making terminology, a match holds part of the pattern and helps shape the separation between mould sections.
collocations: a match for a mould pattern
distinctions: This specialised object is separate from a contest or a small stick for making fire.
usage: Metalworking and mould making; reading recognition.

originalSense.definition: A perforated board, block of plaster, hardened sand, etc., in which a pattern is partly embedded when a mould is made, for giving shape to the surfaces of separation between the parts of the mould.

definition: To agree, correspond or have compatible features.
example: The two descriptions do not match.
distinctions: This use needs no direct object; one description matches the other names the compared object.

originalSense.definition: To agree; to be equal; to correspond.
originalSense.example: Their interests didn't match, so it took a long time to agree what to do together.

definition: To correspond to, be equal to or have features compatible with something.
example: The signature matches the one on the application.
distinctions: Match can concern selected features; a colour match does not imply that two objects are identical in every respect.

originalSense.definition: To agree with; to be equal to; to correspond to.
originalSense.example: His interests didn't match her interests.

definition: To equal or rival someone’s level of achievement.
example: The new runner matched the previous course record.
distinctions: Matching a record reaches that level; breaking it goes beyond it. In broader contexts, matching someone can mean proving an equal or better rival.

originalSense.definition: To equal or exceed in achievement.
originalSense.example: She matched him at every turn: anything he could do, she could do as well or better.

distinctionTask.prompt: Matching a timed record means _____ its level; breaking it means going beyond it.
distinctionTask.explanation: Match a record reaches the record level; break a record improves on it.

definition: To bring together things or people that form a suitable pair.
example: The organiser matched each new student with a mentor.
distinctions: Match pairs items by relevant features or needs; mix merely combines them without necessarily finding suitable partners.

originalSense.definition: To make a successful match or pairing.
originalSense.example: They found out about his color-blindness when he couldn't match socks properly.

definition: To unite in marriage or form a mating pair.
example: In the obsolete marriage sense, match means unite people in marriage.
distinctions: This older marriage verb is distinct from the modern broader match someone with a mentor.

originalSense.definition: To unite in marriage, to mate.
originalSense.example: […]Adam's sons are my brethren; and truly, I hold it a sin to match in my kindred.

definition: To make pieces fit together, especially by cutting tongue-and-groove edges in boards.
example: The workshop matched the boards for the panelled wall.
distinctions: This joinery sense concerns fitting edges together; matching wood colour concerns visual correspondence.

originalSense.definition: To fit together, or make suitable for fitting together; specifically, to furnish with a tongue and groove at the edges.
originalSense.example: to match boards

definition: To satisfy a rule or a regular-expression pattern.

definition: A small treated stick or paper strip that produces a flame when struck on a suitable surface.
example: She used a match to light the candle.
distinctions: A match is a disposable fire-lighting item; a lighter is a different device. A sporting match is a separate word sense.

originalSense.definition: A small wooden stick specially treated with chemicals to produce flame upon contact with another chemical, from the frictional heat produced by striking it against a surface, or both; other similar items made from chemically-treated paper, cardboard, etc.
originalSense.example: He struck a match and lit his pipe.

distinctionTask.prompt: The usual plural of the fire-lighting noun match is _____.

definition: A taper or thin stick used to transfer a flame.

originalSense.definition: Synonym of taper, a thin stick used to transfer flame, as from tender to a candle.

definition: A fuse or long wick used to carry a flame, in an obsolete sense.

originalSense.definition: Synonym of fuse, a long wick used to transfer flame to an explosive device.

definition: A competitive sporting event between players or teams.

originalSense.definition: A competitive sporting event such as a boxing meet, a baseball game, or a cricket match.

definition: Someone who equals or exceeds another person in a relevant ability.

originalSense.definition: Someone with a measure of an attribute equaling or exceeding the object of comparison.

distinctionTask.prompt: “He is no match for her at chess” means he _____ compete successfully against her.
distinctionTask.explanation: Be no match for indicates insufficient competitive ability in the stated context.

definition: A correspondence, equivalent or counterpart.

originalSense.definition: Equivalence; a state of correspondence; a counterpart.

definition: An agreement or compact, in an older recorded use.

definition: A marriage or marital union.

originalSense.definition: A candidate for matrimony; one to be gained in marriage.

definition: A trader or investor who sells in anticipation of falling prices.

definition: A state police officer, in US CB-radio slang.

originalSense.example: It’s everywhere. At this moment, as you sit quietly reading this book, you are awash in it. At work, it’s emanating from your electronic devices; step outside for lunch, and the sun bathes you in it. You may receive an extra dose of it when you visit your doctor, pass through security at the airport, or drive through city streets, but minuscule amounts of it are with you always. You cannot see, hear, smell, or feel it, but there is never a single second when it is not flying through your body. Too much of it will kill you, but without it you wouldn’t live a year. “Invisible light” seems like a contradiction. Like Simon and Garfunkel’s “The Sound of Silence,” it’s an oxymoron. We think of light, by definition, as something seen, something that enables our seeing, illuminating the darkness. Unlike dogs, who sniff in order to “get” what an object is, we depend on vision above all our other senses. We rely on light to tell us about our surroundings. But just as there are frequencies of sound audible to other animals that we cannot hear, there is a whole world of light outside our range of vision, a world that is humming with activity. Though we rarely think about this invisible world, our way of life depends on it. It’s because of invisible light that you can do things such as send a text message, use GPS to find your way to a friend’s house, listen to the radio, or microwave a frozen pizza. Invisible light shows us things we would never otherwise see, including our own skeletons and brains and the history of our universe. I was reminded of just how much we rely on invisible light, and how mysterious it remains to us, during a visit from my sister and her family. It was a lazy summer afternoon, and we were sprawled across a few couches sharing a bowl of popcorn. My niece, her shoulders crimson after a day outdoors, was chatting on her cell phone, holding up a promising finger to her mother, who was scolding her for not using sunscreen. My brother-in-law, meanwhile, was asking my opinion on an article he’d read proposing that Wi-Fi be banned in schools because of its dangers. We were all depending on invisible light (for the microwave popcorn, the cell-phone service) while being concerned that it might harm us (sunburn, mysterious Wi-Fi health threats) and confused about what to do to protect ourselves. We need it, and it surrounds us, yet we remain uneasy about living with invisible light, partly because we fear what is unknown. After all, most of us don’t know much about “all the light we cannot see.” This book aims to change that. My hope is to expose the hidden side of the spectrum, to make the invisible (at least temporarily) visible and vivid to you.

originalSense.example: She had light skin.

distinctionTask.prompt: In “light blue curtains”, light describes _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Light blue is a colour description.

definition: Of coffee, served with extra milk or cream.
example: In the recorded coffee use, light describes coffee with extra milk or cream.
distinctions: Light coffee here concerns added milk or cream. It does not by itself mean weak coffee, low caffeine or low calories.
usage: Coffee-order terminology; interpretation depends on local usage.

originalSense.definition: Served with extra milk or cream.
originalSense.example: Do you want your coffee light or black? -I like mine light.

definition: Having relatively little weight; not heavy.
example: This light suitcase is easy to carry.
distinctions: Light describes weight relative to the comparison. It does not tell us whether the object is pale in colour or lightly packed.

originalSense.definition: Having little or relatively little actual weight; not heavy; not cumbrous or unwieldy.
originalSense.example: a light load ; a lighter backpack after having removed the books ; light weapons

distinctionTask.prompt: A suitcase that is easy to carry because it weighs little is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Light is the weight adjective. Lit is a verb form or an adjective meaning illuminated.

definition: Having little mass for its volume; low in density.
example: For the same volume, cork is lighter than stone.

usage: Material-density sense; compare objects at the same volume.

originalSense.definition: Having little weight as compared with bulk; of little density or specific gravity.
originalSense.example: feathers and cork are light ; oil is lighter than water

distinctionTask.prompt: At equal volume, the material with less mass has _____ density.
distinctionTask.explanation: Density is mass per volume; compare the same volume. A large amount can still have a large total mass.

definition: Below the proper or standard weight.
example: In the older coinage use, a light coin weighs less than the required standard.
distinctions: This sense concerns a shortfall against a specified weight, not simply a conveniently portable object.

originalSense.definition: Of short or insufficient weight; weighing less than the legal, standard, or proper amount; clipped or diminished.
originalSense.example: to issue light coin

definition: Free of a load or burden, or carrying relatively little.
example: The ship sailed light after unloading its cargo.
distinctions: This broad meaning has separate technical uses for unloaded ships, locomotives, lightly built equipment and low-viscosity liquids.
usage: Adjective; source umbrella meaning with more specific children.

originalSense.definition: Lacking that which burdens or makes heavy.

definition: Of bread or cake, airy and well risen rather than dense or soggy.
example: The beaten eggs helped make the sponge cake light.
distinctions: A light cake texture does not automatically mean low calories. The texture and nutritional senses are separate.

originalSense.definition: Not heavy or soggy; spongy; well raised.
originalSense.example: a light bread ; sponge cake is a light cake

distinctionTask.prompt: A light sponge cake has an airy texture; this alone _____ low calories.
distinctionTask.explanation: Texture and nutritional composition are different properties.

definition: Containing relatively little of a stated ingredient or component, such as fat or alcohol.
example: The label describes this beer as light because it contains less alcohol than the standard version.
distinctions: Light needs a stated comparison or product context. It does not universally mean low in every ingredient, alcohol-free or lower in total calories.
usage: Product or food description; standards vary by product and jurisdiction.

originalSense.definition: Low in fat, calories, alcohol, salt, etc.
originalSense.example: This light beer still gets you drunk if you have enough of it.

distinctionTask.prompt: A drink described as light in alcohol is _____ alcohol-free.
distinctionTask.explanation: Light can state a reduction or comparison, not zero alcohol.

definition: Small in amount, degree or intensity.

distinctions: Light rain concerns amount or intensity. A light touch instead emphasises small applied force.

originalSense.definition: Slight, not forceful or intense; small in amount or intensity.
originalSense.example: a light drizzle//a light rain was falling//a light snow set in

definition: Gentle or using little force.
example: Use a light touch when cleaning the delicate surface.
distinctions: A light touch concerns applied force. It does not mean the hand or cleaning tool has little mass.

originalSense.definition: Gentle; having little force or momentum.
originalSense.example: This artist clearly had a light, flowing touch.

distinctionTask.prompt: A light touch uses relatively little _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The stated touch sense concerns force, not brightness.

definition: Easy or relatively undemanding to do or endure.
example: She returned to light duties while rebuilding her strength.
distinctions: Light duties are less demanding in context. Light work does not necessarily mean work involving a small physical object.

originalSense.definition: Easy to endure or perform.
originalSense.example: light duties around the house

definition: Of little importance or seriousness.
example: It began as a light remark about the weather.
distinctions: A light remark is not very serious. A remark can still have an effect despite being intended lightly.

originalSense.definition: Unimportant, trivial, having little value or significance.
originalSense.example: I made some light comment, and we moved on.

definition: Unchaste or sexually wanton, in an obsolete judgmental use.
example: In the obsolete moral judgment, light can describe someone as unchaste.
distinctions: This historical description is separate from cheerful or light-hearted. It should not be treated as a neutral modern description of a person.

originalSense.definition: Unchaste, wanton.
originalSense.example: Long after lay he musing at her mood, / Much grieu'd to thinke that gentle Dame so light, / For whose defence he was to shed his blood.

definition: Unencumbered and able or ready to move quickly.
example: In the older movement use, light describes being unburdened and ready to move.
distinctions: This older description links freedom from burdens with movement. It differs from light meaning pale in colour.

originalSense.definition: Not encumbered; unembarrassed; clear of impediments; hence, active; nimble; swift.
originalSense.example: Unmarried men are best friends, best masters […] but not always best subjects, for they are light to run away.

definition: Quick and nimble in movement.
example: The dancer remained light on her feet.
distinctions: Light on one’s feet means nimble. It is not a measurement of someone’s body mass.

originalSense.definition: Fast; nimble.

distinctionTask.prompt: A dancer who is light on her feet is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This fixed expression concerns movement, not a body-mass measurement.

definition: Unsteady or easily influenced by trivial things, in a dated use.

distinctions: This judgment differs from light meaning cheerful or undemanding. Modern descriptions should state the intended quality directly.

originalSense.definition: Easily influenced by trifling considerations; unsteady; unsettled; volatile.
originalSense.example: a light, vain person; a light mind

definition: Playful or lacking solemnity; intended to amuse rather than be serious.
example: The programme ended with a reading of light verse.
distinctions: Light verse is playful or humorous. The phrase does not describe the physical weight of a poem or its page.

originalSense.definition: Indulging in, or inclined to, levity; lacking dignity or solemnity; frivolous; airy.
originalSense.example: Ogden Nash was a writer of light verse.

definition: Giddy or mentally unsettled, in an older use.
example: In the older phrase light of brain, light can describe giddiness or an unsettled mental state.
distinctions: This historical wording differs from modern light-headed, although the meanings can overlap. The expression alone is not a medical diagnosis.

originalSense.definition: Not quite sound or normal; somewhat impaired or deranged; dizzy; giddy.
originalSense.example: Are his wits safe? Is he not light of brain?

definition: Of sleep or a sleeper, easily disturbed or awakened.
example: I am a light sleeper and wake when a door closes.
distinctions: A light sleeper wakes easily. The phrase does not mean a person who weighs little.

originalSense.definition: Easily interrupted by stimulation.
originalSense.example: light sleep; light anesthesia

distinctionTask.prompt: A light sleeper _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This sleep adjective concerns sensitivity to disturbance.

definition: Cheerful and free from worry.
example: Her heart felt light after the good news.
distinctions: A light heart describes mood, not the physical mass of the organ. Light-hearted is a related adjective.

originalSense.definition: Cheerful.
originalSense.example:
I wish you a good day, and you'll find a way
 To make your spirits light & gay

definition: With little luggage or equipment.
example: We prefer to travel light on short trips.
distinctions: Travel light uses light as an adverb. It does not mean travel only in daylight.

originalSense.definition: Carrying little.
originalSense.example: I prefer to travel light.

distinctionTask.explanation: Light is an adverb describing how much equipment or luggage is carried.

definition: In curling, a stone delivered with too little force to reach the intended position.
example: In the curling noun sense, a light is a stone that falls short because of insufficient delivery weight.
distinctions: Curling weight concerns the force or speed of a delivery, not a reduction in the stone’s physical mass.

originalSense.definition: A stone that is not thrown hard enough.

definition: A recorded cross-reference to lights meaning lungs.

originalSense.definition: See lights (“lungs”).

definition: A low-alcohol lager, in an Australian noun use.

distinctions: The noun identifies a kind of lager in this usage. It does not mean any pale-coloured drink or necessarily an alcohol-free one.

originalSense.definition: A low-alcohol lager.

definition: A member of light cavalry, in a historical use.

distinctions: This person noun is separate from a leading light in a profession and from a lamp.

originalSense.definition: A member of the light cavalry.

definition: To remove cargo or material from a ship so that it becomes lighter.
example: In the recorded nautical verb, light a ship means reduce its load by unloading or discarding material.
distinctions: This nautical verb concerns removing weight. It is separate from lighting a fire aboard a ship.
usage: Nautical reading verb; regular lighted is recorded in this etymological group.

originalSense.definition: To unload a ship, or to jettison material to make it lighter.

definition: To ease a burden or remove something burdensome, in an older verb use.
example: In the source’s older removal use, light means take off a burdensome item.
distinctions: This historical verb differs from illuminate and from the modern adjective light meaning not heavy.

originalSense.definition: To lighten; to ease of a burden; to take off.
originalSense.example: His mailèd habergeon she did undight, / And from his head his heavy burgonet did light.

definition: To leave or depart, in a recorded extended use.

originalSense.definition: To leave; to depart.

definition: With on or upon, to find or encounter something by chance.

usage: Usually light on or upon; past and participle lit or lighted.

originalSense.definition: To find by chance.
originalSense.example: I lit upon a rare book in a second-hand bookseller's.

distinctionTask.prompt: “I lit upon a useful article” means I _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: Light upon means happen to encounter something.

definition: Of eyes or a glance, to come to rest on and notice something.
example: Her eyes lit upon the envelope on the desk.
distinctions: Here the gaze comes to rest on something. Eyes light up is a different expression that can describe excitement.
usage: Literary verb; usually light on or upon.

originalSense.definition: To stop upon (of eyes or a glance); to notice.
originalSense.example: "Sacredam!" he cried, when his eyes lit upon Buck. "Dat one dam bully dog! Eh? How moch?"

definition: To alight or land, in an archaic verb use.
example: In an older narrative, a bird that lit on a branch landed there.
distinctions: This landing sense differs from finding a book by chance and from starting a flame. Modern general prose normally uses land or alight.
usage: Archaic; past and participle lit or lighted.

originalSense.definition: To alight; to land or come down.
originalSense.example: She fell out of the window but luckily lit on her feet.

definition: Light: an honorific capitalised form referring to a contextually understood revered figure.

definition: Light: a surname.

definition: Source grouping: places named Light.

originalSense.definition: A place name:

originalSense.definition: The 24th sura (chapter) of the Qur'an.

definition: A bulb or similar light-emitting device, whether switched on or off.

originalSense.definition: A lightbulb or similar light-emitting device, regardless of whether it is lit.

definition: A traffic signal, or by extension the junction it controls.

usage: Countable noun; often plural lights for a set of signals.

originalSense.definition: A traffic light, or an intersection controlled by traffic lights.

definition: A cigarette lighter, in a slang use.

originalSense.definition: A cigarette lighter.

definition: Free of a burden or impediment.

distinctions: This sense concerns freedom from a burden. It need not mean low material density.

originalSense.definition: Free from burden or impediment; unencumbered.

definition: Built for relatively small loads or agile movement.

originalSense.definition: Lightly built; typically designed for speed or small loads.

definition: Equipped with comparatively light weapons or armour.

distinctions: The relevant classification depends on the period and force. Light does not simply mean a small number of people.

originalSense.definition: Not heavily armed; armed with light weapons.

definition: Of a ship, without cargo and riding relatively high in the water.

originalSense.definition: Riding high because of no cargo; by extension, pertaining to a ship which is light.

definition: Of a locomotive or group of locomotives, running without a train, or with only a caboose.

originalSense.definition: Without any piece of equipment attached or attached only to a caboose.

definition: Of a liquid, relatively low in viscosity.
example: The mechanism calls for a light oil that flows readily.

originalSense.definition: With low viscosity.

both its density and its total mass

definition: Light: an unincorporated community in Greene County, Arkansas.

distinctions: This is the Arkansas community, distinct from the community named Light in Missouri.

originalSense.definition: An unincorporated community in Greene County, Arkansas, the United States.

definition: Light: an unincorporated community in Maries County, Missouri.
example: The source records Light in Maries County, Missouri, as an unincorporated community.
distinctions: This is the Missouri community, distinct from the community named Light in Arkansas.

originalSense.definition: An unincorporated community in Maries County, Missouri, the United States.

originalSense.definition: Light Regional Council, a local government area north of Adelaide, South Australia, named after the River Light.

definition: Light: the River Light in South Australia’s Mid North region.

originalSense.definition: The River Light, a river in the Mid North region, South Australia, named after William Light.

definition: On or relating to the side opposite left, relative to a person or a stated viewpoint.

definition: Turning clockwise in the stated view or changing direction to the right.

originalSense.definition: Clockwise, particularly when describing a change in direction or orientation.

wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

definition: Correct, just or in accordance with what is true or reasonable.

definition: Suitable for a particular purpose or situation.

definition: In a normal or satisfactory physical or mental state.

definition: Of an angle, measuring ninety degrees: one quarter of a full turn.

wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

distinctionTask.prompt: A right angle measures _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A right angle is a quarter of a full 360° turn. A straight angle is 180°.

definition: Of certain geometric figures, having the specified perpendicular relationship between their parts.
example: In a right prism, the lateral edges are perpendicular to the bases.

wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

distinctionTask.prompt: In a right prism, the lateral edges are _____ the bases.

definition: Of a river bank, on the right of a person facing downstream.

definition: Intended to face outward or be seen, especially of fabric.

distinctionTask.explanation: Right side of fabric names a surface, not a compass direction.

definition: Relating to the political right, often associated with conservative positions in context.

originalSense.definition: Pertaining to the political right; conservative.

definition: All right or not needing assistance, in an Australian use.

wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

definition: Favourable or fortunate, in a dated use.

originalSense.definition: Most favourable or convenient; fortunate.

definition: Straight rather than bent, in an archaic use.

originalSense.definition: Straight, not bent.
originalSense.example: a right line
wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

definition: Of or relating to the right whale group.
example: The article describes North Atlantic right whales.

originalSense.definition: Of or relating to the right whale.

wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

definition: On the right side of the stated viewpoint.
example: The image is aligned right rather than centred.
