originalSense.definition: On the right side.
wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

definition: Towards the right-hand side.
example: Turn right at the next junction.
distinctions: The direction is relative to the person or route. It does not always mean travel east.

originalSense.definition: Towards the right side.
wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

definition: Exactly or precisely at the stated point or place.

definition: Immediately or directly, without delay or intervening distance.

definition: Very or extremely, in regional or informal intensifying use.

originalSense.definition: Very, extremely, quite.

definition: Actually, truly or in accordance with fact, in a recorded adverbial use.

originalSense.definition: According to fact or truth; actually; truly; really.

definition: In a correct or proper way.

originalSense.definition: In a correct or proper manner.

wordFamily: Right Arm of the Free World

definition: Used to express agreement or confirm that something is correct.

originalSense.definition: A visual representation of a classification of teams or individuals based on their success over a predetermined period.

distinctionTask.prompt: A league table lists _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The stated sports meaning is a ranking or standings list, not merely a fixture schedule.

definition: A flat elevated region of land; a tableland.
example: In the landscape sense, a table is a flat elevated area of land.
distinctions: This landform sense concerns relief. It is separate from a table of measurements about the land.

originalSense.definition: A tableland; a flat, elevated region.

definition: A horizontal layer of rock.
example: In the recorded geological use, a table is a horizontal rock stratum.
distinctions: This source sense is a rock layer. Water table is a different compound and should not be substituted for it.

originalSense.definition: A horizontal stratum of rock.

definition: A flat plate or length of bone.
example: In anatomical terminology, table can refer to a flat plate of bone.
distinctions: This shape term is separate from a diagram or data table used in an anatomy textbook.

originalSense.definition: A flat length of bone.

definition: The inner or outer compact-bone plate of a cranial bone.
example: In the skull, the inner and outer tables are the two compact-bone plates with diploë between them.
distinctions: Inner and outer refer to anatomical position. They are not the top and bottom rows of a printed table.

originalSense.definition: The inner and outer plates that make up the cranium bones; the outer table and the inner table (vitreous table).

definition: A wide flat obstacle for a horse to jump over.
example: The course included a broad table obstacle after the bend.
distinctions: This equestrian table names an obstacle. It is not a data table or necessarily ordinary household furniture.

originalSense.definition: A wide, flat obstacle for a horse to jump over.

definition: A horizontal band of moulding or decoration around a building; a stringcourse.
example: In the source’s architectural use, a table can mean a horizontal decorative band.
distinctions: This architectural band is separate from a piece of furniture placed inside the building.

originalSense.definition: A stringcourse; a band of horizontal molding or other decoration around a building.

definition: The front or top plate of a stringed instrument, especially one of the violin family.
example: The maker examined the violin’s table for cracks.
distinctions: The table is the instrument’s front plate or soundboard. In a violin, string vibration is transmitted through the bridge rather than by strings lying against the plate.

originalSense.definition: The top of a stringed instrument, particularly a member of the violin family: the side of the instrument against which the strings vibrate.

definition: The flat topmost facet of a cut diamond.
example: The gemologist inspected the diamond’s table.
distinctions: The table is one facet of the cut stone. The term alone does not state the stone’s value or quality.

originalSense.definition: The flat topmost facet of a cut diamond.

definition: A flat gravestone raised on pillars.
example: In the recorded monument sense, a table is a flat gravestone supported by pillars.
distinctions: This monument use is separate from ordinary dining furniture, despite the similarity of the supported slab.

originalSense.definition: A flat gravestone supported on pillars.

definition: The region between the heart line and head line, in palmistry terminology.
example: In palmistry vocabulary, table is a name for the region between the heart and head lines.
distinctions: This is a conventional name within palmistry. It is not an anatomical diagnosis or evidence of future events.

originalSense.definition: The quadrangle, a space between the heart line and head line.

definition: A writing tablet, in an obsolete biblical use.
example: In older biblical language, tables can mean writing tablets.
distinctions: This older table is a tablet for writing. It is separate from a modern electronic tablet or a table of data.

originalSense.definition: A writing tablet.

definition: A flat support for a slab on which printing ink is rolled.
example: In traditional printing, a table can support the slab used for rolling ink.
distinctions: The support and ink slab belong to the printing process. They are separate from a table arranging print-job statistics.

originalSense.definition: A flat surface that supports the slab on which ink is rolled to manipulate its consistency.

definition: An inspection or examination.
example: The technician carried out a safety check before the machine was used.
distinctions: A check examines something; it does not guarantee that every possible fault has been detected.

originalSense.definition: An inspection or examination.
originalSense.example: I don't know if she will be there, but it's worth a check.

definition: A restraint, limit or control.
example: Independent auditors provide a check on the use of public funds.
distinctions: A check on power restrains it. A check of a report examines it; the preposition and context help distinguish these uses.

originalSense.definition: A control; a limit or stop.
originalSense.example: checks and balances

distinctionTask.prompt: “A check on executive power” provides a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The preposition on and the power context select the restraint sense.

definition: A chess position in which a king is attacked by an opposing piece.
example: The rook placed the black king in check.
distinctions: Check requires a legal response that removes the attack. It is not checkmate if such a response is available; the king is not captured.

originalSense.definition: A situation in which the king is directly threatened by an opposing piece.

distinctionTask.prompt: A king in check _____ already be checkmated.
distinctionTask.explanation: Checkmate additionally requires that no legal move can remove the check.

definition: A mark, commonly ✓, used as an indicator.
example: Put a check beside each task you have completed.
distinctions: US check corresponds to UK tick in this marking use. A mark can indicate selection or completion according to the form; it is not automatically a judgement of correctness.

originalSense.definition: A mark (especially a checkmark: ✓) used as an indicator.
originalSense.example: Norton had made a neat, lawyerly check beside each of the items he and Billy had picked up—half a dozen or so, including the milk and a six-pack of Coke.

definition: A written order instructing a bank to pay a specified sum.
example: She wrote a check to pay the membership fee.
distinctions: US check is generally cheque in British banking usage. A restaurant check is the bill requesting payment, rather than the bank payment instrument itself.

originalSense.definition: An order to a bank to pay money to a named person or entity.
originalSense.example: I was not carrying cash, so I wrote a check for the amount.

distinctionTask.prompt: In ordinary British banking spelling, a US check is a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Cheque is the British payment-instrument spelling; Czech refers to a nationality or language.

definition: A bill, especially for a restaurant meal.
example: Could we have the check, please?
distinctions: This chiefly US restaurant noun corresponds to bill in usual British usage. Paying a check does not imply payment by a bank cheque.

originalSense.definition: A bill, particularly in a restaurant.
originalSense.example: I summoned the waiter, paid the check, and hurried to leave.

distinctionTask.prompt: In “Could we have the check, please?”, check means the restaurant _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The US restaurant use requests the bill, regardless of the eventual payment method.

definition: A move that interrupts an opposing player’s participation in play.
example: In a sports report, a check is an action used to impede or separate an opponent from the play.
distinctions: The permitted form of checking depends on the sport, competition and situation. The word itself does not establish that contact was legal.

originalSense.definition: A maneuver performed by a player to take another player out of the play.
originalSense.example: The hockey player gave a good hard check to obtain the puck.

definition: A token used in place of cash or to represent an entitlement.
example: In the source’s token sense, checks may be used in gaming machines or older ration and property systems.
distinctions: A token check is not a bank payment order. Its redemption or accounting function depends on the particular system.

originalSense.definition: A token used instead of cash in various contexts, including sign-out of company property or collection of rations (dated), in gaming machines, or in gambling generally.
originalSense.example: a brass check

definition: A crack or separation in timber, often extending along the grain.
example: In timber inspection, a drying check is a separation in the wood, rather than the act of inspecting it.
distinctions: The source describes a lengthwise separation through growth rings. Do not confuse this defect noun with a quality-control check or assume that every crack has the same cause.

originalSense.definition: A lengthwise separation through the growth rings in wood.

definition: A token, ticket or identifying mark used to prevent mistakes or identify an item.
example: Keep the coat check so that you can collect your jacket.
distinctions: A claim token identifies the stored item. It is separate from the fee charged for storage and from a bank cheque.

originalSense.definition: A mark, certificate, or token by which errors may be prevented, or a thing or person may be identified.
originalSense.example: a check given for baggage

definition: A hawk’s abandonment of its intended quarry to pursue other birds.
example: In falconry terminology, a check is a departure from the intended quarry to chase other birds.
distinctions: This specialised hunting noun describes a change of pursuit; it does not mean inspecting the bird.

originalSense.definition: The forsaking by a hawk of its proper game to follow other birds.

definition: A small crack or narrow opening.
example: In a description of a damaged surface, checks are small cracks or chinks.
distinctions: This physical crack sense is separate from the mark ✓ and from a document inspection.

originalSense.definition: A small chink or crack.

definition: A possible item location in a video-game randomizer.
example: In a randomizer guide, a check is a location that can be visited to discover or collect an item.
distinctions: A location is a check even before its particular item is known. Game rules determine its accessibility and contents.

originalSense.definition: In randomizers, a possible place where an item may be.

definition: To inspect or examine something.
example: Check the date on the form before you submit it.
distinctions: Check whether asks if something is the case. Check for looks for a feature or problem; neither construction by itself proves that a problem exists.

originalSense.definition: To inspect; to examine.
originalSense.example: Check the oil in your car once a month.

distinctionTask.prompt: To look for errors, check _____ them.
distinctionTask.explanation: Check for errors examines whether they are present. Check off marks listed items as dealt with.

definition: To verify a text’s accuracy and make necessary corrections.
example: The editor checked the translation against the original text.
distinctions: Checking accuracy is broader than looking only for typing errors. Proofreading and copyediting can have different scopes; the verb check alone does not specify an exact level of editing.

originalSense.definition: To verify the accuracy of a text or translation, usually making some corrections (proofread) or many (copyedit).

definition: To mark chosen, completed or verified items on a list.
example: She checked off each item after packing it.
distinctions: Marking an item follows the form’s instructions. Check off usually means mark as dealt with; UK usage commonly uses tick off.
usage: Transitive; US check, often with off.

originalSense.definition: To mark items on a list (with a checkmark or by crossing them out) that have been chosen for keeping or removal or that have been dealt with (for example, completed or verified as correct or satisfactory).
originalSense.example: Check the items on the list that interest you.

distinctionTask.prompt: To mark completed list items, check them _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Check off marks items as dealt with; check against compares them with a reference.

definition: To restrain, limit or stop something.
example: The new measures helped check the spread of the disease.
distinctions: Checking the spread aims to curb it. Checking for the disease means looking for it; the two actions are different.

originalSense.definition: To control, limit, or halt.
originalSense.example: Check your enthusiasm during a negotiation.

distinctionTask.prompt: Measures that check the spread of a disease aim to _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: This object-taking restraint sense differs from checking for the disease.

definition: To rebuke or reprimand someone.
example: In an informal rebuke, to check someone is to challenge or reprimand their behaviour.
distinctions: This informal use concerns rebuke, not a medical or identity examination. Tone and context determine how forceful it is.

originalSense.definition: To scold or rebuke someone.

definition: To verify something by comparing it with a source or reference.
example: Check the figures against the original receipts.
distinctions: Check against identifies the comparison reference. Agreement with an unreliable source does not establish independent accuracy.

originalSense.definition: To verify or compare with a source of information.
originalSense.example: Check your data against known values.

distinctionTask.prompt: Verify these figures _____ the original receipts.
distinctionTask.explanation: Checking against identifies the reference used for comparison.

definition: To leave an item in someone’s safekeeping.
example: We checked our coats at the cloakroom.
distinctions: Checking a coat leaves it in storage. Checking the coat for damage instead means inspecting it.

originalSense.definition: To leave in safekeeping.
originalSense.example: Check your hat and coat at the door.

distinctionTask.prompt: “We checked our coats at the cloakroom” means we _____ them.
distinctionTask.explanation: The cloakroom context selects storage rather than inspection.

definition: To hand baggage or goods to an operator for transport.
example: They checked their large suitcase at the airport counter.
distinctions: Checked baggage is handed to the carrier, rather than kept as cabin baggage. Acceptance does not by itself specify fees, connections or where it must be collected.

originalSense.definition: To leave with a shipping agent for shipping.
originalSense.example: Check your bags at the ticket counter before the flight.

distinctionTask.prompt: Checked baggage is normally _____ the carrier for transport.
options: kept beside the passenger throughout the flight
distinctionTask.explanation: The transport sense distinguishes checked baggage from cabin baggage.

definition: In street basketball, to exchange the ball with an opponent to begin or resume play.
example: In the recorded street-basketball use, checking the ball means passing it to an opponent and receiving it back before play starts.
distinctions: The precise restart location and procedure depend on the local rules. This is different from checking an opponent with physical contact.

originalSense.definition: To pass or bounce the ball to an opponent from behind the three-point line and have the opponent pass or bounce it back to start play.
originalSense.example: He checked the ball and then proceeded to perform a perfect layup.

definition: To impede an opponent using the stick or body during play.
example: In hockey commentary, a player checks an opponent to disrupt their play or contest possession.
distinctions: Whether a particular check is permitted depends on the applicable rules and circumstances; the verb does not mean inspect the player.

originalSense.definition: To disrupt another player with the stick or body to obtain possession of the ball or puck.
originalSense.example: The hockey player checked the defenceman to obtain the puck.

definition: To decline an additional bet while remaining in a poker hand when no bet must be matched.
example: With no outstanding bet to call, she checked.
distinctions: A player can check only when there is no outstanding or unmatched bet to call in that betting round. Calling matches a bet; folding gives up the hand. A previous contribution, such as a blind, does not make every later check a new bet.

originalSense.definition: To announce that one is remaining in a hand without betting.
originalSense.example: Tom didn't think he could win, so he checked.

distinctionTask.prompt: A poker player can check when there is _____ bet to match in the current round.
distinctionTask.explanation: Checking adds no bet on that action; calling matches an outstanding bet.

definition: To make a chess move that attacks the opposing king.
example: Moving the rook to the open file checked the black king.
distinctions: Checking is different from checkmating: a checked king may have a legal escape, capture or interposition. The precise legal responses depend on the position.

originalSense.definition: To make a move which puts an adversary's king in check; to put in check.
originalSense.example: After I checked my opponent with a pawn, he resigned immediately.

definition: To chide or reprove someone.
example: In the source’s rebuke sense, to check someone is to reprove them.
distinctions: This recorded reprimand use overlaps the informal rebuke sense. It is distinct from inspecting someone’s documents or health.

originalSense.definition: To chide, rebuke, or reprove.
originalSense.example: The good king, his master, will check him for it.

definition: To slacken or ease a rope or brace.
example: In nautical terminology, to check a brace is to ease its tension.
distinctions: The nautical verb concerns controlled easing, not checking a written measurement for accuracy.

originalSense.definition: To slack or ease off, as a brace which is too stiffly extended.

definition: To develop small cracks or separations.
example: The old varnish had begun to check.
distinctions: Here the material itself cracks. Check the varnish means inspect it, while heat checked the varnish uses check as a cause-of-cracking verb.

originalSense.definition: To crack or gape open, as wood in drying; or to crack in small checks, as varnish, paint, etc.

distinctionTask.prompt: “The varnish has checked” means the varnish has _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The material is the subject of this intransitive cracking sense.

definition: To cause small cracks or separations in a material.
example: In the source’s causative use, drying conditions can check timber by causing separations.
distinctions: This object-taking verb causes a defect. It is separate from checking timber to see whether a defect exists.

originalSense.definition: To make checks or chinks in; to cause to crack.
originalSense.example: The sun checks timber.

definition: To stop or pause, especially in the construction check at.
example: In an older narrative, a person who checks at a threshold pauses there.
distinctions: This recorded intransitive pause use differs from check in at a hotel and from checking a document.
usage: Older or literary construction; often with at.

originalSense.definition: To make a stop; to pause.
originalSense.example: The mind, once jaded by an attempt above its power, either is disabled for the future, or else checks at any vigorous undertaking ever after.

definition: To clash with or interfere with something, in an obsolete use.
example: In the obsolete sense, things that check interfere or clash with each other.
distinctions: This is a reading explanation for an obsolete verb sense, not a recommended modern substitute for interfere.

originalSense.definition: To clash or interfere.
originalSense.example: For if it [Loue] checke once with businesse, it troubleth Mens fortunes.

definition: To serve as a curb or restraint.
example: In the recorded restraint use, something that checks acts as a limit on further action.
distinctions: The subject itself provides restraint. An object-taking construction such as check spending directly names what is restrained.

originalSense.definition: To act as a curb or restraint.
originalSense.example: It [his presence] checks too strong upon me.

definition: Of a hawk, to leave the intended quarry and pursue other birds.
example: In falconry, a hawk that checks changes from the intended quarry to other birds.
distinctions: The verb describes the bird’s change of pursuit, rather than someone inspecting the bird.

originalSense.definition: To turn, when in pursuit of proper game, and fly after other birds.
originalSense.example:
And like the haggard, check at every feather
 That comes before his eye.

definition: To prove consistent or credible after verification.
example: The totals check when we add the individual figures.
distinctions: This means the comparison is consistent. Agreement of totals does not by itself verify every underlying record. Check out is a common related construction.

originalSense.definition: To check out, make sense or prove to be the case after verification or interrogation.
originalSense.example: Didn’t remember that at all. But it sure checks!

definition: To visit and collect an item at a possible location in a randomizer game.
example: In a randomizer guide, checking a location means visiting it to see or collect the item there.
distinctions: This game-specific verb concerns an item location, not a spelling check. Availability and item contents depend on the game.

originalSense.definition: In randomizers, to go to and collect a possible place where an item may be.

definition: An acknowledgment that a requirement or item has been satisfied.
example: Tickets? Check. Passports? Check. We are ready to leave.
distinctions: This interjection confirms an item in a spoken checklist. It does not refer to a bank instrument or necessarily to a chess position.

originalSense.definition: An expression showing that a requirement has been satisfied.
originalSense.example: Keys? Check. Batteries? Check. We are all ready to go!

distinctionTask.prompt: “Tickets? Check.” _____ that the tickets requirement is satisfied.
distinctionTask.explanation: The checklist interjection gives an affirmative completion acknowledgment.

definition: A request for the bill, especially in a restaurant.
example: As a restaurant request in US usage, Check, please asks for the bill.
distinctions: This short request may sound abrupt without appropriate politeness and context. A full question such as Could we have the check, please? is often more suitable.

originalSense.definition: An expression that indicates that the speaker wishes to pay the bill (e.g. in a restaurant).

definition: A pattern formed by a grid of squares in alternating colours.
example: The tablecloth has red and white checks.
distinctions: Checks form a square grid. Stripes run in bands, and a checkmark is the separate symbol ✓.

originalSense.definition: A pattern made up of a grid of squares of alternating colors; a checkered pattern.
originalSense.example: The tablecloth had red and white checks.

distinctionTask.prompt: A textile check pattern uses a grid of _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The pattern meaning is different from a checkmark or stripes.

definition: Fabric woven with a checked pattern.
example: She chose a wool check for the jacket.
distinctions: Here check names the fabric rather than an individual square or a tick mark. The weave and fibre are separate properties.

originalSense.definition: Any fabric woven with such a pattern.

definition: To decorate or mark something with a checked pattern.
example: In the pattern-making sense, to check a surface is to mark it with alternating squares.
distinctions: This design verb is distinct from inspecting the surface and from putting one checkmark beside it.

originalSense.definition: To mark with a check pattern.

definition: A rare recorded heraldic form of chequy, possibly a printing error.
example: The source records check as a rare heraldic form corresponding to chequy and explicitly notes that it may be a printing error.
distinctions: Do not treat this uncertain rare form as a normal modern adjective. Chequy is the usual heraldic term for a field divided into alternating squares.
usage: Heraldry; rare, possibly only a printing error.

originalSense.definition: Checky, i.e. chequy.
originalSense.example: CHECKY, […] Checky, according to Colombiere, is one of the most noble and ancient figures […] Checky is always composed of metal, and colour. […] So that if that be or, and the next gules, the house or family is said to bear check, or, and gules. When the whole shield is not chequered , but only the chief, a bend, cross, or the like, the number of ranges should be expressed.

definition: A regional alternative spelling of chick meaning a window blind or door screen.
example: In the recorded South Asian usage, check can denote the blind or screen otherwise spelled chick.
distinctions: This is a regionally recorded screen noun, not the young-bird meaning of chick or an inspection.
usage: India and Pakistan; source-bound regional reading.

originalSense.definition: Alternative form of chick (“window blind or door screen”).

definition: Check, a surname.
example: The source records Check as a family name.
distinctions: The capitalised surname does not describe a bank payment, an inspection or a nationality. Czech is a separate word.

originalSense.definition: A surname.

definition: A small dot or mark.
example: Each blue point on the map marks a survey site.
distinctions: A drawn point is a visible mark. A mathematical point instead models a position with no size; the visible mark represents it.

originalSense.definition: A small dot or mark.
originalSense.example: The stars showed as tiny points of yellow light.

definition: An individual detail, feature or small division of a larger whole.
example: The proposal contains several points that need clarification.
distinctions: This broad detail sense has more specific uses for topics, main ideas, purposes, scores and units. Select the meaning appropriate to the context.
usage: Countable umbrella noun; specific uses are listed separately.

originalSense.definition: A small discrete division or individual feature of something.
originalSense.example: The Congress debated the finer points of the bill.

definition: A sharp or projecting end of something.
example: The point of the needle was bent.
distinctions: A point can be a physical tip. It is not necessarily the main idea of a discussion or a dimensionless mathematical position.

originalSense.definition: A sharp extremity.
originalSense.example: Cut the skin with the point of the knife.

distinctionTask.prompt: The point of a needle is its _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The tool context selects the physical extremity.

definition: The act or gesture of pointing.
example: The source groups several pointing actions here, including a finger gesture, a dancer’s foot position and a hunting dog’s posture.
distinctions: This broad action noun has specialised child meanings. It is separate from a game score or the tip of a tool.
usage: Action noun; specialised uses listed separately.

originalSense.definition: The act of pointing.

definition: A short length of cord used in reefing a sail.
example: In nautical terminology, reef points are short pieces of line associated with reducing a sail’s exposed area.
distinctions: This source-bound cordage noun is different from a compass point. The word alone is not a rigging procedure.

originalSense.definition: A short piece of cordage used in reefing sails.

definition: A lace or cord historically used to fasten parts of clothing.
example: In historical clothing descriptions, points are laces used to tie garment parts together.
distinctions: Historical points fasten garments; needlepoint lace is a different textile sense.

originalSense.definition: A string or lace used to tie together certain garments.
originalSense.example: pick your purse while they tie your points, and cut your throat while they smooth your pillow

definition: Lace made with a needle.
example: In older textile descriptions, point can mean lace worked with a needle.
distinctions: This lace noun does not name a garment-fastening cord, even though both belong to textile vocabulary.

originalSense.definition: Lace worked by the needle.
originalSense.example: point de Venise; Brussels point

definition: A named player position in certain sports, or the player occupying it.
example: The source groups sport-specific positions called point, including cricket and older hockey or lacrosse terminology.
distinctions: The position depends on the sport and period. Do not infer one shared location or a unit of scoring from this umbrella definition.
usage: Sports noun; specific positions are listed separately.

originalSense.definition: In various sports, a position of a certain player, or, by extension, the player occupying that position.

definition: An acknowledgment meaning point taken or understood.
example: As a brief acknowledgment, Point can mean that the speaker has understood the argument.
distinctions: Understanding an argument does not necessarily mean agreeing with it. Point taken is the fuller, more familiar expression.

originalSense.definition: Point taken; understood; got it.

definition: To indicate something by extending a finger in its direction.
example: She pointed at the notice on the wall.
distinctions: The gesture directs attention. Point out a mistake is a related phrasal expression that need not involve a finger gesture.
usage: Intransitive verb; often with at or to.

originalSense.definition: To extend the index finger in the direction of something in order to show where it is or to draw attention to it.
originalSense.example: It's rude to point at other people.

distinctionTask.prompt: “She pointed at the notice” uses pointed _____.
options: with notice as its direct object
distinctionTask.explanation: The notice is introduced by at in this finger-gesture construction.

definition: To indicate a direction or draw attention to something.
example: The arrow points to the emergency exit.
distinctions: A sign or arrow can point without a person making a finger gesture. Point to evidence can also be figurative.

originalSense.definition: To draw attention to something or indicate a direction.
originalSense.example: The arrow of a compass points north

definition: To face in a particular direction.
example: The camera points towards the entrance.
distinctions: The verb describes orientation. Facing a direction does not by itself mean moving in that direction.

originalSense.definition: To face in a particular direction.

distinctionTask.prompt: A camera that points north _____ be moving north.
distinctionTask.explanation: Orientation and movement are different.

definition: To aim or direct something towards a target.
example: She pointed the torch at the label.
distinctions: In this transitive construction the object is what is aimed. The target follows at or towards.

originalSense.definition: To direct toward an object; to aim.
originalSense.example: to point a gun at a wolf, or a cannon at a fort

distinctionTask.prompt: In “Point the torch at the label”, the torch is _____.
options: the target being illuminated by another named object
distinctionTask.explanation: The direct object is what is directed; at introduces its target.

definition: To sharpen an object or give it a pointed end.
example: The craftworker pointed the wooden pegs before fitting them.
distinctions: This verb changes an object’s tip. It differs from pointing at an object to show where it is.

originalSense.definition: To give a point to; to sharpen; to cut, forge, grind, or file to an acute end.
originalSense.example: to point a dart, a pencil, or (figuratively) a moral

definition: To suggest that something is likely or supported by evidence.
example: The results point to a need for further investigation.
distinctions: Point to indicates support or likelihood in this context; it does not necessarily prove the conclusion or identify a physical direction.

originalSense.definition: To indicate a probability of something.
originalSense.example: Tens of thousands of Portuguese, Greek and Irish people have left their homelands this year, many heading for the southern hemisphere. Anecdotal evidence points to the same happening in Spain and Italy.

distinctionTask.prompt: Evidence that points to a cause _____ that cause on its own.
distinctionTask.explanation: The evidential construction indicates support, not automatic proof.

definition: To repair or renew mortar in masonry joints.
example: In masonry work, to point a wall is to repair or renew its mortar joints.
distinctions: The verb concerns masonry joints, rather than drawing an arrow on the wall. Materials and repair specifications depend on the structure.

originalSense.definition: To repair mortar.

definition: To fill and finish the joints of masonry with mortar or cement.
example: In construction terminology, pointing a wall finishes the joints between its bricks or stones.
distinctions: This more specific finishing sense overlaps mortar repair. It is not the same as sharpening the individual stones.

originalSense.definition: To fill up and finish the joints of (a wall), by introducing additional cement or mortar, and bringing it to a smooth surface.

definition: To cut or dress a surface with a pointed tool.
example: In stone-cutting terminology, pointing a surface works it with a pointed tool.
distinctions: This specialised cutting verb differs from placing a punctuation mark or indicating a direction.

originalSense.definition: To cut, as a surface, with a pointed tool.
originalSense.example: Damaged stone will be removed, and the new stone installed and pointed to ensure a comprehensive match to maintain the integrity of the structure.

definition: To guide or direct someone towards a course of action or destination.
example: The receptionist pointed us towards the registration desk.
collocations: point someone in the right direction
point a learner to a resource
distinctions: The person can be directed by explanation rather than a finger gesture. The expression does not promise that the destination or resource solves every problem.

originalSense.definition: To direct or encourage (someone) in a particular direction.
originalSense.example: If he asks for food, point him toward the refrigerator.

distinctionTask.prompt: To guide a visitor, point them _____ the registration desk.
distinctionTask.explanation: Point someone towards is the intended guidance construction.

definition: To insert a decimal point to separate the whole-number part from the fractional part.
example: In the recorded arithmetic use, pointing a number means inserting its decimal point.
distinctions: Here the separator is a decimal point. Not every locale uses a point as its decimal separator, and moving it changes the represented value.

originalSense.definition: To separate an integer from a decimal with a decimal point.

definition: To add diacritical marks to a written text.
example: A pointed Hebrew text includes vowel or other reading marks in addition to its letters.
distinctions: The marks support reading or pronunciation. They are distinct from ordinary full stops or decimal points.

originalSense.definition: To mark with diacritics.

definition: To mark a psalm or similar text to guide its musical chanting.
example: In Anglican chant, pointing a psalm marks how the words are fitted to the chant.
distinctions: Musical pointing concerns the relation of text to chant, not merely adding punctuation or placing dots on a map.

originalSense.definition: To mark (e.g. an Anglican psalm) with pointing.

definition: To punctuate a text, in a dated use.
example: In dated editorial language, to point a passage can mean to supply punctuation marks.
distinctions: Punctuate is the usual clear modern verb. This historical reading is separate from adding vowel marks in a writing system.

originalSense.definition: To supply with punctuation marks; to punctuate.
originalSense.example: to point a composition

definition: To make a pointer or reference designate a location in memory.
example: The pointer points to the first item in the array.
distinctions: A pointer designates a location; reading the stored value is a separate operation. A valid-looking address does not by itself establish that access is valid.

originalSense.definition: To direct the central processing unit to seek information at a certain location in memory.

distinctionTask.prompt: A pointer that points to an array item identifies a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Designating a location is separate from dereferencing it or copying its contents.

definition: To configure a domain name to resolve to a specified network address.
example: We pointed the subdomain to the new server’s IP address.
distinctions: DNS resolution maps a name to address information. It does not by itself redirect a URL path, move website content or configure HTTPS. The exact record type matters.

originalSense.definition: To direct requests sent to a domain name to the IP address corresponding to that domain name.

distinctionTask.prompt: Pointing a domain to an address with DNS _____ move the website files.
distinctionTask.explanation: Name resolution and content migration are separate operations.

definition: To sail close to the wind.
example: In sailing terminology, a boat that points well can sail at a relatively close angle to the wind.
distinctions: The sailing sense concerns the angle a vessel can maintain. It is separate from a compass point used as a unit of bearing.

originalSense.definition: To sail close to the wind.
originalSense.example: Bear off a little, we're pointing.

definition: Of a hunting dog, to indicate game by holding a fixed posture.
example: The dog pointed towards the hidden birds.
distinctions: The dog’s posture indicates the game’s location. The verb does not imply that the dog extends a human-like index finger.

originalSense.definition: To indicate the presence of game by a fixed and steady look, as certain hunting dogs do.
originalSense.example: Novv the vvarm Scent aſſures the Covey near, / He [the dog] treads vvith Caution, and he points vvith Fear; […]

definition: Of an abscess, to approach the surface and form a head.
example: In medical description, an abscess that points is becoming superficial and forming a visible head.
distinctions: This describes an appearance or stage, rather than a recommendation for treatment or a pointing gesture.

originalSense.definition: To approximate to the surface; to head.

definition: To give particular force or prominence to words or actions.
example: In dated literary description, a detail may point a remark by giving it extra force.
distinctions: This figurative verb sharpens the effect of an expression rather than physically sharpening an object.

originalSense.definition: To give point to (something said or done); to give particular prominence or force to.
originalSense.example: He points it, however, by no deviation from his straightforward manner of speech.

definition: To appoint, in an obsolete use.
example: The source records point as an obsolete verb meaning appoint.
distinctions: Use appoint in ordinary modern writing; the obsolete form is retained for reading recognition.

originalSense.definition: To appoint.
originalSense.example:
And he, that points the Centinel his room,
Doth license him depart at sound of morning Droom.

definition: Point, an informal military reference to the United States Military Academy at West Point.
example: In the recorded informal military use, Point refers to the US Military Academy at West Point, New York.
distinctions: This proper-name reference is not a direction, a numerical score or every place whose name contains Point.

originalSense.definition: USMA (United States Military Academy) in West Point, New York.
originalSense.example: Study goes on until tattoo, which, when Pops was at the Point, was sounded at 9.30, followed by taps at 10.

definition: Point Township in Posey County, Indiana, United States.
example: The source records Point Township in Posey County, Indiana.
distinctions: This is the Indiana township, distinct from Point Township in Pennsylvania. The source also records a geographical explanation of its name.

originalSense.definition: A township in Posey County, Indiana, United States, so-named for being the southernmost and westernmost point in the state.

definition: Point Township in Northumberland County, Pennsylvania, United States.
example: The source records Point Township in Northumberland County, Pennsylvania.
distinctions: This township is distinct from Point Township in Indiana and the city named Point in Texas.

originalSense.definition: A township in Northumberland County, Pennsylvania, United States.

definition: Point, a city in Rains County, Texas, United States.
example: The source records the city of Point in Rains County, Texas.
distinctions: The capitalised place name refers to this Texas city, not to a generic position or promontory.

originalSense.definition: A minor city in Rains County, Texas, United States.

definition: Point, a coastal settlement in Feock parish, Cornwall, England.
example: The source records Point in Feock parish in south-west Cornwall, England.
distinctions: This Cornish settlement is distinct from the US places named Point. The source gives the grid reference SW8138.

originalSense.definition: A coastal settlement in Feock parish, south-west Cornwall, England (OS grid ref SW8138).
originalSense.example: Cornwall County Council asked for a decision on objections raised by property owners to its proposal to convert the site of the railway into a public road for a distance of 1 mile 86 yards from Devoran to Point (Restronguet Creek).

definition: Point, a surname of French origin.
example: The source records Point as a family name derived from French.
distinctions: The surname is capitalised and does not itself identify a place, a score or someone’s opinion.

originalSense.definition: A surname from French.

definition: A very small mark or speck.
example: A tiny point of light appeared in the distance.
distinctions: This is a small visible feature. A mathematical point has no magnitude and is represented by a mark rather than literally being a speck.

originalSense.definition: Something tiny, as a pinprick; a very small mark.

definition: A full stop or another terminal punctuation mark.
example: In the recorded punctuation sense, point can mean a full stop or another mark ending an utterance.
distinctions: Full stop in British usage and period in US usage are more specific common terms for the ordinary sentence-ending dot.

originalSense.definition: A full stop or other terminal punctuation mark.

definition: A decimal point, especially when a number is read aloud.
example: Read 3.5 as three point five.
distinctions: The digits after a decimal point are commonly read individually. A decimal point is not a claim about percentage points or a punctuation mark ending the sentence.

originalSense.definition: A decimal point (now especially when reading decimal fractions aloud).

distinctionTask.prompt: Read 3.5 as three point _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: After the decimal separator, this single digit is read five.

definition: A diacritical mark added to a letter, especially in a Semitic writing system.
example: In a pointed Hebrew text, points can mark vowels or other reading information alongside the consonant letters.
distinctions: These marks belong to the writing system and are distinct from decimal points or sentence-ending punctuation.

originalSense.definition: Each of the marks or strokes written above letters, especially in Semitic languages, to indicate vowels, stress etc.

definition: A musical dot or mark; in modern notation, a dot that adds half a note’s undotted duration.
example: In ordinary modern notation, a dotted crotchet lasts one and a half crotchet units.
distinctions: A single augmentation dot adds half the original duration. Other musical dots, including staccato markings, have different functions; position and notation matter.
usage: Music reading terminology; historical uses are broader.

originalSense.definition: A dot or mark used to designate certain tones or time. In ancient music, it distinguished or characterized certain tones or styles (points of perfection, of augmentation, etc.). In modern music, it is placed on the right of a note to raise its value, or prolong its time, by one half.

definition: A musical note or tune, in a historical or specialised use.
example: In the recorded older musical use, point can denote a note or a tune.
distinctions: This meaning is separate from an augmentation dot and from a unit of scoring. Use note or tune for clear ordinary modern description.
usage: Historical or specialised music reading noun.

originalSense.definition: A note; a tune.

definition: A mathematical position with no size or extent.
example: The point P has coordinates two, three on the diagram.
distinctions: A mathematical point has position but no length, area or volume. A visible dot drawn to represent it has size, which is a feature of the drawing.

originalSense.definition: A zero-dimensional mathematical object representing a location in one or more dimensions; something considered to have position but no magnitude or direction.

distinctionTask.prompt: A mathematical point has _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A visible dot represents a position; its ink size is not the mathematical point’s size.

definition: A particular detail, thought or feature within a larger subject.
example: Her final point concerned the cost of maintenance.
distinctions: A point can be one detail among several. The main point is the central idea; the point of an activity can instead be its purpose.

originalSense.definition: An individual element in a larger whole; a particular detail, thought, or quality.

definition: A particular moment or stage in an event.
example: At that point, the meeting was interrupted.
distinctions: This temporal point is a moment or stage. A meeting point is usually a place, unless the surrounding context supplies a temporal meaning.

originalSense.definition: A particular moment in an event or occurrence; a juncture.

distinctionTask.prompt: “At that point, the meeting stopped” locates a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The context makes this a temporal juncture.

definition: A condition or state, in an archaic use.
example: In an older passage, point can denote a person’s condition or a state of affairs.
distinctions: This older state sense is distinct from a present-day score or an item in an argument.

originalSense.definition: Condition, state.

definition: A topic, proposition or issue for discussion.
example: The committee debated each point in turn.
distinctions: The point is the matter being considered. It does not have to be a numerical score or the main idea of the entire conversation.

originalSense.definition: A topic of discussion or debate; a proposition; a count.

definition: A piece of private information or a tip, in dated US slang.
example: In the dated slang sense, a point can be a privately supplied tip or hint.
distinctions: This historical information sense is separate from a percentage-point change and does not guarantee that the information is reliable.

originalSense.definition: An item of private information; a hint; a tip; a pointer.

definition: The central idea or focus of a discussion.
example: The main point is that the water supply must remain reliable.
distinctions: The main point is the central idea. The point of an action can instead be its purpose or benefit.

originalSense.definition: A focus of conversation or consideration; the main idea.

distinctionTask.prompt: “The main point of her argument” is its _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The discussion context selects the main-idea sense.

definition: A purpose or objective that makes an activity worthwhile.
example: There is little point in printing a form that must be submitted online.
distinctions: Point in doing something concerns purpose or benefit. It is distinct from one detail in a list or a mark on a map.
usage: Purpose noun; often uncountable in expressions.

originalSense.definition: A purpose or objective, which makes something meaningful.

distinctionTask.prompt: “There is little point in doing this twice” questions its _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Point in doing something concerns whether the activity serves a useful purpose.

definition: The smallest quantity of something; a jot or whit.
example: In the obsolete quantity use, point denotes an extremely small amount.
distinctions: This is not a modern standard measurement unit. Its scale cannot be inferred from a typographic point or a compass point.

originalSense.definition: The smallest quantity of something; a jot, a whit.

definition: A very short interval of time; a moment.
example: In the obsolete temporal quantity use, point means a very small amount of time.
distinctions: The source distinguishes this obsolete tiny-interval use from a point meaning a particular stage or moment in an event.

originalSense.definition: A tiny amount of time; a moment.

definition: A particular location considered as a position in space.
example: We agreed to meet at the same point on the path.
distinctions: A spatial point locates something. It need not be a sharp promontory or a mathematical object considered in strict geometric terms.

originalSense.definition: A specific location or place, seen as a spatial position.

distinctionTask.prompt: A meeting point usually identifies a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The people agree on a location where they will meet.

definition: A distinguishing quality or characteristic.
example: Clear explanation is one of her strong points.
distinctions: A strong point is a favourable characteristic, rather than a game score or a physical sharp tip.

originalSense.definition: A distinguishing quality or characteristic.

distinctionTask.prompt: “Patience is her strong point” names a favourable _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Strong point describes a characteristic or ability.

definition: The principal or excellent features, in a dated plural use.
example: In an older description of an animal’s points, the word can refer to its chief or excellent features.
distinctions: This dated evaluation sense is separate from coloured markings on the fur and from points scored in a competition.

originalSense.definition: The chief or excellent features.

definition: An area of contrasting colour on an animal’s coat.
example: In a coat description, an animal’s dark points are its contrasting darker markings.
distinctions: These points are colour areas, not bony tips or a numerical rating. The exact pattern depends on the animal and description.

originalSense.definition: An area of contrasting colour on an animal, especially a dog; a marking.

definition: A tenth, or historically a twelfth, in restricted expressions.
example: The source records point as a fractional use meaning a tenth, formerly also a twelfth, now restricted to phrases.
distinctions: Do not apply one universal fraction to every point: decimal, scoring, financial and typographic uses have separate conventions.

originalSense.definition: A tenth; formerly also a twelfth.

definition: A unit expressing the numerical difference between two percentages.
example: A rise from twenty per cent to twenty-five per cent is a rise of five percentage points.
distinctions: From 20% to 25% is an increase of 5 percentage points, but a relative increase of 25%: (25 − 20) / 20. State which comparison is intended.

originalSense.definition: Ellipsis of percentage point.

distinctionTask.prompt: A rise from 20% to 25% is an increase of _____ percentage points.
distinctionTask.explanation: The absolute percentage-point difference is 25 − 20 = 5; the relative increase is 25%.

definition: A unit of scoring in a game or competition.
example: The team scored six points in the final round.
distinctions: Points follow the rules of the game or competition. One scoring event does not necessarily earn exactly one point.

originalSense.definition: A unit of scoring in a game or competition.

distinctionTask.prompt: The number of points awarded for a scoring event depends on _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Different games and scoring events can award different numbers of points.

definition: A unit of a numerical game attribute, such as health or experience.
example: In a game, losing ten health points changes the character’s health parameter rather than necessarily changing the match score.
distinctions: Game attributes and victory scores are different quantities even when both are counted in points. Rules define how each changes.

originalSense.definition: A unit of various numerical parameters used in a game, e.g. health, experience, stamina, mana.

definition: A quoted unit used to describe a difference in a stock or share price.
example: In a quotation using one dollar per point, a one-point change is one dollar, rather than one per cent.
distinctions: The unit depends on the quotation and instrument. A one-point price change is not universally a one-per-cent relative change.

originalSense.definition: A unit used to express differences in prices of stocks and shares.

definition: A typographic unit, equal to one twelfth of a pica; digitally, one seventy-second of an inch.
example: In the digital typographic convention, 72 points equal one inch.
distinctions: Digital 1 pt = 1/72 inch and 12 pt = 1 pica. Font size does not guarantee that every visible glyph is that tall; historical point systems also differ.

originalSense.definition: A unit of measure equal to 1/12 of a pica, or approximately 1/72 of an inch (exactly 1/72 of an inch in the digital era).

definition: An electrical power socket, in British usage.
example: There is a power point beside the desk.
distinctions: This is a place for an electrical connection, not a dot on the wall or the presentation software PowerPoint.

originalSense.definition: An electric power socket.

distinctionTask.prompt: In British usage, a power point is an electrical _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The phrase can refer to a wall electrical connection.

definition: An obsolete rainfall unit equal to one hundredth of an inch, or 0.254 millimetres.
example: In the recorded older rainfall unit, ten points equal 2.54 millimetres.
distinctions: Here 1 point = 0.01 inch = 0.254 mm. This is not the digital typographic point of 1/72 inch.
usage: Obsolete UK, Australian and New Zealand rainfall unit.

originalSense.definition: A unit of measure for rain, equal to 0.254 mm or 0.01 of an inch.

definition: A contact surface in a mechanical ignition distributor, usually referred to in the plural.
example: In an older ignition distributor, the points open and close the primary circuit associated with the ignition coil.
distinctions: This is mechanical ignition terminology; it does not describe every modern electronic ignition system or provide an adjustment procedure.

originalSense.definition: Either of the two metal surfaces in a distributor which close or open to allow or prevent the flow of current through the ignition coil. There is usually a moving point, pushed by the distributor cam, and a fixed point, and they are built together as a unit.

definition: The sharp tip of an object.
example: Be careful not to damage the point of the pencil.
distinctions: The physical tip is separate from the pencil mark it produces and from the purpose of writing.

originalSense.definition: The sharp tip of an object.

definition: A projecting end or extremity of an object.
example: The star-shaped badge has five points.
distinctions: A projecting point need not be dangerously sharp. This is a shape or extremity sense, rather than the zero-dimensional geometric model.

originalSense.definition: Any projecting extremity of an object.

distinctionTask.prompt: A five-pointed star has five projecting _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The shape context selects its projecting tips.

definition: An object with a sharp or tapering tip.
example: In the source’s object sense, a point can denote a pointed implement rather than only its tip.
distinctions: The source includes separate archaeological and historical medical child uses. Context is needed to identify the object.

originalSense.definition: An object which has a sharp or tapering tip.

definition: A spearhead or similar object fixed to a handle or shaft.
example: In archaeology, a projectile point is a shaped implement such as a spearhead or arrowhead.
distinctions: The object is the point, not necessarily a complete spear or arrow. Shape alone need not identify the exact original weapon.

originalSense.definition: A spearhead or similar object hafted to a handle.

definition: A vaccine point, in an obsolete medical use.
example: In historical medical terminology, a vaccine point was a pointed item carrying material for vaccination.
distinctions: This is obsolete terminology retained for interpreting historical texts, rather than a description of current vaccination equipment or practice.

originalSense.definition: A vaccine point.

definition: One of the triangular playing positions on a backgammon board.
example: A standard backgammon board has 24 points, arranged as four quadrants of six points.
distinctions: There are 24 points in total, 12 on each broad half and 6 in each inner or outer quadrant. The preserved source’s “twelve ... in either table” uses table ambiguously; do not confuse a half-board with a six-point quadrant.
usage: Backgammon reading terminology; source division clarified.

originalSense.definition: Each of the twelve triangular positions in either table of a backgammon board, on which the stones are played.

definition: A piece of land projecting into the water; a headland or promontory.
example: The lighthouse stands on a rocky point.
distinctions: A coastal point projects from the land. The word alone does not specify its height, geological origin or safe route around it.

originalSense.definition: A peninsula or promontory.

distinctionTask.prompt: A rocky point on a coast is a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The geographic point projects from land into water.

definition: The front or vanguard position in an advancing group.
example: In a description of a patrol, point is its leading position.
distinctions: This position is at the front of the group, rather than a compass direction or a numerical score.

originalSense.definition: The position at the front or vanguard of an advancing force.

definition: A leading operational or public role in a risky undertaking.
example: In a figurative account, taking point means accepting the leading role in a difficult undertaking.
distinctions: This figurative leadership use extends the vanguard sense. It does not specify formal authority or guarantee that the leader acts alone.

originalSense.definition: An operational or public leadership position in a risky endeavor.

definition: Short for point man, a person in a leading position or role.
example: In the recorded shortened use, the point can mean the person serving as point man.
distinctions: This use names the person, unlike point meaning the position. Point person is a common gender-neutral alternative for a lead contact in modern organisational contexts.

originalSense.definition: Ellipsis of point man.

definition: A direction on a traditional compass rose.
example: On a traditional 32-point compass rose, north and north by east are adjacent named points.
distinctions: Compass roses may display different subdivisions. The traditional 32-point convention is the one used here; it is not the number of directions every instrument must label.

originalSense.definition: Each of the main directions on a compass, usually considered to be 32 in number; a direction.

definition: A traditional bearing unit equal to one thirty-second of a full circle: 11.25 degrees.
example: On the traditional 32-point system, two points span 22.5 degrees.
distinctions: 360° / 32 = 11.25° per point. A point in this convention is not one degree, and left or right still needs a stated reference frame.

originalSense.definition: The difference between two points of the compass; a unit of bearing equal to one thirty-second of a circle, i.e. 11.25°.

definition: A penetrating, incisive or decisive quality of speech or writing.
example: In literary criticism, a remark with point has a sharp or effective quality of expression.
distinctions: This evaluative quality is distinct from the topic being discussed and from a physical pointed object.

originalSense.definition: Pointedness of speech or writing; a penetrating or decisive quality of expression.

definition: A railway switch that guides trains between tracks.
example: In British railway usage, the points set the route from one track to another.
distinctions: The plural points names a track-switch assembly. It is not a score or a guarantee that a route is clear; operation depends on the railway system.

originalSense.definition: A railroad switch.

definition: A projecting tine or branch of an antler.
example: In an antler description, each point is one of its projecting tines.
distinctions: This is a projection of an antler, not a scored evaluation of the animal. Counting conventions can depend on the description or system.

originalSense.definition: A tine or snag of an antler.

definition: A named area at the base or a qualified corner of a heraldic shield.
example: In heraldry, an unqualified point can refer to the shield’s lower central area; qualified forms name other positions.
distinctions: Heraldic dexter and sinister use the bearer’s viewpoint, so they reverse the viewer’s right and left. The term here names a shield area rather than a geometric point.

originalSense.definition: One of the "corners" of the escutcheon: the base (bottom center) unless a qualifier is added (point dexter, point dexter base, point sinister, point sinister base), generally when separately tinctured.

definition: A heraldic ordinary rising from the base of a shield, similar to a pile.
example: In the recorded heraldic use, a point pointed is a charge extending upward from the shield’s base.
distinctions: This is a heraldic shape or charge, distinct from a named corner of the shield and from an ordinary geometric point.

originalSense.definition: An ordinary similar to a pile (but sometimes shorter), extending upward from the base.

definition: The act of extending or directing the foot downwards in a dance position.
example: In the recorded dance use, a point is an action or position of the foot, rather than a competition score.
distinctions: This action sense differs from pointe, the specialised ballet term, and does not describe every possible movement of the foot.

originalSense.definition: The act of pointing, as of the foot downward in certain dance positions.

definition: A finger gesture indicating a direction or object.
example: A quick point towards the sign showed us where to go.
distinctions: This noun names the gesture. The corresponding verb is point, as in she pointed towards the sign.

originalSense.definition: The gesture of extending the index finger in a direction in order to indicate something.

definition: The fixed pointing posture assumed by a hunting dog after locating game.
example: In a hunting description, the dog holds a point when it indicates the location of game.
distinctions: The posture is distinct from the hunter’s gesture and from a point awarded in a trial or competition.

originalSense.definition: The attitude assumed by a pointer dog when he finds game.

definition: A hawk’s vertical rise above a place where its quarry has taken cover.
example: In the recorded falconry sense, point names the hawk’s upward movement above covered quarry.
distinctions: This source-bound movement noun is separate from a hawk’s check, which involves leaving the intended quarry for other birds.

originalSense.definition: The perpendicular rising of a hawk over the place where its prey has gone into cover.

definition: A movement made with a foil or sabre.
example: In the recorded fencing action sense, point names a movement with a foil or sabre.
distinctions: This broad source use is distinct from the tip of the weapon and from a point awarded in scoring. The entry does not specify one modern rule-defined action.

originalSense.definition: A movement executed with the sabre or foil.

definition: A cricket fielding position square on the off side, between gully and cover.
example: In cricket, point is an off-side fielding position near square of the batter.
distinctions: Off side depends on the batter’s handedness. Point is a fielding position here, not a unit of runs or points on a compass.

originalSense.definition: A fielding position square of the wicket on the off side, between gully and cover.

definition: A player position in front of the goalkeeper in the recorded hockey or lacrosse use.
example: The source records point as a position in front of the goalkeeper in certain hockey and lacrosse terminology.
distinctions: Names and locations depend on the sport, period and formation. Do not apply this historical or specialised gloss to every modern hockey use of the point.

originalSense.definition: The position of the player of each side who stands a short distance in front of the goalkeeper.

definition: The pitcher-and-catcher position, in a recorded baseball use.
example: The source records point for the baseball pitcher-and-catcher position.
distinctions: This older or specialised position use is not the normal scoring term: baseball scores are normally counted in runs.

originalSense.definition: The position of the pitcher and catcher.

definition: A destination or straight run in hunting, including a cross-country run from point to point.
example: In a hunting account, a run from point to point links one destination with another across country.
distinctions: This recorded run or destination use is distinct from a hunting dog’s fixed point and from a game score.

originalSense.definition: A spot to which a straight run is made; hence, a straight run from point to point; a cross-country run.

definition: Senses relating to exerting force or pulling.
example: This source heading organises pulling uses. Choose a concrete meaning such as pulling a curtain, drawing a bow or a vessel’s draught.
distinctions: The heading is an index to different meanings, not one definition suitable for an exercise.
usage: Source organisation heading; choose a concrete meaning.

originalSense.definition: Senses relating to exerting force or pulling.
originalSense.example: He drew a sheaf of papers from his bag.

draw a sponge over the slate

definition: Senses relating to attracting.
example: This source heading groups attracting attention, people, reactions and physical material.
distinctions: The concrete object and context determine the meaning; the group heading is not itself a practice target.
usage: Source organisation heading; choose a concrete meaning.

originalSense.definition: Senses relating to attracting.
originalSense.example: From the moment she entered the room, all eyes were drawn to her.
wordFamily: draw a line in the sand
draw a sponge over the slate

definition: Senses relating to extending or protracting.
example: This source heading groups stretching, lengthening and certain manufacturing uses.
distinctions: A group title does not specify whether the context is physical length, duration or a historical expression.
usage: Source organisation heading; choose a concrete meaning.

originalSense.definition: Senses relating to extending or protracting.
originalSense.example: The dough was run through the pasta machine and drawn into a long ribbon.
wordFamily: draw a line in the sand
draw a sponge over the slate

definition: Senses relating to extracting or selecting.
example: This source heading groups extraction, selection, inference and related uses.
distinctions: Extracting water, selecting a ticket and drawing a conclusion are distinct concrete meanings.
usage: Source organisation heading; choose a concrete meaning.

originalSense.definition: Senses relating to extracting or selecting.
wordFamily: draw a line in the sand
draw a sponge over the slate

definition: Senses relating to moving or travelling.
example: This source heading groups motion and approach, such as a train drawing into a station or an event drawing near.
distinctions: The heading is retained as source organisation. Choose a concrete movement or time meaning to practise.
usage: Source organisation heading; choose a concrete meaning.

originalSense.definition: Senses relating to moving or travelling.
originalSense.example: She thought she heard a noise in her chamber, and she drew herself within the casement.
wordFamily: draw a line in the sand
draw a sponge over the slate

definition: Senses relating to depicting or representing.
example: This source heading groups picture-making, comparison, document-writing and verbal portrayal.

originalSense.definition: To drag (something), especially along the ground.

originalSense.definition: To pull (blinds, a curtain, etc.) open or closed.

definition: To attract people or act as an inducement, without a stated direct object.

definition: To take a drink, especially of an alcoholic beverage.
