distinctionTask.explanation: Date from introduces its origin.

definition: Date as a family name.
example: In a person’s name, Date may be the family name.
distinctions: Capitalisation and naming context identify the surname. It is separate from dates as fruit or calendar information.

originalSense.definition: A surname.

definition: Date, a ghost town in Perkins County, South Dakota, United States.
example: In the geographical entry, Date names a ghost town in Perkins County, South Dakota.
distinctions: This capitalised name identifies the preserved geographical entry. It is not an instruction to arrange a meeting or supply a calendar date.

originalSense.definition: A ghost town in Perkins County, South Dakota, United States.

definition: To move or burst forth suddenly.
example: Water sprang from a crack in the pipe.
distinctions: The subject moves or emerges suddenly. The phrase spring a leak has a direct object and describes developing a leak; it is not the same grammatical construction.
usage: Intransitive; common past sprang, past participle sprung.

originalSense.definition: To move or burst forth.
originalSense.example: The boat sprang a leak and began to sink.

distinctionTask.prompt: Water suddenly emerged from a crack: it _____ from the crack.
distinctionTask.explanation: Here sprang describes sudden emergence.

definition: To cause something to move or act suddenly.
example: The released catch sprang the lid open.
distinctions: Here the subject causes the lid’s movement. The lid sprang open instead describes the lid moving without a direct object.

originalSense.definition: To cause to spring (all senses).

distinctionTask.prompt: The catch caused the lid to open suddenly: it _____ the lid open.
distinctionTask.explanation: This is the causative transitive construction.

definition: To leap over an obstacle.
example: In the preserved village story, I sprang the fence means I jumped over the fence.
distinctions: The fence is the direct object in this older construction. Modern jump over the fence is more familiar than spring the fence.
usage: Contextual reading of a less common transitive use.

originalSense.definition: To leap over.
originalSense.example: I sprang the fence, and was soon in the village street.

definition: In obsolete horse-breeding usage, to mate with or impregnate a mare.
example: In the 1585 passage, horses were sought to spring their mares, meaning to mate with them.
collocations: spring their mares in the passage
distinctions: This historical verb does not describe jumping over a mare or the season when breeding occurs.

originalSense.definition: To breed with, to impregnate.
originalSense.example: ...[they] sought the fairest stoned horses to spring their mares...

definition: In obsolete usage, to wet or moisten.
example: In the preserved obsolete gloss, spring means to wet or moisten something.
collocations: spring in the obsolete wetting sense
distinctions: This note explains the recorded definition rather than presenting a newly attested modern sentence. Use wet or moisten in ordinary current writing.

originalSense.definition: To wet, to moisten.

definition: To burst apart or suddenly open.
example: The overloaded case sprang open on the platform.
distinctions: The subject opens or comes apart suddenly. A person springs something open instead uses the transitive causative construction.

originalSense.definition: To burst into pieces, to explode, to shatter.
originalSense.example: On the 22nd the mines sprang, and took very good effect.

distinctionTask.prompt: The case suddenly opened: it _____ open.
distinctionTask.explanation: Sprang is a standard past tense of the motion verb.

definition: In the preserved obsolete military sense, to go off or discharge.
example: The obsolete military gloss uses spring for go off, as of a device discharging.
distinctions: This explains the historical definition. It gives no operating procedure and should not be inferred from every modern use of spring apart.
usage: Obsolete military vocabulary; lexicographical reading note.

originalSense.definition: To go off.
originalSense.example: The whole contraption appears liable to spring apart at any moment.

definition: Of a mast or spar, to crack or cause it to crack.
example: In the 1582 diary, the ship sprang her foremast means that the foremast cracked.
distinctions: This nautical damage use differs from a spring fitted as an elastic component. A sprung mast has suffered damage; the word alone does not determine its condition.

originalSense.definition: To crack.
originalSense.example: The Edward sprang hir foremast.

definition: To discover and flush a bird or animal from cover.
example: The dog sprang a pheasant from the long grass.
distinctions: Here the bird is flushed into the open. It does not mean the dog gave birth to the bird or merely jumped beside it.

originalSense.definition: To come upon and flush out.
originalSense.example: For generations of men the springer spaniel has been looked upon as the dog for springing pheasants in covert and finding and retrieving dead birds or winged runners when ordered to do so. The properly broken dog will not chase, but drop to wing and shot.

definition: In Australian slang, to catch someone in wrongdoing or a compromising situation.
example: In the preserved Australian passage, nobody would spring him means nobody would catch him out.
distinctions: This catch-out sense differs from freeing someone from custody in American slang. Context and regional usage distinguish the opposing actions.

originalSense.definition: To catch in an illegal act or compromising position.
originalSense.example: He figured that nobody would ever spring him, but he figured wrong.

definition: In obsolete usage, to begin.
example: The preserved obsolete gloss records spring in the sense begin.
collocations: spring in the obsolete beginning sense
distinctions: The recorded bare verb is obsolete in this sense. Modern spring into action remains a separate familiar construction.

originalSense.definition: To begin.

definition: In obsolete slang, to put counterfeit or otherwise bad money into circulation.
example: The preserved obsolete slang gloss uses spring for putting bad money into circulation.
collocations: spring bad money in the old gloss
distinctions: The note explains a historical meaning, without describing a method. It differs from spring a sum meaning spend money.

originalSense.definition: To put bad money into circulation.

definition: To tell someone news or present something to them unexpectedly.
example: Please do not spring a surprise on me just before the meeting.
distinctions: The construction often stresses unexpected timing or lack of warning. It is more specific than simply sharing any information.

originalSense.definition: To tell, to share.
originalSense.example: Sorry to spring it on you like this but I've been offered another job.

distinctionTask.prompt: Do not announce unexpected news without warning: do not spring it _____ me.
distinctionTask.explanation: Spring something on someone stresses surprise.

definition: To free someone from imprisonment, especially by arranging an escape.
example: In the novel, the gang planned to spring their leader from prison.
distinctions: The slang verb names obtaining someone’s freedom. This selected use can concern an escape; another use can concern a lawyer obtaining lawful release.

originalSense.definition: To free from imprisonment, especially by facilitating an illegal escape.
originalSense.example: His lieutenants hired a team of miners to help spring him.

definition: In rare slang, to get free of imprisonment or escape.
example: The preserved rare intransitive gloss records spring for becoming free of imprisonment.
collocations: spring in the rare escape sense
distinctions: The subject is the person who becomes free. Spring someone uses a direct object for a person whose release someone else obtains.

originalSense.definition: To be free of imprisonment, especially by illegal escape.

definition: To secure someone’s release from custody, including through bail or legal assistance.
example: Her lawyer managed to spring her from custody that afternoon.
distinctions: This informal verb does not necessarily mean an illegal escape. The legal basis for release must come from the surrounding facts.

originalSense.definition: To secure a person's release from custody; to free or bail out of jail.
originalSense.example: The Big Man, of course, had had an alibi as solid as Fort Knox. He had been held and questioned, but was quickly sprung by the best lawyer in Harlem.

distinctionTask.prompt: A lawyer secured her release: the lawyer _____ her from custody.
options: necessarily arranged an illegal escape for
distinctionTask.explanation: This informal use can concern lawful release.

definition: To construct or begin the curve of an arch.
example: The builders sprang an arch from the two supports.
distinctions: Here builders form the arch. The arch springs from the supports instead describes where the arch begins to rise.

originalSense.definition: To build, to form the initial curve of.
originalSense.example: They sprung an arch over the lintel.

definition: Of an arch, to rise or curve from its supporting point.
example: The arches spring from the stone columns.
distinctions: From names the support where the curve begins. The arch is not jumping, and the verb does not identify an elastic coil.

originalSense.definition: To extend, to curve.
originalSense.example: The arches spring from the front posts.

distinctionTask.prompt: The arches begin their curves at the columns: they spring _____ the columns.
distinctionTask.explanation: From introduces the supporting point.

definition: To turn a vessel by means of a spring line attached to its anchor cable.
example: The preserved nautical gloss uses spring for turning a vessel with a spring on its anchor cable.
collocations: spring a vessel in the old gloss
a spring on the anchor cable
distinctions: This is the recorded ship-handling term, distinct from a mooring spring led to a berth. The note identifies vocabulary without giving manoeuvring instructions.

originalSense.definition: To turn a vessel using a spring attached to its anchor cable.

definition: To pay or spend a stated sum.
example: He would not spring ten pounds for a ticket.
distinctions: An amount can be the direct object. In the familiar spring for construction, for introduces what someone agrees to pay for; the verb does not describe jumping toward it.

originalSense.definition: To pay or spend a certain sum, to yield.
originalSense.example: He wouldn't spring a nickel for a bag of peanuts.

distinctionTask.prompt: I will pay for lunch: I will spring _____ lunch.
distinctionTask.explanation: Spring for names what someone agrees to pay for.

definition: In obsolete slang, to increase an offered price.
example: The preserved obsolete gloss records spring as raising the price being offered.
collocations: spring in the old price-raising sense
distinctions: This concerns increasing an offer, rather than simply paying a stated amount or the modern seasonal noun.

originalSense.definition: To raise an offered price.

definition: A dialectal American form of sprain.
example: In the preserved American dialect record, spring is an alternative form of sprain.
distinctions: This is a recorded dialect form, not automatically a misspelling. Sprain is the standard modern form for the corresponding injury verb.

originalSense.definition: Alternative form of sprain.

definition: A dialectal American form of strain.
example: In the preserved American dialect record, spring is an alternative form of strain.
distinctions: This record corresponds to strain, while the adjacent dialect record corresponds to sprain. They remain separate source meanings and should not be merged as one injury type.

originalSense.definition: Alternative form of strain.

definition: In obsolete usage, to rebound strongly as a spring does.
example: The preserved obsolete gloss records spring in the sense act as a spring and rebound.
collocations: spring in the old rebound sense
distinctions: This explains the recorded historical classification. It does not make every modern use of spring back obsolete.
usage: Obsolete recorded sense; lexicographical reading note.

originalSense.definition: To act as a spring: to strongly rebound.

definition: To fit something, especially a vehicle, with springs or spring suspension.
example: The carriage was sprung with leaf springs.
distinctions: Sprung here describes being equipped with springs. It differs from a sprung mast, where the same form can describe cracking or damage.
usage: Rare transitive verb, often seen as sprung.

originalSense.definition: To equip with springs, especially (of vehicles) to equip with a suspension.

distinctionTask.prompt: A carriage equipped with spring suspension is a _____ carriage.
distinctionTask.explanation: Sprung has an equipment sense as well as a damage sense in other contexts.

definition: In rare obsolete figurative usage, to inspire or motivate.
example: The preserved figurative gloss records spring as inspire or motivate.
collocations: spring in the old motivating sense
distinctions: The historical meaning is distinct from motives that spring from a source. The note is a definition explanation, not a new claim of modern usage.
usage: Rare and obsolete; lexicographical reading note.

originalSense.definition: to inspire, to motivate.

definition: To bend or warp under pressure, or bend something into position.
example: The timber sprang as it dried and no longer lay flat.
distinctions: The shape changes under stress or during fitting. The context determines whether it returns to shape; spring does not guarantee that every deformation is elastic.

originalSense.definition: To deform owing to excessive pressure, to become warped; to intentionally deform in order to position and then straighten in place.
originalSense.example: Don't drive it in too hard, as it will ‘spring’ the plane-iron, and make it concave.

definition: In British dialect, especially of a cow, to swell with pregnancy or developing milk.
example: In Patrick White’s passage, the heifer is springing: the speakers are describing her swelling.
collocations: a heifer springing in the passage
distinctions: This describes the animal’s condition in the regional vocabulary. It does not mean the heifer is jumping or establish an exact stage of pregnancy.
usage: British dialect cattle terminology; contextual reading.

originalSense.definition: To swell with milk or pregnancy.
originalSense.example:
“Gee, Dad, Nancy’s springing all right,” Ray said and paused in spontaneous pleasure.
Stan Parker came, and together they looked at their swelling heifer.

definition: In archaic use, to sound or play a rattle.
example: In the preserved nineteenth-century story, the cook had sprung the rattle, meaning sounded it.
distinctions: This older use describes making the rattle sound. It does not mean a modern mechanical spring necessarily broke.

originalSense.definition: To sound, to play.
originalSense.example: I do not know how John and his mistress would have settled the fate of the thief, but just at this moment a policeman entered — for the cook had sprung the rattle, and had been screaming "Murder" and "Thieves."

definition: Of an animal, to obtain enough food during springtime.
example: The preserved animal-husbandry gloss records spring for finding enough food during springtime.
distinctions: This lexical note explains a specialised feeding sense. It differs from spending the spring in a place and from the motion verb leap.
usage: Specialised animal sense; lexicographical reading note.

originalSense.definition: To find or get enough food during springtime.

definition: A leap or jump.
example: With one spring, the cat reached the low wall.
distinctions: This countable noun names one jumping movement. It is separate from the season, a water source and a mechanical part.

originalSense.definition: An act of springing: a leap, a jump.

distinctionTask.prompt: The cat made one leap: it reached the wall with one _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This noun names a jumping movement.

definition: The season between winter and summer, associated in temperate regions with increasing daylight and new growth.
example: The garden fills with flowers in spring.
distinctions: Spring falls at different times in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Meteorological and astronomical definitions use different boundaries, and not every species reproduces in spring.
usage: Season name, normally lower case except at the start of a sentence or in a name.

originalSense.definition: The season of the year in temperate regions in which temperatures and daylight hours rise, and plants spring from the ground and into bloom and dormant animals spring to life.
originalSense.example: Spring is the time of the year most species reproduce.

distinctionTask.prompt: The season between winter and summer is _____.
options: a mechanical coil in every context
distinctionTask.explanation: The context is the seasonal noun.

definition: Figuratively, an early period of growth or development.
example: In Shakespeare’s phrase this spring of love, spring compares the early growth of love with the season.
collocations: the spring of the day in older text
distinctions: The figurative meaning can concern a beginning rather than a calendar season. Political spring is a related but separately recorded use.

originalSense.definition: The time of something's growth; the early stages of some process.
originalSense.example: ...and it came to passe about the spring of the day, that Samuel called Saul to the top of the house...

definition: In a seasonal colour-analysis scheme, a person classified in a palette called spring.
example: In the preserved fashion scheme, a spring is someone classified as suiting a spring colour palette.
distinctions: This is terminology within a styling system. It is not a biological season or an objective test that every person with a stated skin, hair or eye colour must fit one category.
usage: Fashion and styling terminology; contextual reading.

originalSense.definition: Someone with ivory or peach skin tone and eyes and hair that are not extremely dark, seen as best suited to certain colors of clothing.

definition: Something that springs forth, up or back.
example: The broad preserved noun definition introduces things that spring forth, up or back, followed by concrete water-source, tide, device and other uses.
distinctions: The general definition is preserved as a lexical record. Select a concrete child meaning when studying a water source or mechanical device; the source does not explicitly mark this line as a non-gloss heading.

originalSense.definition: Something which springs, springs forth, springs up, or springs back, particularly
originalSense.example: This beer was brewed with pure spring water.

definition: In slang, an erection of the penis.
example: The preserved slang gloss records spring as a noun for an erection.
distinctions: This explains a slang definition rather than presenting an attested quotation. It is separate from the season and mechanical-device meanings.

originalSense.definition: An erection of the penis.

definition: In obsolete nautical use, a crack in a mast, spar or occasionally a plank or seam.
example: The 1846 Nautical Dictionary calls the crack in a sprung spar a spring.
distinctions: The noun names damage. It differs from a flexible spring fitted as a working mechanical component.

originalSense.definition: A crack which has sprung up in a mast, spar, or (rare) a plank or seam.
originalSense.example: A spar is said to be sprung, when it is cracked or split,... and the crack is called a spring.

definition: The quality of being able to spring or rebound.
example: There was still some spring in the old mattress.
distinctions: This abstract noun describes springiness. It remains a genuine lexical sense even though the source also lists more specific property and force uses beneath it.

originalSense.definition: Springiness: an attribute or quality of springing, springing up, or springing back, particularly
originalSense.example: the spring of a bow

definition: A source or origin of an action, feeling or supply.
example: Curiosity was the spring of her interest in science.
distinctions: This figurative spring is a source or origin. It need not be a water outlet, even though the metaphor draws on something flowing from a source.

originalSense.definition: The source from which an action or supply of something springs.
originalSense.example: As wel the singers as the players on instruments shall bee there: all my springs are in thee.

distinctionTask.prompt: The origin of her interest was curiosity: curiosity was its _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The metaphorical noun identifies a source.

definition: Something that causes another thing or person to spring forth or into action.
example: The broad preserved definition introduces something prompting movement or action, followed by motive and musical submeanings.
distinctions: This broad source record is not explicitly marked as a non-gloss heading. Concrete motives and the obsolete musical use remain independent child meanings; an introductory definition is not a substitute for their exact context.

originalSense.definition: Something which causes others or another to spring forth or spring into action, particularly
originalSense.example: Our Author ſhuns by vulgar Springs to move / The Hero's Glory, or the Virgin's Love; […]

definition: To spend the spring season in a place.
example: In the preserved travel passage, springed at Vienna means spent the spring in Vienna.
collocations: springed at Vienna in the passage
distinctions: This seasonal verb takes regular springed in the quotation. It is separate from the motion verb with sprang or sprung forms.

originalSense.definition: To spend the springtime somewhere.
originalSense.example: True it is that, owing to the migratory propensities of our countrymen, every third man has wintered at Naples, springed at Vienna, summered in Switzerland, and autumned on the banks of the Lago Maggiore;

definition: Spring as a family name.
example: In a person’s name, Spring may be the family name.
distinctions: A naming context identifies the surname. It is separate from a lower-case season or mechanical part.

originalSense.definition: A surname.

definition: Spring, a census-designated place in Harris County, Texas, United States.
example: In the geographical entry, Spring names the census-designated place in Harris County, Texas.
distinctions: This capitalised name identifies the preserved place entry. It is not a reference to the season or a water source merely because the spelling matches.

originalSense.definition: A census-designated place in Harris County, Texas, United States.

definition: A capitalised written form of spring, the season.
example: In the preserved historical passage, Spring is capitalised as the name of the season.
distinctions: This is a recorded capitalised form, not automatically a spelling error or a distinct fifth season. Modern prose normally writes the season lower case unless another capitalisation rule applies.

originalSense.definition: Alternative form of spring, the season of warmth and new vegetation following winter.
originalSense.example: There the roſy-finger'd Spring, by the liquid mirror of a cryſtalline pool, was attiring her fair daughters in ſeven-fold ornaments, while the love-whiſpering breezes ſtole kiſſes as they paſſed, and fanned their glowing beauties.

definition: To appear or emerge.
example: In the preserved biblical wording when the day began to spring, spring means begin to appear.
distinctions: The subject is the appearing daylight. The phrase does not mean that a calendar season has begun or that day physically jumps.
usage: Older or literary use; contextual reading.

originalSense.definition: To appear.

definition: To grow or sprout.
example: New shoots sprang from the ground after the rain.
distinctions: This use concerns plant growth or emergence. The season spring is a noun; here sprang is the past tense of a verb.

originalSense.definition: To grow, to sprout.

distinctionTask.prompt: Shoots began to grow from the soil: new shoots _____ from it.
distinctionTask.explanation: This verb describes growing or sprouting.

definition: In British dialect, to mature.
example: The nested British-dialect gloss records spring with the meaning mature.
collocations: spring in the dialect maturity sense
distinctions: The note identifies the recorded maturity sense. It does not supply an invented dialect quotation or make every growth use regional.

originalSense.definition: To mature.

definition: To arise or come into existence.
example: New problems sprang up after the rules changed.
distinctions: A problem can arise figuratively without moving through physical space. Spring up often stresses its appearance or emergence.

originalSense.definition: To arise, to come into existence.

distinctionTask.prompt: New problems appeared: problems sprang _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Spring up means arise or come into existence.

definition: To become active or lively.
example: The old engine sprang to life at the first turn of the key.
distinctions: Spring to life can describe something starting to operate. It does not assert that an engine is a living organism.

originalSense.definition: To enliven.

distinctionTask.prompt: The engine began working: it sprang to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Spring to life is figurative activation.

definition: To move with great speed and energy.
example: She sprang from her chair when the phone rang.
distinctions: The verb describes a sudden energetic movement. It need not refer to a mechanical spring or a change of season.

originalSense.definition: To move with great speed and energy.

distinctionTask.prompt: She rose energetically from the chair: she _____ to her feet.
distinctionTask.explanation: Sprang is a standard motion-verb past tense.

definition: To descend or originate from a stated source.
example: The proposal sprang from a discussion among local residents.
distinctions: From introduces the source or origin. With people it can concern ancestry; with ideas it commonly concerns what produced them.

originalSense.definition: To be born, descend, or originate from

distinctionTask.prompt: The idea originated in a discussion: it sprang _____ that discussion.
distinctionTask.explanation: From introduces the origin.

definition: In obsolete usage, to rise in social position or military rank.
example: The preserved obsolete gloss records spring as rise in rank or be promoted.
collocations: spring in the old rank sense
distinctions: This is a historical recorded meaning. Use rise, advance or be promoted in ordinary current prose rather than inventing a modern spring promotion construction.

originalSense.definition: To rise in social position or military rank, to be promoted.

definition: To make a mechanism work or open by sudden pressure or release.
example: Releasing the catch sprang the small lid open.
distinctions: Here an action triggers a mechanism. The note describes the word’s causative meaning, not a procedure for operating a hazardous device.

originalSense.definition: To cause to work or open by sudden application of pressure.

definition: The astronomical season from the local spring equinox to the summer solstice.
example: In the Northern Hemisphere, astronomical spring runs from the March equinox to the June solstice.
distinctions: In the Southern Hemisphere the corresponding season runs from the September equinox to the December solstice. Exact dates vary by year and time zone; March 21 and June 21 are approximate labels, not fixed annual dates.

originalSense.definition: The period from the moment of vernal equinox (around March 21 in the Northern Hemisphere) to the moment of the summer solstice (around June 21); the equivalent periods reckoned in other cultures and calendars.

distinctionTask.prompt: Astronomical spring begins at the local _____.
options: first day of March in every hemisphere
distinctionTask.explanation: Astronomical seasons are defined by equinoxes and solstices.

definition: The three-month meteorological season: March to May in the Northern Hemisphere, September to November in the Southern Hemisphere.
example: Northern Hemisphere meteorological spring includes all of March, April and May.
distinctions: Meteorological seasons use complete calendar months. This differs from astronomical spring beginning at an equinox; the two boundaries should not be merged.

originalSense.definition: The three months of March, April, and May in the Northern Hemisphere and September, October, and November in the Southern Hemisphere.

distinctionTask.prompt: Northern Hemisphere meteorological spring includes _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The meteorological convention groups complete calendar months by hemisphere.

definition: A period described as political liberalisation or democratisation.
example: The term Prague Spring names the 1968 period of attempted political liberalisation in Czechoslovakia.
distinctions: The seasonal metaphor names a political period or aspiration. The word does not guarantee a successful transition or mean that every event bearing Spring happened in the same calendar season.

originalSense.definition: A period of political liberalization and democratization.

definition: A natural outlet where groundwater emerges at the ground surface.
example: A small spring fed the stream beside the path.
distinctions: A spring is a groundwater outlet, not simply any puddle or stream. Spring water is not automatically safe to drink or warmer than other water.

originalSense.definition: A spray or body of water springing from the ground.

distinctionTask.prompt: Groundwater naturally emerges at the surface through a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This selected sense is a natural groundwater outlet.

definition: In obsolete oceanographic usage, the sea’s rising at high tide.
example: The preserved obsolete gloss records spring for the rising of the sea at high tide.
collocations: spring in the old rising-tide sense
distinctions: This old noun is distinct from the modern spring-tide cycle. It does not mean every high tide is a spring tide.
usage: Obsolete oceanographic use; lexicographical reading note.

originalSense.definition: The rising of the sea at high tide.

definition: A spring tide, when the tidal range is greater than usual around new and full moons.
example: At spring tides, high waters are generally higher and low waters lower than at neap tides.
distinctions: Spring tides occur through the year, roughly twice each lunar month. The name is unrelated to the season; it concerns increased tidal range, not a rule that every location’s highest water occurs at the exact instant of new or full moon.

originalSense.definition: Ellipsis of spring tide, the especially high tide shortly after full and new moons.

distinctionTask.prompt: A spring tide has a larger _____ than a neap tide.
distinctionTask.explanation: Spring tides have higher high waters and lower low waters relative to neaps.

definition: An elastic mechanical component that resists deformation and tends to return toward its original shape.
example: The compressed spring pushed the button back into place.
distinctions: Springs can be coiled, flat or other shapes. They store recoverable elastic energy within their working range; excessive deformation can cause permanent damage.

originalSense.definition: An elastic mechanical part or device in any shape (e.g., flat, curved, coiled), made of flexible material (usually spring steel) that exerts force and attempts to spring back when bent, compressed, or stretched.

distinctionTask.prompt: The elastic part pushing the button back is a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This spring is a mechanical component.

definition: A line led from a vessel to its anchor cable to help control or turn the vessel.
example: In Marryat’s passage, springs on the anchor cable helped the vessel warp round.
distinctions: This anchor-cable arrangement is distinct from a mooring spring led along a berth. The note explains the nautical term without specifying line handling or manoeuvring steps.

originalSense.definition: A line from a vessel's end or side to its anchor cable used to diminish or control its movement.

definition: A mooring line led diagonally along a vessel to limit its fore-and-aft movement at a berth.
example: The springs limited the boat’s fore-and-aft movement at the berth.
distinctions: Mooring springs primarily restrain fore-and-aft movement. Breast lines primarily restrain movement toward or away from the berth; actual arrangements depend on the vessel and berth.

originalSense.definition: A line laid out from a vessel's end to the opposite end of an adjacent vessel or mooring to diminish or control its movement.

distinctionTask.prompt: A mooring spring primarily restrains a vessel’s _____ movement.
options: movement only toward and away from the berth
distinctionTask.explanation: Mooring springs run along the vessel to limit fore-and-aft movement.

definition: A race or line of descent.
example: The preserved figurative gloss records spring as a race or lineage.
distinctions: This less familiar noun sense concerns descent, not a water source or a person jumping. The note explains the glossary rather than inventing a historical quotation.
usage: Figurative lineage sense; lexicographical reading note.

originalSense.definition: A race, a lineage.

definition: A young person.
example: The preserved figurative gloss records spring as a youth.
distinctions: This recorded noun names a person. It is distinct from someone’s youth as a period of life and from a spring colour-analysis classification.

originalSense.definition: A youth.

definition: A shoot or young tree.
example: The preserved plant gloss records spring as a shoot or young tree.
distinctions: This botanical noun names the plant or shoot. It differs from the verb spring meaning sprout and from the seasonal noun.

originalSense.definition: A shoot, a young tree.

definition: A grove of trees or a forest.
example: The preserved source gloss records spring as a grove or forest.
distinctions: This recorded noun names an area of trees. It should not be inferred from every place name ending in Spring or Springs.
usage: Less familiar wooded-area sense; lexicographical reading note.

originalSense.definition: A grove of trees; a forest.

definition: A group of teal.
example: The preserved wildfowling accounts use a spring of teal for a group of those birds.
distinctions: This traditional collective name concerns the birds as a group. It does not state that they are present in the season spring or all jumping at once.

originalSense.definition: A group of teal.

definition: Elasticity: the ability to return toward the original form after deformation.
example: The spring in the cushion helped it recover its shape after the weight was removed.
distinctions: This names a property of resilience, rather than a separate coil component. Recovery occurs within the material’s limits; not every deformation is reversible.

originalSense.definition: Elasticity: the property of a body springing back to its original form after compression, stretching, etc.

distinctionTask.prompt: A cushion recovering its shape shows _____.
options: that force and energy have identical units
distinctionTask.explanation: This spring is a material property.

definition: Force, vigour or energy associated with springing movement.
example: In Dryden’s phrase what a spring was in his arm, spring conveys the force or vigour of the movement.
distinctions: The older source groups energy, power and force as loose senses. In physics these are different quantities: energy in joules, power in watts and force in newtons; do not use them as interchangeable units.
usage: Often older or literary; contextual reading.

originalSense.definition: Elastic energy, power, or force.

definition: A cause or motive that prompts action.
example: In the preserved prologue, vulgar springs are the ordinary motives used to move the characters.
distinctions: This spring prompts behaviour. It is figurative and differs from the literal elastic component that can move a mechanism.

originalSense.definition: A cause, a motive, etc.

definition: In obsolete musical use, a lively piece of music.
example: In the preserved ballad, the first spring the fiddle played means the first lively tune it played.
collocations: a spring played on a fiddle
distinctions: This is a historical tune-name sense. It does not identify a spring fitted inside the instrument or a season when the tune was played.

originalSense.definition: A lively piece of music.

definition: To hold something up or help keep it from falling.
example: Two columns support the balcony.
distinctions: The subject holds up the object. Supporting an opinion or providing evidence uses a different, figurative sense.

originalSense.definition: To help keep from falling.
originalSense.example: Don’t move that beam! It supports the whole platform.

distinctionTask.prompt: The columns hold the balcony up: they _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: This selected meaning is physical holding up.

definition: To favour or back a person, cause, group or proposal.
example: Most residents support the plan for a new park.
distinctions: This expresses approval or backing. It does not by itself prove that the proposal is correct or identify a financial payment.

originalSense.definition: To back or favor a cause, party, etc., mentally or with concrete aid
originalSense.example: I support France in the World Cup.

distinctionTask.prompt: Residents favour the park proposal: they _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: Supporting a proposal expresses backing, without establishing proof.

definition: To provide what someone or something needs to live or continue.
example: These small farms support four families.
distinctions: Here support concerns maintaining a livelihood or existence. A structure supporting weight instead holds something up physically.

originalSense.definition: To provide sustenance or maintenance for; to sustain in integrity or livelihood.
originalSense.example: Mars does not currently support human habitation.

definition: To help someone or something financially, including through a subsidy.
example: Local grants support the community theatre.
distinctions: Financial assistance is explicit in this sense. Simply saying that someone supports a cause can instead describe agreement without a payment.

originalSense.definition: To help, particularly financially; to subsidize.
originalSense.example: The government supports the arts in several ways.

distinctionTask.prompt: The grant pays part of the theatre’s costs: it provides _____ support.
distinctionTask.explanation: Money makes the kind of assistance financial.

definition: To provide evidence for a statement or explanation.
example: The new measurements support the proposed explanation.
distinctions: Evidence can strengthen a claim without proving it conclusively. The sentence does not describe a beam holding up a physical object.

originalSense.definition: To provide evidence for; to lend credibility to.
originalSense.example: The testimony is not sufficient to support the charges.

distinctionTask.prompt: Measurements lend credibility to the explanation: they _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: Support can strengthen an explanation without proving it conclusively.

definition: To provide a service or assistance to an organisation or its users.
example: Our IT teams support staff at both campuses.
distinctions: The team supplies assistance to the people or organisation. Device support can instead describe a product’s technical compatibility.

originalSense.definition: To serve, as in a customer-oriented position; to give support to.
originalSense.example: The IT Department supports the research organization, but not the sales force.

definition: To assist with an activity without having primary responsibility for it.
example: I support the coordinator by arranging meeting rooms.
distinctions: The person contributes to the activity. Supporting its coordinator does not make that person the lead decision-maker.

originalSense.definition: To assist or be involved with, but not be responsible for.
originalSense.example: I support the administrative activities of the executive branch of the organization.

distinctionTask.prompt: An assistant helps the coordinator but does not lead: the assistant _____ the coordinator.
distinctionTask.explanation: Supporting the lead describes an assisting role.

definition: To answer users’ questions and resolve problems with a product.
example: The supplier continues to support the old model and answer users’ technical questions.
distinctions: The supplier provides help with use and problems. A device supports a file format instead describes compatibility.

originalSense.definition: To answer questions and resolve problems regarding something sold.
originalSense.example: Sure they sell the product, but do they support it?

definition: To have the capacity or compatibility needed to use a feature, format or component.
example: Many readers support PDF files.
distinctions: This states a technical capability. It does not mean the manufacturer has promised continuing customer assistance or that every possible operation on that format is available.

originalSense.definition: To be designed to provide capacity for; to work or be compatible with (a part, accessory, file type, program, algorithm, etc.).
originalSense.example: Early personal computers did not support voice-recognition hardware or software.

distinctionTask.prompt: The reader can open this file format: it _____ PDF files.
distinctionTask.explanation: A product supporting a format concerns compatibility.

definition: (Archaic) To endure or tolerate something without being overcome.
example: In Dryden’s passage, patience that could not support insolence means patience that could not endure it.
collocations: support in the older endurance sense
distinctions: This older sense means bear or tolerate. It differs from approving the insolence or providing help to the person responsible.

originalSense.definition: To endure without being overcome; bear; undergo; tolerate.
originalSense.example: This fierce demeanour and his insolence / The patience of a god could not support.

definition: To perform a lesser role alongside a leading performer in a production.
example: Several young actors support the leading performer in the production.
distinctions: The performer acts alongside the lead in a subordinate role. Financially supporting a production is a separate use.

originalSense.definition: To play a lesser part in the same production with (a star performer).
originalSense.example: to support the character of King Lear

definition: Something that holds up or helps sustain another thing.
example: The shelf needs an extra support at its centre.
distinctions: Here the noun names the supporting thing. The broad definition remains a lexical sense rather than automatically becoming a source directory.

originalSense.definition: Something which supports.
originalSense.example: Don't move that beam! It's a support for the whole platform.

definition: Financial or other assistance.
example: The charity offers financial support to students.
distinctions: The kind of help depends on the phrase and context. Financial support is money; emotional support need not involve payment.

originalSense.definition: Financial or other help.
originalSense.example: The government provides support to the arts in several ways.

distinctionTask.prompt: The charity provides money to help students: it offers financial _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The context specifies monetary assistance.

definition: Help with questions or problems involving a product or service.
example: Contact technical support if you cannot reset your password.
distinctions: This can name the assistance or the service providing it. Software support for a format instead concerns capability or compatibility.

originalSense.definition: Answers to questions and resolution of problems regarding something sold.
originalSense.example: Sure they sell the product, but do they provide support?

distinctionTask.prompt: For help fixing an account problem, contact technical _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Technical support is help with use and problems.

definition: In mathematics, a function’s nonzero set, or, under another common convention, the closure of that set.
example: For a function equal to x(1 − x) on 0 < x < 1 and zero elsewhere, the nonzero set is (0, 1), while its closure is [0, 1].
distinctions: Specify the convention in use. Closing the nonzero set includes its boundary; it does not mean the function must take nonzero values at every point of that closed support.

originalSense.definition: in relation to a function, the set of points where the function is not zero; the closure of that set.

definition: In fuzzy-set theory, the ordinary set of elements whose membership grade in the fuzzy set is greater than zero.
example: If membership grades are μ(a) = 0, μ(b) = 0.3 and μ(c) = 1, the fuzzy set’s support is {b, c}.
collocations: the support of a fuzzy set
distinctions: Support includes partial and full membership but excludes zero membership. The support is an ordinary set; membership grades do not become equal merely because both elements belong to it.

originalSense.definition: A set whose elements are at least partially included in a given fuzzy set (i.e., whose grade of membership in that fuzzy set is strictly greater than zero).
originalSense.example: If the membership function of a fuzzy set is continuous, then that fuzzy set's support is an open set.

definition: For a module M over a commutative ring R, the prime ideals at which the localised module is nonzero.
example: The formula Supp_R(M) = {p ∈ Spec R : M_p ≠ 0} describes the module’s support.
distinctions: Here p denotes a prime ideal and M_p a localisation. This algebraic set is distinct from a function’s nonzero set and from evidence supporting an assertion.

originalSense.definition: The set of all prime ideals of R such that the localization of M at the prime is nonzero, denoted operatorname SuppM

definition: Evidence that strengthens a statement or explanation.
example: She supplied documentary support for her account of the event.
distinctions: The noun names supporting evidence. The evidence’s existence does not by itself establish that every part of the account is proven.

originalSense.definition: Evidence.
originalSense.example: The new research provides further support for our theory.

distinctionTask.prompt: Documents offered as evidence are documentary _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The documents are supporting evidence whose strength must still be assessed.

definition: Technical compatibility or functionality for a product or feature.
example: The application has support for offline storage.
distinctions: This concerns capability. Customer support instead concerns help with questions and problems; the phrases can refer to different services or properties.

originalSense.definition: Compatibility and functionality for a given product or feature.
originalSense.example: This game has no mouse support.

distinctionTask.prompt: The application can work offline: it has _____ for offline storage.
distinctionTask.explanation: This selected noun meaning concerns functionality.

definition: An actor performing a subordinate role alongside a leading actor.
example: In the preserved cinema gloss, a support means an actor playing a subordinate part with a star.
collocations: a support in the cinema gloss
distinctions: This noun names a performer rather than money, a physical prop or a technical help service. Supporting actor is the clearer ordinary phrase.

originalSense.definition: An actor playing a subordinate part with a star.

definition: An accompaniment in music.
example: The strings provided harmonic support for the melody.
distinctions: The accompaniment sustains or complements the musical line. This is not financial sponsorship of the performers.

originalSense.definition: An accompaniment in music.

definition: In gymnastics, a shortened form of support position.
example: The preserved gymnastics gloss uses support as a shortened name for a support position.
distinctions: This note identifies the source’s shortened expression. It does not equate every general movement described as supporting with the named gymnastics position.

originalSense.definition: Clipping of support position.
originalSense.example: Dip down as far as you are able, aiming to descend to the bottom of your sternum. Press back up to a support.

definition: In structural analysis, a restraint that limits specified translations or rotation of a structure.
example: The preserved structural glossary distinguishes movable, hinged and fixed supports.
distinctions: Support types are distinguished by which movements they restrain. The constraints depend on the model and dimensional assumptions; the glossary alone is not a complete engineering model.

originalSense.definition: Horizontal, vertical or rotational support of structures: movable, hinged, fixed.

definition: An upright piece of timber, metal or similar material set in the ground.
example: A wooden post holds up this section of fence.
collocations: set a post in the ground
distinctions: This is a physical upright. A job, a postal delivery and an online message are separate meanings.

originalSense.definition: A long dowel or plank protruding from the ground; a fencepost; a lightpost.
originalSense.example: ram a post into the ground

definition: A projecting terminal on a battery to which an electrical connection can be made.
example: The cable is attached to the positive battery post.
distinctions: Here post names the physical terminal. Positive identifies its polarity, not whether it is an online message.

originalSense.definition: A pole in a battery.

definition: In chiefly a cappella singing, a prolonged final melody note while the harmony notes change.
example: The preserved singing gloss calls the held final melody note a post while other voices move through changing harmony.
collocations: a post in a cappella singing
distinctions: The melody note is sustained while the harmony moves. This specialised noun does not name a postal service or a written notice.

originalSense.definition: A prolonged final melody note, among moving harmony notes.

definition: A traditional printing-paper size of 19.25 by 15.5 inches.
example: The preserved paper glossary gives post as 19.25 × 15.5 inches.
distinctions: These dimensions belong to the source’s named printing size. They are not the dimensions of every sheet suitable for postal delivery, nor an ISO A-series size.

originalSense.definition: A printing paper size measuring 19.25 inches x 15.5 inches.

definition: The vertical body of a crochet stitch.
example: The crochet gloss calls the vertical part of a stitch its post.
distinctions: The term identifies part of a stitch. It does not mean that a wooden upright is inserted into the fabric.

originalSense.definition: The vertical part of a crochet stitch.

definition: To display a notice where people can see it.
example: Please post the notice beside the entrance.
distinctions: This means display written information publicly. Sending a letter through the postal service is a different action.

originalSense.definition: To hang (a notice) in a conspicuous manner for general review.
originalSense.example: Post no bills.

distinctionTask.prompt: To display the notice where everyone can see it, _____ it beside the entrance.
options: send it through the postal service by fastening
distinctionTask.explanation: The selected verb means display a notice publicly.

definition: To announce or publish information, including a result.
example: The company expects to post a profit of £2 million.
distinctions: Posting a result means announcing or recording it publicly. The verb does not require a physical notice or an Internet forum.

originalSense.definition: To announce publicly; to publish.
originalSense.example: The company posted record profits this quarter.

distinctionTask.prompt: The company announced its result: it _____ a profit of £2 million.
distinctionTask.explanation: Here posted means announced or published a result.

definition: To denounce someone publicly or expose them to public reproach.
example: The source’s expression post someone for cowardice means publicly denounce that person as cowardly.
distinctions: This is the source’s older public-reproach use. It differs from assigning the person to a job or merely publishing a neutral message about them.

originalSense.definition: To hold up to public blame or reproach; to advertise opprobriously; to denounce by public proclamation.
originalSense.example: to post someone for cowardice

definition: To transfer an accounting entry from a journal to the appropriate ledger account.
example: The bookkeeper will post the journal entry to the ledger.
distinctions: The entry is recorded in the ledger. Posting is an accounting recording step; it does not itself establish that a bank payment has cleared.

originalSense.definition: To carry (an account) from the journal to the ledger.
originalSense.example: You have not poſted your Books theſe Ten years; hovv is it poſſible for a Man of Buſineſs to keep his Affairs even in the VVorld at this rate?

distinctionTask.prompt: Transfer the journal entry to the ledger: _____ the entry.
distinctionTask.explanation: This is the accounting recording step.

definition: To inform someone or make them acquainted with the details of a subject.
example: The source describes someone as posted up in the politics of the day: well informed about those politics.
distinctions: The preserved example uses posted up for being informed. Keep someone posted is a familiar related expression; neither describes physically fastening the person to a wall.
usage: Contextual reading; the source often uses up.

originalSense.definition: To inform; to give the news to; to make acquainted with the details of a subject; often with up.
originalSense.example: thoroughly posted up in the politics and literature of the day

definition: To deposit money or provide a payment, sometimes subject to conditions about its return.
example: The bidder had to post a deposit before the auction.
distinctions: Post describes providing the deposit or security. Whether it is returned depends on the arrangement; the verb does not promise a refund.

originalSense.definition: To deposit a payment that may or may not be returned.
originalSense.example: Since Jim was new to the game, he had to post $4 in order to receive a hand.

definition: Historically, a person stationed along a route to relay official letters and dispatches.
example: The source’s obsolete plural posts can mean the people ready at successive places to pass dispatches onward.
distinctions: This source meaning names the relay personnel. A post can separately name a station or a courier travelling with a message.

originalSense.definition: Each of a series of men stationed at specific places along a postroad, with responsibility for relaying letters and dispatches of the monarch (and later others) along the route.

definition: A station on an established route where travellers could obtain refreshments or accommodation.
example: The source’s phrase a stage or railway post names a station serving travellers along a route.
distinctions: This dated sense names a stopping place. It differs from a single upright pole and from the people who relay letters.

originalSense.definition: A station, or one of a series of stations, established for the refreshment and accommodation of travellers on some recognized route.
originalSense.example: a stage or railway post

definition: A military station or base, or the troops stationed there.
example: The soldiers returned to their military post.
distinctions: The context can identify the station or its garrison. A guard’s assigned position is a related, separately listed sense.

originalSense.definition: A military base; the place at which a soldier or a body of troops is stationed; also, the troops at such a station.
originalSense.example: September 6th.—The English mail of the 10th of July arrived to-day, and while Mr. Hart was at the Foreign Office engaged on business with Wan-se-ang and Hang-Ki, he received his Shang-hai letters, one of which contained the news of the recapture by the Imperial forces of the cities of Woo-tu and Nan-ching, two important rebel posts.

definition: Historically, a courier carrying letters or dispatches quickly along a fixed route.
example: In the preserved Shakespeare passage, a worthless post means the messenger carrying the writer’s lines.
distinctions: Here post names a travelling person. It is distinct from the station where a courier stops and from the letter being carried.

originalSense.definition: Someone who travels express along a set route carrying letters and dispatches; a courier.
originalSense.example:
I fear my Julia would not deign my lines,
Receiving them from such a worthless post.

definition: The organisation or service that delivers letters and parcels.
example: I sent the documents by post.
distinctions: This is the delivery service. The post can also mean the letters in a particular delivery; American English commonly uses mail.
usage: Especially British, Irish, Indian, Australian and New Zealand English.

originalSense.definition: An organisation for delivering letters, parcels etc., or the service provided by such an organisation.
originalSense.example: I sent a parcel via/by post.

distinctionTask.prompt: The documents were sent through the postal service: they went by _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: By post identifies the delivery service.

definition: A delivery or batch of letters and parcels.
example: The morning post included a letter from the college.
distinctions: Here post means delivered items or a delivery. By post usually describes the service used to send them.
usage: Especially British, Irish, Indian, Australian and New Zealand English.

originalSense.definition: A single delivery of letters; the letters or deliveries that make up a single batch delivered to one person or one address.
originalSense.example: Royal Mail worker Evette Chapman gathered a team of 12 colleagues to deliver post in fancy dress and raise money for a nurses' charity and patients in Musgrove Park Hospital, Taunton.

distinctionTask.prompt: The letters delivered this morning are the morning _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This noun names the delivery or its contents.

definition: A message or item published on an Internet forum, blog or similar service.
example: Her latest blog post explains how to grow tomatoes.
distinctions: The noun names the published item. To post a message is the related verb, and a physical notice is a separate use.

originalSense.definition: A message posted in an electronic or Internet forum, or on a blog, etc.
originalSense.example: Oli conceded defeat and, in a post on X Saturday, congratulated Shah. “Balen Babu, Congratulations to you for the victory! May your five-year tenure be smooth and successful—heartfelt best wishes!”

distinctionTask.prompt: An item published on a blog is a blog _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The selected noun names an online item.

definition: In American football, a receiving route that first goes downfield and then cuts inward towards the goalposts.
example: The source describes a post route as a downfield run followed by a cut towards the middle, typically around 45 degrees.
distinctions: The route name describes the receiver’s path. The source’s distance and angle are typical descriptions, not a compulsory geometry for every play.

originalSense.definition: A moderate to deep passing route in which a receiver runs 10-20 yards from the line of scrimmage straight down the field, then cuts toward the middle of the field (towards the facing goalposts) at a 45-degree angle.
originalSense.example: Two of the receivers ran post patterns.

definition: In obsolete use, haste or speed associated with a messenger.
example: In the preserved Romeo and Juliet passage, in post means in haste.
distinctions: This noun describes haste. It is not the ordinary modern instruction to put something in the post.

originalSense.definition: Haste or speed, like that of a messenger or mail carrier.
originalSense.example: And then in post he came from Mantua.

definition: In obsolete use, a person in charge of a station, especially a postal station.
example: The source’s obsolete station-manager gloss uses post for the person responsible for that station.
collocations: a post in charge of a station
distinctions: This names the person in charge. A courier and an assigned station are separate source senses.

originalSense.definition: One who has charge of a station, especially a postal station.
originalSense.example: there he held the office of postmaster, or, as it was then called, post, for several years.

definition: To travel using relays of horses changed along a route.
example: In the preserved Frankenstein passage, post the remainder of our way means continue the journey using post horses.
distinctions: This historical verb concerns changing horses along a journey. It does not mean sending the travellers as parcels.

originalSense.definition: To travel with relays of horses; to travel by post horses, originally as a courier.
originalSense.example: Beyond Cologne we descended to the plain of Holland; and we resolved to post the remainder of our way […].

definition: To travel quickly or hurry.
example: Shakespeare’s instruction Post speedily means hurry to the person addressed.
distinctions: This is the source’s rapid-travel sense. Modern everyday English normally uses hurry or travel quickly.

originalSense.definition: To travel quickly; to hurry.
originalSense.example: Post speedily to my lord your husband.

definition: To send a letter or parcel through the postal service.
example: I need to post the application today.
distinctions: This concerns postal delivery. Posting an application online instead uses the publishing or uploading sense.
usage: Especially British, Irish, Indian, Australian and New Zealand English.

originalSense.definition: To send (an item of mail etc.) through the postal service.
originalSense.example: Mail items posted before 7.00pm within the Central Business District and before 5.00pm outside the Central Business District will be delivered the next working day.

distinctionTask.prompt: To send the letter through the postal service, _____ it.
options: publish it on a forum by definition
distinctionTask.explanation: This selected verb concerns physical mail.

definition: To rise and sit rhythmically in the saddle in time with a horse’s movement, especially at a trot.
example: The riding gloss uses post for the rider’s rhythmic rising and sitting during a trot.
collocations: rise and sit in the saddle
distinctions: This names the rider’s movement. It is separate from travelling between stations on relays of post horses.

originalSense.definition: To rise and sink in the saddle, in accordance with the motion of the horse, especially in trotting.

definition: To publish a message on an Internet service.
example: She plans to post a question on the forum.
distinctions: This verb describes publishing the message. A post is the resulting item; sending a physical letter is another sense.

originalSense.definition: To publish (a message) to a newsgroup, forum, blog, etc.
originalSense.example: I couldn't figure it out, so I posted a question on the mailing list.

distinctionTask.prompt: To publish a question on the forum, _____ it.
distinctionTask.explanation: This selected verb concerns online publication.

definition: By a relay of horses and, by extension, rapidly or express.
example: In the preserved Austen passage, travel Post describes continuing the journey with changes of horses.
distinctions: This historical adverb modifies how someone travels. It differs grammatically from the noun in a fence post.

originalSense.definition: With the post, on post-horses; by a relay of horses (changing at every staging-post); hence, express, with speed, quickly.
originalSense.example: His highness comes post from Marseilles,

definition: By the postal service.
example: The source lists an adverbial post meaning sent through the postal service.
distinctions: This identifies the preserved grammatical use. The clearer everyday phrase by post uses post as a noun after by.

originalSense.definition: Sent via the postal service.

definition: An assigned place of duty, especially a guard’s station.
example: The guard remained at her post beside the gate.
distinctions: The post is the assigned place of duty. A job title or appointment is a separate sense.

originalSense.definition: An assigned station; a guard post.
originalSense.example: From the ground, Colombo’s port does not look like much. Those entering it are greeted by wire fences, walls dating back to colonial times and security posts. For mariners leaving the port after lonely nights on the high seas, the delights of the B52 Night Club and Stallion Pub lie a stumble away.

distinctionTask.prompt: The guard’s assigned place of duty is her _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: A post can be the place where a guard is assigned to stand.

definition: An appointed job or position in an organisation.
example: She applied for the post of research assistant.
distinctions: Here post means a job or appointment. It is distinct from a message on a website and from the physical place where a guard stands.

originalSense.definition: An appointed position in an organization, job.
originalSense.example: As hard as this may seem for some people to understand, my adamant stand in favor of President Clinton leaving his post was not personal.

distinctionTask.prompt: An appointed job as research assistant is a _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Here post means an organisational appointment.

definition: To enter a person’s name on a list, for example for service or promotion.
example: The source’s listing gloss uses post a name for entering it on a service or promotion list.
collocations: post a name on a list
distinctions: This names entering the name, not necessarily completing the appointment or publishing the list to everyone.

originalSense.definition: To enter (a name) on a list, as for service, promotion, etc.

definition: To assign someone to a station or position.
example: They will post a guard at the entrance.
distinctions: The person is assigned to a place of duty. Posting a notice at the entrance means displaying written information instead.

originalSense.definition: To assign to a station; to set; to place.
originalSense.example: Post a sentinel in front of the door.

distinctionTask.prompt: To assign a guard to the entrance, _____ a guard there.
options: paste a written notice instead of
distinctionTask.explanation: This verb assigns a person to a station.

definition: After a specified date, event or period.
example: The manuscript must have been written post 1327.
distinctions: As a separate preposition, post means after. The sentence sets a lower time boundary and does not give an exact composition date.

originalSense.definition: Synonym of after, particularly used with historical dating.
originalSense.example: The chronicle mentions the defenestration of the local bishop, indicating a composition sometime post 1327.

distinctionTask.prompt: Written post 1327 means written _____ 1327.
distinctionTask.explanation: Post supplies an after-boundary, not an exact year.

definition: Informally, post-production work on a film or recording.
example: They corrected the colour in post.
distinctions: This shortened noun refers to work after filming or recording. It does not mean that every problem can be corrected at that stage.

originalSense.definition: Post-production.
originalSense.example: We'll fix it in post.

distinctionTask.prompt: Film colour correction done in post happens during _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This informal noun shortens post-production.

definition: Informally, a post-mortem examination to investigate a body’s cause of death.
example: In the source’s morgue passage, do a post means perform a post-mortem examination.
distinctions: The medical context identifies the shortened expression. It is distinct from film post-production and an online post.

originalSense.definition: A post mortem (an investigation of a body's cause of death).
originalSense.example: I gotta run. Yes, send the kid to the morgue. We'll do a post on Monday.

definition: POST: power-on self-test, a computer’s startup diagnostic checks.
example: The capitalised source entry expands POST as power-on self-test.
distinctions: The acronym identifies startup checks. Passing POST does not by itself establish that the operating system will load or that every component works correctly.

originalSense.definition: Acronym of power-on self-test.

definition: Of a computer, to complete its power-on self-test successfully.
example: The source’s computing verb POST means successfully perform the power-on self-test.
distinctions: This is successful completion of startup checks. It is distinct from publishing a message and does not guarantee successful operating-system startup.

originalSense.definition: To successfully perform a power-on self-test.
originalSense.example: The computer had a bunch of strange components, but it still POSTed so I assumed everything worked.

definition: Post as part of the name of a newspaper or periodical.
example: The Washington Post and the New York Post use Post in their newspaper names.
distinctions: The capitalised word belongs to a title. It does not mean that each newspaper article is a postal delivery.

originalSense.definition: A common name (often in combination) for a newspaper or periodical, such as The Washington Post or the New York Post.

definition: Post as a surname.
example: The preserved capitalised entry lists Post as a family name.
distinctions: This is a surname. Its appearance alone does not identify a particular person or imply a job in the postal service.

originalSense.definition: A surname.

definition: Post as the name of a village in Iran.
example: The preserved capitalised place entry identifies a village in Iran named Post.
distinctions: This source record identifies a place. The short gloss does not establish a province or coordinates, which are not supplied here.

originalSense.definition: A village in Iran.

definition: Post, an unincorporated community in Crook County, Oregon.
example: The preserved place entry identifies Post in Crook County, Oregon, and gives Walter H. Post as its namesake.
distinctions: This Oregon place is distinct from the city of Post in Texas. The preserved source describes it as an unincorporated community.

originalSense.definition: An unincorporated community in Crook County, Oregon, named after Walter H. Post.

definition: Post, a city and the county seat of Garza County, Texas.
example: The preserved place entry identifies Post in Garza County, Texas, and names C. W. Post as its namesake.
collocations: the county seat of Garza County
distinctions: This Texas city is distinct from the Oregon community and the source’s village in Iran.

originalSense.definition: A city, the county seat of Garza County, Texas, named after C. W. Post.

definition: A pole erected to mark a particular place or boundary.
example: A post marks the boundary of the property.
distinctions: This post marks a location. A fence post may also support fencing, but marking and supporting are distinct functions.

originalSense.definition: A pole erected to mark a spot.

definition: A stake marking the start or finish of a horse race.
example: The source’s racing gloss uses post for the stakes at the beginning or end of a race.
distinctions: This is a race marker. The finishing post is not an online result announcement, even though the race result may later be posted.

originalSense.definition: The stakes that mark the beginning or end of a horse race

definition: In obsolete use, an inn doorpost on which customers’ debts were marked, and by extension the account or debt.
example: In the preserved Rowlands passage, discharge your poast concerns settling the debt.
collocations: chalk a score on the post
distinctions: The gloss links a physical tally location to the account or debt recorded there; the quoted poast is an older spelling in that passage. It is not a modern postal bill.

originalSense.definition: The doorpost of a victualler's shop or inn, on which were chalked the scores of customers; hence, a score; a debt.

definition: A goalpost.
example: The shot hit the post and rebounded into play.
distinctions: Post names part of the goal structure. Hitting it does not by itself mean a goal was scored.

originalSense.definition: A goalpost.

distinctionTask.prompt: The ball struck the goal frame’s upright: it hit the _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This selected noun means goalpost.

definition: A narrow component inserted into a tooth’s root canal to help retain a crown restoration.
example: The dental gloss describes a post placed in a root canal to provide retention for a crown.
distinctions: This describes a restorative component. It does not imply that every root-treated tooth needs a post or that the post strengthens the root.

originalSense.definition: A long, narrow piece inserted into a root canal to provide retention for a crown.

definition: In the source’s construction use, a stud or a two-by-four.
example: The construction gloss lists post as a stud or two-by-four.
collocations: a post in the construction gloss
distinctions: This identifies the source’s construction use. Two-by-four is a nominal lumber name; the gloss does not establish exact finished dimensions or a universal structural role.

originalSense.definition: A stud; a two-by-four.

definition: The slender metal stem of an earring.
example: The earring gloss calls its wire-like metal core a post.
collocations: the metal stem of an earring
distinctions: This post is part of the jewellery. It is distinct from the earring’s decorative front and from a fence upright.

originalSense.definition: The wire-like core of metal in an earring.

definition: In gambling, to put up a required stake or blind.
example: The new player must post the required blind before receiving a hand.
distinctions: Posting a blind supplies a required wager. It does not mean the player has won or is guaranteed to recover that money.

originalSense.definition: To pay (a stake or blind).

distinctionTask.prompt: Before receiving a hand, the player must _____ the required blind.
distinctionTask.explanation: Posting supplies the required stake; it does not guarantee a return.

definition: To provide bail or the required security for it.
example: The source’s expression post bail concerns supplying the required bail payment or security.
distinctions: This concerns security for release under the applicable process. It is not a finding of innocence; the form, conditions and return of funds depend on the jurisdiction and arrangement.

originalSense.definition: To pay bail.

definition: A drawing or diagram that conveys information.
example: Figure 2 shows the parts of the flower.
distinctions: In a report, figure names an illustration or diagram. It need not be a numerical amount; table and figure may be separately numbered.

originalSense.definition: A drawing or diagram conveying information.
originalSense.example: For example, while Figure 1 shows information for 516 visitor groups, Figure 3 presents data for 1,625 individuals. A note above each graph or table specifies the information illustrated. ... For example, although Joshua Tree NP visitors returned 525 questionnaires, Figure 1 shows data for only 516 respondents.

distinctionTask.prompt: The labelled illustration in the report is referred to as _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: In this selected meaning, figure names an information diagram.

definition: A representation of a form, especially a human body, in art.
example: The painting contains a small human figure.
distinctions: The figures are representations within the artwork. They are distinct from the actual people and from the numbered diagram sense.

originalSense.definition: The representation of any form, as by drawing, painting, modelling, carving, embroidering, etc.; especially, a representation of the human body.
originalSense.example: a figure in bronze; a figure cut in marble

definition: A person, thing or action that represents or stands for something else.
example: The campaign used the worker as a symbolic figure of resilience.
distinctions: The context gives the representative role. A person being a figure does not imply that the person is physically a drawing.

originalSense.definition: A person, thing, or action representative of another
originalSense.example: Seeing the British establishment struggle with the financial sector is like watching an alcoholic […]. Until 2008 there was denial over what finance had become. When a series of bank failures made this impossible, there was widespread anger, leading to the public humiliation of symbolic figures.

definition: The impression someone makes through their appearance, conduct or public role.
example: He cut a confident figure at the ceremony.
distinctions: Cut a figure concerns the impression made. It does not literally describe cutting a diagram or calculating a number.

originalSense.definition: The appearance or impression made by the conduct or career of a person.
originalSense.example: He cut a sorry figure standing there in the rain.

distinctionTask.prompt: He made a confident impression: he cut a confident _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Cut a figure describes an impression.

definition: In obsolete use, distinguished appearance, magnificence or show.
example: The source’s obsolete gloss uses figure for impressive outward display or splendour.
collocations: figure in the obsolete display sense
distinctions: This is the source’s older display meaning. It should not be substituted automatically for an ordinary number or report diagram.

originalSense.definition: Distinguished appearance; magnificence; conspicuous representation; splendour; show.
originalSense.example: that he may live in figure and indulgence

definition: The shape of a person’s body.
example: The tailor adjusted the jacket to fit his figure.
distinctions: Here figure describes body shape. It is separate from the impression described by cut a confident figure.

originalSense.definition: A human figure, which dress or corset must fit to; the shape of a human body.
originalSense.example: The origin of the corset is lost in remote antiquity. The figures of the early Egyptian women show clearly an artificial shape of the waist produced by some style of corset.

definition: A written numeral or numerical character.
example: Write the figure 8 clearly on the form.
distinctions: This concerns numerical notation. In the amount 507, the three decimal digits are figures; the whole amount is also a figure in another sense.
