definition: Evidence or demonstration taken as establishing a fact or truth.
example: The missing signature is not proof that the document is a forgery.
distinctions: Proof is stronger than mere supporting evidence in this meaning, but what establishes a claim depends on the context and standard. A missing signature alone need not establish forgery. Ordinary conclusive proof is uncountable.

originalSense.definition: The degree of evidence which convinces the mind of any truth or fact, and produces belief; a test by facts or arguments which induce, or tend to induce, certainty of the judgment; conclusive evidence; demonstration.
originalSense.example: I'll have some proof.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: The missing signature is not proof of forgery. This says _____.
options: that fact alone does not establish forgery
the document has been conclusively shown genuine
distinctionTask.answer: that fact alone does not establish forgery
distinctionTask.explanation: Lack of proof for one claim does not prove its opposite.

definition: The quality of having been tested and resisting force or impression.
example: In this physical-quality meaning, proof concerns tested firmness or resistance, rather than a logical demonstration.
distinctions: The source preserves a physical quality. Do not infer complete resistance to every force or use it as a modern engineering rating without specified test conditions.

originalSense.definition: The quality or state of having been proved or tried; firmness or hardness which resists impression, or does not yield to force; impenetrability of physical bodies.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: An obsolete meaning: experience of something.
example: In the older quotation, proof refers to experience, not a printing sheet or an argument establishing a theorem.
distinctions: The source marks the experience meaning obsolete. Modern proof of experience would usually mean evidence that someone has experience, a different construction.

originalSense.definition: Experience of something.
originalSense.example: But the chaste damzell, that had never priefe / Of such malengine and fine forgerye, / Did easely beleeve her strong extremitye.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: An obsolete meaning: firmness of mind or unshakable resolve.
example: This older proof describes firmness of mind, rather than evidence supporting a belief.
distinctions: The source marks this mental-firmness meaning obsolete. Firm conviction is not itself proof that a belief is true.

originalSense.definition: Firmness of mind; stability not to be shaken.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: A trial printed impression or sheet used for checking and correction.
example: The editor marked a spelling error on the proof before publication.
distinctions: A printing proof is a version for checking. It can contain errors and is separate from conclusive evidence or the final published copy.

originalSense.definition: A proof sheet; a trial impression, as from type, taken for correction or examination.
originalSense.example: And these men scour the printed proof for error, blunder, and misspelling.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: The editor corrects a printing proof. The proof is _____.
options: a trial version that may contain errors
distinctionTask.answer: a trial version that may contain errors
distinctionTask.explanation: A printing proof is made for examination and correction.

definition: A specially made, high-quality coin strike, now commonly produced for collectors.
example: The collector examined a proof from the new coin set.
distinctions: Proof describes the special method or quality of the strike. It does not inherently mean the coin has circulated, is unique, or will increase in financial value.

originalSense.definition: A limited-run high-quality strike of a particular coin, originally as a test run, although nowadays mostly for collectors' sets.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: A proof in a collectors’ coin set is _____.
options: necessarily a coin worn by circulation
distinctionTask.explanation: Proof concerns the special strike; circulation and value require separate information.

definition: A logical sequence from stated premises to the proposition being established.
example: For any integer n, 2n is divisible by 2; this is a proof that 2n is even.
distinctions: The definition of even is divisibility by 2. The premise that n is an integer supplies the needed domain. One example such as n = 3 alone would not prove the claim for every integer.

originalSense.definition: A sequence of statements consisting of axioms, assumptions, statements already demonstrated in another proof, and statements that logically follow from previous statements in the sequence, and which concludes with a statement that is the object of the proof.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: For every integer n, 2n is divisible by 2. The proof that 2n is even uses _____.
options: the definition of even and the stated integer domain
only a numerical check at n = 3
distinctionTask.answer: the definition of even and the stated integer domain
distinctionTask.explanation: A general proof applies to every integer in the stated domain.

definition: A check on the accuracy of a performed arithmetic operation.
example: After 48 ÷ 6 = 8, multiplying 8 by 6 gives 48 as a proof of the division.
distinctions: This checks the stated division by reversing it with multiplication. It does not by itself prove the correctness of every division algorithm or every calculation.

originalSense.definition: A process for testing the accuracy of an operation performed. Compare prove, transitive verb, 5.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: Checking 48 ÷ 6 = 8 by 8 × 6 = 48 checks _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: An inverse-operation check has a limited stated scope.

definition: An obsolete meaning: armour of tested quality, considered resistant to penetration.
example: In older writing, lapped in proof describes someone clothed in armour of tried quality.
distinctions: The source marks this armour noun obsolete. The historical judgement does not establish resistance to every weapon or modern ballistic certification.

originalSense.definition: Armour of excellent or tried quality, and deemed impenetrable; properly, armour of proof.
originalSense.example: Till that Bellona's bridegroom, lapped in proof
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: An alcohol-strength scale: in the United States, twice the alcohol percentage by volume.
example: On the US scale, 80 proof corresponds to 40% alcohol by volume.
distinctions: US proof is twice ABV. The historical British scale was different: 100 proof was about 57.1% ABV. Do not read 80 proof as 80% ABV or combine the two scales.
usage: US scale; historical British scale retained for comparison.

originalSense.definition: A measure of the alcohol content of liquor. Originally, in Britain, 100 proof was defined as 57.1% by volume (no longer used). In the US, 100 proof means that the alcohol content is 50% of the total volume of the liquid; thus, perfectly pure absolute alcohol would be 200 proof.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: A spirit labelled 80 proof on the US scale has _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: US proof is twice the alcohol percentage by volume.

definition: Used for testing or proving something.
example: The laboratory applied a proof load during the structural test.
distinctions: Proof modifies load: the load is used in a test. The phrase alone supplies no load value, safety factor, test result or rating for later use.

originalSense.definition: Used in proving or testing.
originalSense.example: a proof load; a proof charge
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: In proof load, proof describes _____.
options: the conclusive result of a test that always passed
distinctionTask.explanation: The adjective describes use; no result follows from the label.

definition: Resistant to the specified harm or influence.
example: She seemed proof against flattery.
distinctions: Proof against names resistance to the specified influence. Here seemed makes it an impression, and it does not mean she is resistant to every influence or that a belief is logically proved.

originalSense.definition: Firm or successful in resisting.
originalSense.example: proof against harm
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: She seemed proof against flattery means _____.
options: every claim she made was mathematically proved
distinctionTask.explanation: This adjective concerns resistance to a specified influence.

definition: Having a stated alcohol strength on a proof scale.
example: The US label describes the spirit as 80-proof.
distinctions: The adjectival number uses a proof scale, not a percentage sign. On the US scale 80-proof means 40% ABV. The historical British scale uses a different conversion.

originalSense.definition: Being of a certain standard as to alcohol content.
originalSense.example: 60% proof liquor
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: An 80-proof spirit on a US label uses _____.
options: a statement that 80% of the liquid is alcohol
distinctionTask.explanation: A proof number is not the same as the ABV percentage.

definition: To read and check text for errors; to proofread.
example: Please proof the final page before it is printed.
distinctions: Proof means check the text here. It does not certify that every factual claim is true or refer to making a material resistant to water.

originalSense.definition: To proofread.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: Please proof the page asks someone to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The text context selects the proofreading verb.

definition: To make something resistant, especially to water.
example: The treatment is intended to proof the fabric against water.
distinctions: Proof is a treatment verb here, not proofreading. Intended to does not establish that the treatment worked, and actual resistance depends on the material and conditions.

originalSense.definition: To make resistant, especially to water.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: A treatment intended to proof fabric against water aims to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The material and water context select the resistance-treatment verb.

definition: To subject a firearm to a specialised high-pressure test to establish its resistance to service pressures.
example: In firearms terminology, proof names a specialised pressure test rather than a routine accuracy test.
distinctions: This source meaning concerns testing resistance to pressure. It does not establish aim accuracy, the absence of every defect, or unlimited resistance under all conditions.

originalSense.definition: To test-fire with a load considerably more powerful than the firearm in question's rated maximum chamber pressure, in order to establish the firearm's ability to withstand pressures well in excess of those expected in service without bursting.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: To allow yeast-containing dough to rise, especially after shaping.
example: The baker will proof the shaped rolls before baking.
distinctions: This baking verb concerns dough rising. It differs from testing yeast activity, even though active yeast contributes to the rise; timing depends on the recipe and conditions.

originalSense.definition: To allow (yeast-containing dough) to rise, especially after it has been shaped
originalSense.example: dough proofing
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: Proof the shaped rolls asks for _____.
options: a separate test of yeast before any dough exists
distinctionTask.explanation: Dough rising and a yeast-activity test are separate baking uses.

definition: To test whether yeast is active.
example: The baker will proof the yeast before mixing the dough.
distinctions: Testing yeast activity and allowing shaped dough to rise are separate operations. The sentence gives no universal requirement to test every yeast product or a particular method or temperature.

originalSense.definition: To test the activeness of (yeast).
originalSense.example: yeast proofing
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

distinctionTask.prompt: Proof the yeast before mixing the dough means _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The object yeast selects the activity-test meaning.

definition: Proof: the English title of the 98th sura, or chapter, of the Qur’an.
example: Capitalised Proof names the 98th chapter of the Qur’an in this source entry.
distinctions: This proper name retains the capitalised source identity. It is separate from lowercase proof meaning conclusive evidence and is not an assertion about the truth of a particular argument.

originalSense.definition: The 98th sura (chapter) of the Qur'an.
wordFamily: the proof of the pudding is in the eating

definition: A process of reasoning or argumentation.
example: Through careful argument, she challenged the proposed rule.
distinctions: This meaning concerns reasoning as a process. A challenge need not be angry, and the existence of a line of argument does not establish that it is sound or persuasive.

originalSense.definition: A process of reasoning; argumentation.
originalSense.example: Indeed, I cannot commend my life; for I am conſcious to my ſelf of many failings: therein, I know alſo that a man by his converſation, may ſoon overthrow what by argument or perſwaſion he doth labour to faſten upon others for their good: […]

distinctionTask.prompt: Careful argument used to challenge a rule refers to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Reasoning and quarrelling are separate meanings.

definition: A prefatory summary of a literary work or section; figuratively, its contents.
example: A literary argument can be a summary printed before a poem or chapter; the source also records a figurative extension to the contents themselves.
distinctions: The literary summary is separate from a disagreement or a logical reason. The figurative extension is retained within this source record rather than silently removed.

originalSense.definition: An abstract or summary of the content of a literary work such as a book, a poem or a major section such as a chapter, included in the work before the content itself; (figuratively) the contents themselves.
originalSense.example: If I would broach the veſſels of my loue, / And try the argument of hearts, by borrowing, / Men, and mens fortunes, could I frankely vſe / As I can bid thee ſpeake.

definition: A verbal disagreement or quarrel.
example: They had an argument about where to park.
distinctions: This sense concerns disagreement between people. It is different from an argument for a policy, which may simply be a reason; a verbal argument need not become physical.

originalSense.definition: A verbal dispute; a quarrel.
originalSense.example: The neighbours got into an argument about the branches of the trees that extended over the fence.

distinctionTask.prompt: They had an argument about parking means they _____.
options: supplied a value to a mathematical function
distinctionTask.explanation: The people and disagreement context select the quarrel meaning.

definition: By humorous or euphemistic extension, a dispute, altercation or collision.
example: The report jokingly called the van’s collision with a bollard an argument.
distinctions: The source allows a jocular or euphemistic extension beyond words. The bollard does not literally speak, and the wording should not conceal whether an actual collision occurred.

originalSense.definition: Any dispute, altercation, or collision.
originalSense.example: Steve got in a physical argument with his neighbor and came away with a black eye.

distinctionTask.prompt: Calling a van’s collision with a bollard an argument is _____.
options: a jocular extension beyond a verbal disagreement
a literal conversation between the van and bollard
distinctionTask.answer: a jocular extension beyond a verbal disagreement
distinctionTask.explanation: The source preserves humorous and euphemistic extensions.

definition: In linguistics, a phrase syntactically connected to a clause’s verb as an argument.
example: In “Maya opened the door”, the phrase “the door” is an argument of “opened”.
distinctions: In this English example, the door is an object argument, while an added yesterday is a time adjunct. Arguments are not defined simply as every nearby word or every phrase that cannot be omitted. Analyses and constructions vary.

originalSense.definition: Any of the phrases that bear a syntactic connection to the verb of a clause.
originalSense.example: In numerous works over the past two decades, beginning with the pioneering work of Gruber (1965), Fillmore (1968a), and Jackendoff (1972), it has been argued that each Argument (i.e. Subject or Complement) of a Predicate bears a particular thematic role (alias theta-role, or θ-role to its Predicate), and that the set of thematic functions which Arguments can fulfil are drawn from a highly restricted, finite, universal set.

distinctionTask.prompt: In Maya opened the door yesterday, the door is an object argument, while yesterday is _____.
options: a time adjunct in this example
another object argument merely because it is nearby
distinctionTask.answer: a time adjunct in this example
distinctionTask.explanation: Syntactic role, rather than proximity, distinguishes this example.

definition: The independent variable of a function.
example: In f(x) = x², x is the argument of f.
distinctions: The argument supplies the function’s input. It differs from the output f(x); at x = 3 the input is 3 and the output is 9. This mathematical use need not involve a software function call.

originalSense.definition: The independent variable of a function.

distinctionTask.prompt: In f(x) = x² at x = 3, the argument value and output are _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The argument is the input; f(3) is the output.

definition: The phase angle of a complex number.
example: The complex number 1 + i has principal argument π/4 radians.
distinctions: The modulus of 1 + i is √2, not π/4. Its arguments differ by integer multiples of 2π; a principal argument selects a branch convention. Zero has no defined argument.

originalSense.definition: The phase of a complex number.

distinctionTask.prompt: For 1 + i, principal argument π/4 names _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Complex argument is phase angle, not magnitude.

definition: A quantity on which the calculation of another quantity depends.
example: In the refraction table, altitude is the argument used to look up the correction.
distinctions: The argument is the input used in the table or calculation, not the resulting correction. A table’s stated conditions matter; the wording alone gives no universal refraction formula.

originalSense.definition: A quantity on which the calculation of another quantity depends.
originalSense.example: The altitude is the argument of the refraction.

distinctionTask.prompt: Altitude used as an argument in a correction table is _____.
options: the input used to look up the correction
necessarily the correction returned by the table
distinctionTask.answer: the input used to look up the correction
distinctionTask.explanation: The argument is an input quantity.

definition: A value, or reference to a value, supplied to a function.
example: In the call square(3), 3 is the argument.
distinctions: In a definition such as square(x), x is a formal parameter; 3 is the argument supplied in the call. Languages differ in how values or references are passed.

originalSense.definition: A value, or a reference to a value, passed to a function.
originalSense.example: Parameters are like labelled fillable blanks used to define a function whereas arguments are passed to a function when calling it, filling in those blanks.

distinctionTask.prompt: Given definition square(x) and call square(3), the argument is _____.
options: 3, while x is a formal parameter
x, while 3 is the definition’s formal name
distinctionTask.answer: 3, while x is a formal parameter
distinctionTask.explanation: The roles are supplied argument and named formal parameter.

definition: An actual parameter supplied in a function call, rather than a formal parameter in its definition.
example: In add(2, 5), each supplied number is an argument, also called an actual parameter.
distinctions: If the definition is add(a, b), a and b are the formal parameters. The call supplies arguments 2 and 5. The older term actual parameter does not make the formal name and supplied value the same role.
usage: Programming; terminology overlaps with the value sense.

originalSense.definition: A parameter at a function call; an actual parameter, as opposed to a formal parameter.

distinctionTask.prompt: In add(2, 5), actual parameters are _____.
options: only the formal names in add(a, b)
distinctionTask.explanation: Actual parameter is an alternative term for a supplied argument.

definition: An obsolete meaning: the matter in question or business at hand.
example: In older writing, argument can name the matter being considered, rather than a quarrel or function input.
distinctions: This child meaning inherits the source’s obsolete heading. A modern reason supporting a proposition remains a separate use.

originalSense.definition: A matter in question; a business in hand.
originalSense.example:
As neere as I could ſift him on that argument,
 On ſome apparent danger ſeene in him,
 Aimde at your highnes, no inueterate malice.

definition: An obsolete meaning: the subject matter or theme of a work, discourse or representation.
example: In the older thematic use, argument names what a work or discourse is about.
distinctions: This thematic child inherits the source’s obsolete heading. It differs from the independently preserved literary prefatory summary.

originalSense.definition: The subject matter of an artistic representation, discourse, or writing; a theme or topic.
originalSense.example: [I]n vttering the ſtuffe ye receiued of the one, in declaring the order ye tooke with the other, ye ſhall neuer lacke, neither matter, nor maner, what to write, nor how to write in this kinde of Argument.

definition: An archaic meaning: evidence or proof, including a countable item of it.
example: In this older use, argument can mean evidence or proof; a particular item can be an argument.
distinctions: The source marks the broad use archaic and retains a countable item extension. Do not apply the countable grammar to ordinary uncountable evidence or treat every modern argument as conclusive proof.
usage: Archaic noun; countable item extension retained.

originalSense.definition: Evidence, proof; (countable) an item of such evidence or proof.
originalSense.example: [F]or louing me, by my troth it is no addition to her wit, nor no great argument of her follie, for I will be horribly in loue with her, […]

definition: To put forward an argument; to argue.
example: The source’s older verb argument describes arguing, rather than passing a software function an input.
distinctions: The source labels this intransitive verb obsolete and now nonstandard in some learner usage. Use argue in standard modern writing. Its label does not make the ordinary noun obsolete.
usage: Obsolete; now nonstandard in the source’s stated usage.

originalSense.definition: To put forward as an argument; to argue.
originalSense.example: [I]t is moſt certaine, that after Herodotus and other auncient writers, it is ſafer to call theſe [elephants' tusks] teeth, then hornes; and I will breefly ſet downe the reaſons of Philoſtratus, that will haue them to be teeth, and afterward of Grapaldus [i.e., Francesco Mario Grapaldi], Aelianus, and Pauſanias, that would make them horns, and ſo leaue the reader to conſider whether opinion he thinketh moſt agreeable to truth. […] Thus they argument for the horns of Elephants.

definition: An obsolete verb meaning: to adduce evidence or provide proof.
example: In the older source use, argument as a verb concerns providing evidence or proof.
distinctions: The source labels this intransitive verb obsolete. Keep it separate from both ordinary argue and the modern noun naming a reason or a function input.

originalSense.definition: To adduce evidence, to provide proof.
originalSense.example: Albeit that it apperteneth to the apoſtolis, be the puiſtoun of God to tak ordour in all materis off debait cõcernyng ye faith, & ſpecialie to iterprete ye ſcripturis, as yat quhilkis had yͤ ſpreit of god, & wer yͤ trew kirk: It argumẽtis [argumentis] not yat vtheris, quha hes ꝯuenit [conuenit] ſenſyne in generale ꝯſales [consales] had the ſpreit of GOD, or wer the trew kirk: […]

definition: In logic, premises arranged with a conclusion intended to follow from them.
example: All squares are rectangles; this figure is a square; therefore it is a rectangle: this is a valid argument.
distinctions: An argument can be invalid, or have false premises. Validity concerns whether the conclusion follows; soundness also requires true premises. The stated example uses the standard inclusive definition of rectangle.
usage: Logic and philosophy; restored child meaning.

originalSense.definition: A series of propositions organized so that the final proposition is a conclusion which is intended to follow logically from the preceding propositions, which function as premises.

distinctionTask.prompt: An argument is valid when _____.
options: its conclusion follows logically from its premises
every premise is guaranteed true merely by being written
distinctionTask.answer: its conclusion follows logically from its premises
distinctionTask.explanation: Validity concerns the logical relation; soundness additionally requires true premises.

definition: A belief, judgement or perspective formed about a topic, person or thing.
example: In my opinion, the revised plan is more practical.
distinctions: An opinion can be informed by evidence or reflect subjective judgement. Calling it an opinion does not by itself make it false, baseless or beyond criticism. An opinion is not automatically conclusive proof.
usage: Countable or uncountable according to construction.

originalSense.definition: A belief, judgment or perspective that a person has formed, either through objective or subjective reasoning, about a topic, issue, person or thing.
originalSense.example: I would like to know your opinions on the new filing system.

distinctionTask.prompt: An informed opinion can _____.
options: draw on evidence while remaining a judgement
distinctionTask.answer: draw on evidence while remaining a judgement
distinctionTask.explanation: An opinion may use objective or subjective reasoning.

definition: An estimation or judgement of a person or thing.
example: She has a high opinion of her new colleague.
distinctions: This estimation concerns how someone regards the colleague. It does not independently establish the colleague’s performance or concern the obsolete noun meaning public reputation itself.

originalSense.definition: The judgment or sentiment which the mind forms of persons or things; estimation.
originalSense.example: I haue bought / Golden Opinions from all ſorts of people, […]

distinctionTask.prompt: A high opinion of a colleague describes _____.
options: a favourable estimation of that person
independent proof of every claim the person makes
distinctionTask.answer: a favourable estimation of that person
distinctionTask.explanation: An estimation does not establish every external fact.

definition: An obsolete meaning: favourable reputation, public esteem or renown.
example: In older writing, losing one’s opinion can mean losing public esteem or reputation.
distinctions: The source marks this reputation meaning obsolete. It differs from changing one’s opinion in modern English, which usually means changing a belief or judgement.

originalSense.definition: Favorable estimation; hence, consideration; reputation; fame; public sentiment or esteem.
originalSense.example: Thou haſt redeemed thy loſt opinion, […]

definition: An obsolete meaning: obstinate or conceited adherence to one’s views.
example: In the older expression learned without opinion, opinion refers to conceited or obstinate attachment to one’s views.
distinctions: The source marks this meaning obsolete. Merely having or expressing a modern opinion does not imply obstinacy or conceit.

originalSense.definition: Obstinacy in holding to one's belief or impression; opiniativeness; conceitedness.
originalSense.example: […] your reaſons at Dinner haue been ſharpe & ſententious: pleaſant without ſcurillitie, wittie without affection, audatious without impudencie, learned without opinion, and ſtrange without hereſie: […]

definition: A formal decision or expression of views by someone officially asked to consider a matter.
example: The doctor gave a second opinion on the diagnosis.
distinctions: A professional opinion is more than an ordinary preference, but its authority and effect depend on the role and context. A medical opinion is not a court judgment; not every legal opinion is binding.

originalSense.definition: The formal decision, or expression of views, of a judge, an umpire, a doctor, or other party officially called upon to consider and decide upon a matter or point submitted.

distinctionTask.prompt: A second medical opinion is _____.
options: a professional assessment in its medical context
distinctionTask.answer: a professional assessment in its medical context
distinctionTask.explanation: The role and context determine the kind of formal opinion.

definition: In EU law, an Advocate General’s proposed legal solution in a case before the Court of Justice.
example: The Advocate General delivered an opinion proposing how the case should be resolved.
distinctions: The Advocate General independently proposes a solution. The opinion is not binding on the Court and is separate from its judgment. Not every case requires an Advocate General’s opinion.

originalSense.definition: A judicial opinion delivered by an Advocate General to the European Court of Justice where he or she proposes a legal solution to the cases for which the court is responsible.

distinctionTask.prompt: An Advocate General’s opinion before the Court of Justice is _____.
options: a proposed solution that does not bind the Court
the Court’s final binding judgment itself
distinctionTask.answer: a proposed solution that does not bind the Court
distinctionTask.explanation: The independent opinion and the Court’s judgment are distinct.

definition: An archaic verb meaning: to hold or express a view.
example: In older writing, the verb opinion can mean to hold or express a view; modern writing usually uses think, believe or opine.
distinctions: The source labels this transitive verb archaic. The ordinary noun opinion remains current; opine is a different modern verb form, not the same source identity.

originalSense.definition: To have or express as an opinion.
originalSense.example: Philoſophers that opinioned the vvorlds deſtruction by fire, did never dreame of annihilation, vvhich is beyond the povver of ſublunary cauſes; for the laſt and proper action of that element [fire] is but vitrification, or a reduction of a body into Glaſſe, and therefore ſome of our Chymicks factiouſly affirme; yea, and urge Scripture for it, that at the laſt fire all ſhall be cryſtallized and reverberated into Glaſſe, vvhich is the utmoſt action of that element.

definition: To review previously learned material, usually in preparation for an examination.
example: I study for the exam every evening.
distinctions: This use concerns revision of material already learned. Study can take an object such as the notes, or occur without one in study for an exam. Time spent revising does not guarantee a pass.
usage: Transitive or intransitive verb; academic revision.

originalSense.definition: To review materials already learned in order to make sure one does not forget them, usually in preparation for an examination.
originalSense.example: Students are expected to start studying for final exams in March.

distinctionTask.prompt: I study for the exam every evening describes _____.
options: a guarantee that the exam has been passed
distinctionTask.explanation: The revision activity does not establish its outcome.

definition: To take a course or courses in a subject.
example: She plans to study engineering at university.
distinctions: Studying a subject means taking courses here. Plans to leaves enrolment and completion open; the verb does not say that a degree has already been awarded.

originalSense.definition: To take a course or courses on a subject.
originalSense.example: I study medicine at the university.

distinctionTask.prompt: She plans to study engineering states _____.
options: an intended course of learning, with completion still open
that she has already been awarded an engineering degree
distinctionTask.answer: an intended course of learning, with completion still open
distinctionTask.explanation: Plans and completed qualifications are different.

definition: To acquire knowledge about a subject with the intention of applying it.
example: We study local building methods before designing the shelter.
distinctions: This source meaning includes an intention to apply the learning. It does not establish that the methods have already been used successfully. Study and learn overlap, but study names the activity and does not guarantee mastery.

originalSense.definition: To acquire knowledge on a subject with the intention of applying it in practice.
originalSense.example: Biologists study living things.

distinctionTask.prompt: We study methods before designing a shelter describes learning _____.
options: with an intention to apply it
which already proves the finished shelter is successful
distinctionTask.answer: with an intention to apply it
distinctionTask.explanation: Intended application is separate from a completed successful outcome.

definition: To examine something closely and carefully.
example: Please study the map before choosing a route.
distinctions: Study here means look at or examine closely. It need not mean enrol in a course about maps, and examining a map does not guarantee that the chosen route is suitable.

originalSense.definition: To look at carefully and minutely.
originalSense.example: He studied the map in preparation for the hike.

distinctionTask.prompt: Please study the map asks for _____.
options: necessarily enrolment in a university map course
distinctionTask.explanation: The object and context select close examination.

definition: To direct sustained thought towards a subject; to ponder it.
example: I need time to study what this decision might mean for us.
distinctions: This meaning emphasises sustained thought. It can overlap with examination or learning; the sentence does not say the question has already been resolved or that a course is involved.

originalSense.definition: To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to dwell upon anything in thought; to muse; to ponder.
originalSense.example:
July 10, 1732, Jonathan Swift, letter to Mr. Gay and The Duchess of Queensberry
I found a moral first, and studied for a fable.

distinctionTask.prompt: Time to study what a decision might mean is time to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: This use emphasises sustained thought.

definition: An archaic meaning: to strive diligently or be zealous.
example: In the older phrase study to be quiet, study means strive or endeavour, rather than take a course in quietness.
distinctions: The source marks this intransitive effort meaning archaic. Its label does not make the ordinary academic verb archaic.

originalSense.definition: To endeavor diligently; to be zealous.
originalSense.example: And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you […]

definition: Mental effort devoted to acquiring knowledge or learning.
example: Regular study helps her understand the subject.
distinctions: The noun names learning effort. Helps does not guarantee complete understanding, and study in this construction is not the countable noun for a room or a publication.

originalSense.definition: Mental effort to acquire knowledge or learning.
originalSense.example: The study of languages is fascinating.

distinctionTask.prompt: Regular study names _____.
options: a particular room in every use
distinctionTask.explanation: The noun here names mental effort.

definition: The act of examining or investigating something.
example: A careful study of the plans revealed a missing exit.
distinctions: The noun names an examination or investigation. The example states a finding in the plans, rather than a room for reading or necessarily the publication reporting that finding.

originalSense.definition: The act of studying or examining; examination.
originalSense.example: I made a careful study of his sister.

distinctionTask.prompt: A careful study of plans that revealed a missing exit is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The finding arises from the stated examination.

definition: A branch of learning or an object of attentive consideration.
example: Astronomy was her favourite study.
distinctions: Study here names what receives attention or learning. It differs from the effort of studying, although the meanings are related; a subject of study need not be a room, artwork or research publication.

originalSense.definition: Any particular branch of learning that is studied; any object of attentive consideration.
originalSense.example: The Holy Scriptures, especially the New Testament, are her daily study.

distinctionTask.prompt: Astronomy was her favourite study identifies _____.

definition: A room in a home intended for reading, writing or similar work.
example: She keeps her reference books in the study.
distinctions: This countable room noun is separate from the activity of studying. The source’s traditional association with a male householder is historical context, not a modern restriction on who can use the room.

originalSense.definition: A room in a house intended for reading and writing; traditionally the private room of the male head of household.
originalSense.example: Father spends all his time in the study poring over manuscripts.

distinctionTask.prompt: Reference books kept in the study are kept _____.
options: in a room used for reading or writing
inside a learning activity rather than a room
distinctionTask.answer: in a room used for reading or writing
distinctionTask.explanation: The preposition and books context select the room.

definition: An artwork made to practise or demonstrate a subject or technique.
example: The artist made a study of hands before painting the portrait.
distinctions: An artistic study is a work for practice or demonstration. It can be preparatory, but the term does not require that every study later becomes part of a finished painting.

originalSense.definition: An artwork made in order to practise or demonstrate a subject or technique.
originalSense.example: a study of heads or of hands for a figure picture

distinctionTask.prompt: An artist’s study of hands is _____.
options: an artwork for practice or demonstration
distinctionTask.answer: an artwork for practice or demonstration

definition: A face with an expression an observer finds amusingly typical of an emotion or state of mind.
example: His face was a study in comic bewilderment.
distinctions: This figurative use focuses on the facial expression. It does not mean his face is a room or an academic publication, and the observer’s interpretation does not independently establish his exact feelings.

originalSense.definition: The human face, bearing an expression which the observer finds amusingly typical of a particular emotion or state of mind.
originalSense.example: Geoffrey's face was a study.

distinctionTask.prompt: His face was a study in comic bewilderment refers to _____.

distinctionTask.explanation: The figurative use concerns the observed expression.

definition: A musical piece intended for focused practice; an étude.
example: The pianist practised a study for the left hand.

distinctions: A musical study is a practice piece, not simply any piece someone happens to practise. Such pieces may also be performed in concert; practice purpose does not rule out artistic value.

originalSense.definition: A piece for special practice; an etude.

distinctionTask.prompt: A piano study for the left hand is _____.
options: a piece intended for focused practice
every song that anyone happens to rehearse
distinctionTask.answer: a piece intended for focused practice
distinctionTask.explanation: A study has a practice purpose as a kind of composition.

definition: An academic publication reporting research or analysis.
example: The journal published a study of urban travel patterns.

originalSense.definition: An academic publication.

distinctionTask.prompt: A journal published a study. Publication alone _____.

definition: A person considered in terms of learning a theatrical role by heart.
example: The actor is a quick study and memorised the part overnight.

originalSense.definition: One who commits a theatrical part to memory.

distinctionTask.prompt: An actor described as a quick study is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The phrase describes the actor’s learning speed.

definition: A composed chess endgame problem whose intended task is to find a win or a draw.
example: A chess study is an artistic endgame composition with a stated win-or-draw task, rather than necessarily a position from a played game.
distinctions: The source concerns composed endgame problems. The task and solution require the actual position and rules; this reading note supplies no invented position, legal move sequence or automatic guarantee that one line wins.

originalSense.definition: An endgame problem composed for artistic merit, where one side is to play for a win or for a draw.

definition: An obsolete meaning: perplexity or worried thought.

definition: An archaic meaning: purposeful thought or one’s concern.

originalSense.definition: Thought, as directed to a specific purpose; one's concern.

definition: Careful inquiry or examination to discover, check or revise facts, theories or applications.
example: The team conducts research into ways to reduce food waste.
distinctions: Academic research is normally uncountable in general standard usage: research or a piece of research. The source also preserves countable use in some dialects. Inquiry can revise earlier claims; calling work research does not guarantee a discovery or a correct conclusion.
usage: Usually uncountable; source notes countability in some dialects.

originalSense.definition: Diligent inquiry or examination to seek or revise facts, principles, theories, applications, etc. (that are currently available, or that are familiar to oneself).

distinctionTask.prompt: The team conducts research into waste reduction. This describes _____.

a guaranteed discovery merely from the word research

distinctionTask.explanation: Research names inquiry, not automatic success or certainty.

definition: A dated countable meaning: a particular investigation or piece of research.

distinctions: The source marks this instance meaning dated. Prefer a study or a piece of research in ordinary contemporary academic writing, while retaining the separate source qualification that countable research exists in some dialects.

definition: To search or examine something with sustained care.

originalSense.definition: To search or examine with continued care; to seek diligently.

in a way that makes all transitive uses incorrect
distinctionTask.answer: without a direct object, with a prepositional topic
distinctionTask.explanation: The intransitive and transitive constructions coexist.

definition: A separate meaning: to search again.

distinctions: The source preserves search again separately. Read this record as a repeat search; do not infer that every use of research means repetition or that the word’s presence alone establishes which meaning is intended.

originalSense.definition: To search again.

originalSense.definition: A suburb of Melbourne in the Shire of Nillumbik, Victoria, Australia

definition: A test under controlled conditions to demonstrate a result or investigate a hypothesis or untried effect.
example: The class conducted an experiment to compare how two materials retain heat.
distinctions: The experiment is a test, rather than accumulated practical experience. A controlled test can examine a hypothesis without confirming it, and the conclusion still depends on design, observations and analysis.

the same thing as years of work experience

originalSense.definition: To conduct an experiment.

distinctionTask.prompt: Students experiment on insulation materials. The materials are _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: On introduces the object of testing in this sentence.

definition: An obsolete meaning: to experience, feel, perceive or detect something.
example: In older writing, the transitive verb experiment can describe experiencing or perceiving something.
distinctions: The source marks this experiencing verb obsolete. Use experience, feel or perceive as appropriate in modern writing; the current verb experiment has its own testing meanings.

originalSense.definition: To test or ascertain by experiment; to try out; to make an experiment on.

definition: To try something in order to observe what happens.
example: You can experiment with different layouts before choosing one.
distinctions: This exploratory use need not describe a formal controlled scientific experiment. With introduces what is tried; the sentence leaves the final choice and whether any layout improves the result open.

originalSense.definition: To try something to observe the results.
originalSense.example: I want to experiment with psychedelics.

options: try layouts and observe the results
necessarily perform a controlled scientific study
distinctionTask.answer: try layouts and observe the results

definition: The personal impressions or effects of directly witnessing or participating in events.
example: Reading about the storm was different from the experience of being there.
distinctions: Direct experience differs from a second-hand description. It can involve enjoyment, distress or mixed feelings, and the person’s impressions need not be a complete or infallible account of the event.

originalSense.definition: The effect upon the judgment or feelings produced by any event, whether witnessed or participated in; personal and direct impressions as contrasted with description or fancies; personal acquaintance; actual enjoyment or suffering.
originalSense.example: It was an experience he would not soon forget.

distinctionTask.prompt: The experience of being at the storm differs from reading about it because it involves _____.
options: a guarantee of an infallible account
distinctionTask.explanation: Direct participation and accuracy of interpretation are separate.

definition: An activity a person has performed or participated in.
example: Teaching abroad was a valuable experience for her.

originalSense.definition: An activity one has performed.

distinctionTask.prompt: Teaching abroad was a valuable experience uses experience as _____.
options: a noun that can never take an or a plural
distinctionTask.explanation: The individual-activity meaning is countable.

definition: Accumulated events or activities from which knowledge, views or skills may be gained.
example: Her experience of working in small teams shaped her approach.
distinctions: This meaning concerns the events or activities someone has been through. It is usually uncountable, but the source says usually, rather than declaring every plural form wrong. Participation does not guarantee expertise.

originalSense.definition: A collection of events and/or activities from which an individual or group may gather knowledge, opinions, and skills.
originalSense.example: Virtually all employers now require jobseekers to have work experience even for entry-level roles. Many believe this will hurt companies in the long run.

distinctionTask.prompt: Experience of working in teams concerns _____.
options: proof that every experienced worker is an expert
distinctionTask.explanation: Participation can inform learning without guaranteeing expertise.

definition: Knowledge gained through participation in events or activities.
example: Her experience helps her recognise common errors quickly.
distinctions: The emphasis is the knowledge gained, rather than a single countable event. Experience can help judgement without guaranteeing that every decision is right or that a qualification has been awarded.

originalSense.definition: The knowledge thus gathered.

distinctionTask.prompt: Experience that helps recognise common errors emphasises _____.

definition: A business offering focused on the customer’s interaction throughout the transaction.

originalSense.example: CDNOW's custom music selection and Levi Strauss & Co.'s custom-fit jean service are also good examples of giving customers more than just the product, but an experience as well.

distinctionTask.prompt: A pottery-making experience offered by a business focuses on _____.
options: the customer’s participation as well as the outcome
only ownership of the finished bowl

definition: In games, experience points awarded or accumulated by a character or player.

originalSense.definition: Synonym of experience points
originalSense.example: As your troops conquer the enemy, they'll earn experience and gain levels. Each time they level up, their stats will increase.

distinctionTask.prompt: A quest that earns experience in a game earns _____.

distinctionTask.answer: game experience points under that game’s rules
distinctionTask.explanation: The gaming alias does not establish real-world skill or qualifications.

definition: An obsolete meaning: a trial, test or experiment.

originalSense.definition: To observe certain events; undergo a certain feeling or process; or perform certain actions that may alter one or contribute to one's knowledge, opinions, or skills.
originalSense.example: A 2022 report published by the Scottish Borders Council states: "Hawick has been affected more by depopulation than any other Borders town, with all parts of the town experiencing population loss, and Hawick Central is currently experiencing the highest depopulation out of the 30 Intermediate Zones in Scottish Borders."

all passengers certainly enjoy the delays

definition: General understanding of or familiarity with a subject, place or situation.

distinctions: Knowledge usually names understanding or information and is uncountable in this ordinary use. A good knowledge of is an established construction; it does not make every piece of information a knowledge. Familiarity need not be complete or based on direct experience.

originalSense.definition: Awareness of a particular fact or situation; a state of having been informed or made aware of something.

definition: Intellectual understanding or appreciation of information or truth.
