distinctionTask.explanation: A taxonomic description sets out distinguishing characteristics; naming-code requirements vary.

definition: In an obsolete use, to divide or arrange into parts, groups or classes.
example: In this obsolete use, describe concerns dividing or classifying something into parts or groups, rather than merely saying what it is like.
distinctions: The ordinary modern words divide, classify or mark off express this meaning more clearly. The historical sense is distinct from a modern description in words.

originalSense.definition: To distribute into parts, groups, or classes; to mark off; to class.
originalSense.example: Passed through the land, and described it by cities into seven parts in a book.

definition: To make a meaning, idea or process clear and understandable.
example: Could you explain the rule to me?
distinctions: Put the thing explained directly after the verb and introduce the recipient with to: explain the rule to me. In standard English, explain me the rule does not use the normal object pattern.

originalSense.definition: To make plain, manifest, or intelligible; to clear of obscurity; to illustrate the meaning of.
originalSense.example: The issue was explained to the governor in detail.

distinctionTask.prompt: Choose the standard object pattern: _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The rule is the direct object; the recipient follows to.

definition: To give a reason, justification or cause for something.
example: The broken signal may explain the train delay.
distinctions: May presents the broken signal as a possible cause. An offered explanation is not automatically confirmed, and explaining conduct does not necessarily excuse it. A reason can explain why something happened without describing every detail.

originalSense.definition: To give the reason for, justification for, or cause of.
originalSense.example: It is tempting to speculate about the incentives or compulsions that might explain why anyone would take to the skies in [the] basket [of a balloon]: perhaps out of a desire to escape the gravity of this world or to get a preview of the next; […].

distinctionTask.prompt: The broken signal may explain the delay presents _____.
options: a possible cause, not an automatically confirmed one
a confirmed cause simply because someone proposes it
distinctionTask.answer: a possible cause, not an automatically confirmed one
distinctionTask.explanation: May makes the proposed cause tentative; explaining is not by itself independent confirmation.

definition: In an obsolete use, to make flat or smooth out.
example: In this obsolete physical use, explain means flatten or smooth out, rather than make an idea understandable.
distinctions: Read the verb as a physical action where the older context supports it. Modern English normally uses flatten or smooth out for this action.

originalSense.definition: To make flat, smooth out.

definition: In an obsolete use, to unfold or make visible.
example: In this obsolete use, explain can mean unfold, as in an older description of a leaf opening.
distinctions: This older physical sense concerns something opening or becoming visible. It is separate from explaining the meaning of a word or the reason for an event.

originalSense.definition: To unfold or make visible.
originalSense.example:
April 14, 1684, John Evelyn, a letter sent to the Royal Society concerning the damage done to his gardens by the preceding winter
The horse-chestnut is […] ready to explain its leaf.

definition: To make something understandable, with no direct object stated.
example: Please let me explain before you decide.
distinctions: No direct object follows explain in this sentence; the topic comes from the situation. Compare the transitive pattern explain the rule, where the thing explained is stated.
usage: Intransitive; the topic is understood from context.

originalSense.definition: To make something plain or intelligible.
originalSense.example: She tried to explain but he wouldn’t listen.

distinctionTask.prompt: In Please let me explain before you decide, explain has _____.
options: no direct object stated in the sentence
the direct object me after explain
distinctionTask.answer: no direct object stated in the sentence
distinctionTask.explanation: Me belongs to let me; explain has no stated direct object in this clause.

definition: To make something clearer by giving, or serving as, an example or comparison.
example: This missed connection can illustrate how a bus delay affects a journey.
distinctions: An example makes the point concrete. A single missed connection does not prove that every bus delay disrupts every journey. Illustrate can introduce an example or describe a case that serves as one.
usage: Figurative; clarification by example or comparison.

originalSense.definition: To clarify something by giving, or serving as, an example or a comparison.
originalSense.example: We illustrate our definitions by including quotations or simple examples.

distinctionTask.prompt: A missed connection used to illustrate a bus delay gives _____.
options: one example, not proof of what happens on every journey
proof that every delay disrupts every journey
distinctionTask.answer: one example, not proof of what happens on every journey
distinctionTask.explanation: An illustrative case can clarify a point without establishing a universal claim.

definition: To supply a book or other publication with pictures, diagrams or other explanatory or decorative features.
example: The artist will illustrate the book with drawings of local birds.
distinctions: This meaning concerns adding visual material to a publication. The features can explain the text or be decorative; they do not all have to be charts or logical examples.

originalSense.definition: To provide a book or other publication with pictures, diagrams or other explanatory or decorative features.
originalSense.example: The economics textbook was illustrated with many graphs.

distinctionTask.prompt: To illustrate the book with drawings is to add _____.
options: pictures or diagrams to the publication
only spoken explanations with no visual features
distinctionTask.answer: pictures or diagrams to the publication
distinctionTask.explanation: The publication sense includes explanatory or decorative visual material.

definition: In an obsolete use, to shed light on or illuminate something.
example: In this obsolete use, illustrate concerns literal illumination, as when light brightens the sky.
distinctions: The physical light sense differs from the modern figurative sense of clarifying a point with an example. Modern English usually uses illuminate or light up for the physical action.

originalSense.definition: To shed light upon.
originalSense.example: Here, when the morn illustrates all the sky.

definition: In an obsolete use, to bring renown or honour to someone or something.
example: In this obsolete use, illustrate means make illustrious or bring honour, rather than provide pictures.
distinctions: The emphasis is on distinction or glory. This historical meaning is separate from drawing illustrations and from clarifying an argument with an example.

originalSense.definition: To give renown or honour to; to make illustrious.
originalSense.example: Matter to me of glory, whom their hate / Illustrates.

definition: To show someone how to use something or perform an operation.
example: The instructor will demonstrate how to use the new tool.
distinctions: This meaning focuses on showing the procedure in action. A demonstration can accompany an explanation, but explaining a word alone need not show how to operate a tool.

originalSense.definition: To show how to use (something).
originalSense.example: Can you demonstrate the new tools for us?

distinctionTask.prompt: To demonstrate how to use a tool is to _____.
options: show how to use it in practice
only supply the dictionary definition of tool
distinctionTask.answer: show how to use it in practice
distinctionTask.explanation: The procedural sense shows the operation rather than merely defining the word.

definition: To show the steps of a logical argument or a mathematical derivation.
example: We demonstrate the solution of x + 3 = 7 by subtracting 3 from both sides.
distinctions: Subtracting 3 from both sides preserves the equality and gives x = 4. A valid demonstration shows justified steps; checking a single example is not a proof of every case of a general claim.

originalSense.definition: To show the steps taken to create a logical argument or equation.

distinctionTask.prompt: To demonstrate the solution of x + 3 = 7, _____.
options: subtract 3 from both sides to obtain x = 4
subtract 3 from only the left side to obtain x = 7
distinctionTask.answer: subtract 3 from both sides to obtain x = 4
distinctionTask.explanation: Applying the same subtraction to both sides preserves equality.

definition: To take part in or organise a public demonstration, such as a protest.
example: Residents plan to demonstrate against the closure of the library.
distinctions: Here against introduces what the residents oppose. The verb has no direct object in this sentence. Plan to does not establish that the protest has already happened or that the closure will be reversed.

originalSense.definition: To participate in or organize a demonstration.
originalSense.example: Those people outside are demonstrating against the election results.

distinctionTask.prompt: Residents who demonstrate against the closure take part in _____.
options: a public protest opposing the closure
a lesson showing how to operate the library building
distinctionTask.answer: a public protest opposing the closure
distinctionTask.explanation: Demonstrate against introduces the object of a public protest.

definition: To show, display or present something, or make something evident.
example: She can demonstrate her patience by listening without interrupting.
distinctions: Here demonstrate means display a quality through behaviour. In claims about proof, the strength of a demonstration depends on its evidence and reasoning; the verb alone does not guarantee a conclusion.

originalSense.definition: To show, display, or present; to prove or make evident
originalSense.example: The debate was not long on policy, as questions about the Affordable Care Act and the war in Syria demonstrated.

distinctionTask.prompt: Demonstrate her patience by listening means _____.
options: solve an equation by subtracting from both sides
distinctionTask.explanation: The quality is made evident through behaviour, not mathematical steps.

previousSenses.definition: To show something clearly.
previousSenses.example: These results demonstrate the need for change.

definition: To examine two or more things to identify similarities and differences.
example: We compare the two courses in terms of cost and content.
distinctions: A comparison can find similarities, differences or both. With and to have overlapping uses; compare with is common when examining alternatives, while compare to is common when likening one thing to another. These are guides rather than an absolute rule.
usage: Transitive; examination of similarities and differences.

originalSense.definition: To assess the similarities and differences between two or more things [“to compare X with Y”]. Having made the comparison of X with Y, one might have found it similar to Y or different from Y.
originalSense.example: Compare the tiger's coloration with that of the zebra.

distinctionTask.prompt: To compare courses in terms of cost and content is to examine _____.
options: similarities and differences between the courses
only evidence that the courses are identical
distinctionTask.answer: similarities and differences between the courses
distinctionTask.explanation: Comparing can reveal differences as well as similarities.

definition: To liken one thing to another by pointing out a similarity.
example: The writer will compare the city to a maze.
distinctions: The city is likened to a maze because of a shared feature, such as a confusing layout. The comparison does not identify the two things as literally the same or claim they share every property.
usage: Transitive; likening one thing to another.

originalSense.definition: To declare two things to be similar in some respect [“to compare X to Y”].
originalSense.example: Astronomers have compared comets to dirty snowballs.

distinctionTask.prompt: To compare a city to a maze highlights _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The writer likens the layout to a maze rather than equating the two things.

definition: In grammar, to form or state the positive, comparative and superlative forms of an adjective.
example: In grammar, we compare good as good, better, best.
distinctions: Good, better and best are the three forms in this example. They are irregular, so they do not establish a rule that every adjective takes -er and -est.

originalSense.definition: To form the three degrees of comparison of (an adjective).
originalSense.example: We compare “good” as “good”, “better”, “best”.

distinctionTask.prompt: The three degrees of good are _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Good has the irregular comparative better and superlative best.

definition: To be similar or comparable in quality, value or other respects.
example: The two performances do not compare in quality.
distinctions: No direct object follows compare here; in quality identifies the respect being considered. The negative says the performances are not comparable in that respect without specifying which is better.

originalSense.definition: To be similar (often used in the negative).
originalSense.example: A sapling and a fully-grown oak tree do not compare.

distinctionTask.prompt: The performances do not compare in quality means _____.
options: they are not comparable in that respect
the sentence necessarily identifies which is better
distinctionTask.answer: they are not comparable in that respect
distinctionTask.explanation: The negative comparison does not itself identify the better performance.

definition: In an obsolete use, to get or obtain something.
example: In this obsolete use, compare means acquire or obtain, rather than examine similarities and differences.
distinctions: Read the verb as getting something where the older context supports it. Modern English normally uses acquire, get or obtain for this action.

originalSense.definition: To get; to obtain.
originalSense.example: To fill his bags, and richesse to compare.

definition: Comparison, especially in expressions such as beyond compare.
example: Her generosity is beyond compare.
distinctions: Compare is a noun in beyond compare. The phrase praises a quality as unequalled rather than reporting a measured ranking of every person.
usage: Uncountable noun; especially in fixed expressions.

originalSense.definition: Comparison.
originalSense.example: His mighty Champion, ſtrong above compare,

distinctionTask.prompt: Beyond compare uses compare as _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Beyond compare is a fixed expression praising something as unequalled.

definition: In computing, an instruction or command that compares values or states.
example: The program uses a compare to test whether two values are equal.
distinctions: A compare is countable in this technical noun use. The exact result, flags or later branch behaviour depends on the instruction set or programming environment; comparison need not itself change either operand.

originalSense.definition: An instruction or command that compares two values or states.
originalSense.example: […] including addition and subtraction, memory operations, compares, shifts, logic operations, and condition operations.

distinctionTask.prompt: A compare in a program is _____.
options: an instruction or command for comparing values or states
a guarantee that both input values are equal
distinctionTask.answer: an instruction or command for comparing values or states
distinctionTask.explanation: A compare tests a relation; it does not guarantee one particular outcome.

definition: In an obsolete noun use, an illustrative comparison or simile.
example: In this obsolete noun use, compare means illustration by comparison or simile.
distinctions: This historical figure-of-speech meaning is separate from the programming instruction and from the modern fixed expression beyond compare.

originalSense.definition: Illustration by comparison; simile.
originalSense.example: Rhymes full of protest, of oath, and big compare.

definition: A visual difference in lightness, brightness or hue that helps distinguish one colour from another.
example: The dark lettering creates a clear contrast with the pale background.
distinctions: This sense concerns a visual difference. Contrast can involve lightness, brightness or hue, so two colours need not be black and white to contrast. The example does not claim a measured accessibility ratio.

originalSense.definition: A difference in lightness, brightness or hue between two colours that makes them more or less distinguishable.
originalSense.example: The red and the orange don't have much contrast between them — I can hardly tell them apart.

distinctionTask.prompt: The lettering and background have a clear contrast because of _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The sentence describes visible contrast without a numerical ratio.

definition: A difference between people, things or ideas.
example: There is a clear contrast between the two proposals on cost.
distinctions: The contrast identifies a difference in cost without giving the amounts or deciding which proposal is better overall. Compare can examine similarities too; contrast focuses on differences.

originalSense.definition: A difference between two objects, people or concepts.
originalSense.example: Israel is a country of many contrasts.

distinctionTask.prompt: A contrast between proposals on cost identifies _____.
options: a difference in one stated aspect
the best proposal on every criterion
distinctionTask.answer: a difference in one stated aspect
distinctionTask.explanation: A difference in cost does not establish an overall choice.

definition: A person or thing that is strikingly different from another.
example: The quiet garden is a contrast to the busy street.
distinctions: The garden itself is the contrasting item, rather than just the abstract difference between the two places. A contrast can concern one aspect without making the places opposite in every respect.
usage: Countable noun; the contrasting person or thing.

originalSense.definition: Something that is opposite of or strikingly different from something else.
originalSense.example: Why this denunciation of idolatry at this point? And why are Shabbat and the sanctuary mentioned as contrasts to idol worship?

distinctionTask.prompt: In The garden is a contrast to the street, the garden is _____.
options: the display control for the street
distinctionTask.explanation: A person or thing can itself be described as a contrast.

definition: In rhetoric, antithesis: the juxtaposition of contrasting ideas or expressions.
example: The contrast between easy to promise and hard to deliver creates an antithesis.
distinctions: The paired ideas are set against each other for rhetorical effect. This use concerns the expression of opposition rather than a display setting or a medical substance.

originalSense.definition: Antithesis.

distinctionTask.prompt: The pairing easy to promise and hard to deliver uses _____.
options: a medical medium administered for imaging
distinctionTask.explanation: Rhetorical contrast can form an antithesis between ideas or expressions.

definition: In medicine, a contrast medium used to make structures or differences more visible in medical imaging.
example: The scan may require contrast to improve the visibility of some structures.
distinctions: The suitable substance and method of administration depend on the imaging method and clinical circumstances. Contrast is not always injected, and using it does not guarantee that a scan establishes a diagnosis.

originalSense.definition: Contrast medium

distinctionTask.prompt: Medical contrast refers to _____.
options: a medium used to improve visibility in imaging
only the contrast adjustment on a television
distinctionTask.answer: a medium used to improve visibility in imaging
distinctionTask.explanation: The medical substance is distinct from visual contrast settings.

definition: To set things side by side or in opposition in order to show their differences.
example: We contrast the two proposals on cost and delivery time.
distinctions: The verb directs attention to differences. Cost and delivery time are the chosen dimensions here; the sentence does not supply the values or decide which proposal should be adopted.

originalSense.definition: To set in opposition in order to show the difference or differences between; to counterpoint.

distinctionTask.prompt: Contrast the proposals asks the reader to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The transitive verb focuses on differences.

definition: To differ in a way that forms a contrast.
example: The quiet garden and the busy street contrast sharply.
distinctions: Here contrast has no direct object. A subject can contrast with another thing, or two subjects can contrast with each other. This pattern differs from the transitive instruction contrast the two proposals.

originalSense.definition: To form a contrast.
originalSense.example: Foreground and background strongly contrast.

distinctionTask.prompt: In The garden and street contrast sharply, contrast has _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Sharply modifies the verb; it is not its object.

definition: The degree or strength of a visual difference between colours or areas.
example: The image has little contrast, so the two shades are hard to distinguish.
distinctions: Here contrast names the strength of the visual difference, rather than a particular pair of colours or a control. The schematic shades illustrate lower and higher lightness contrast without supplying a measured ratio.

originalSense.definition: The degree of this difference.

distinctionTask.prompt: In The image has little contrast, contrast concerns _____.
options: how strong the visual difference is
the physical control used to adjust a display
distinctionTask.answer: how strong the visual difference is
distinctionTask.explanation: The degree of contrast is distinct from the adjustment control.

definition: A display control or setting that adjusts the contrast of the displayed image.
example: Use the contrast control to adjust the display.
distinctions: The control changes how the display presents contrast. Its precise effect depends on the display; changing it is not the same as modifying the objects or lighting in the scene that was recorded.

originalSense.definition: A control on a television, etc, that adjusts the amount of contrast in the images being displayed.

distinctionTask.prompt: The contrast control is _____.
options: the display setting that adjusts contrast
a claim that the real scene has changed
distinctionTask.answer: the display setting that adjusts contrast
distinctionTask.explanation: The control changes the displayed image rather than the recorded scene itself.

definition: To recognise someone or something as different by identifying its characteristics.
example: Can you distinguish the original from the copy?
distinctions: Distinguish the original from the copy and distinguish between the original and the copy are both useful patterns. Recognising a difference does not require changing the objects or awarding anyone an honour.

originalSense.definition: To recognize someone or something as different from others based on its characteristics.
originalSense.example: It had begun to take a leading place even in the days of the Ptolemies, and in scientific, as distinguished from purely literary work, it had assumed a position of primary importance early in the Christian era.

distinctionTask.prompt: Distinguish the original from the copy means _____.
options: recognise a difference that identifies them
necessarily change the copy into a different object
distinctionTask.answer: recognise a difference that identifies them
distinctionTask.explanation: Recognition of a difference does not require changing either object.

definition: To see or perceive someone or something clearly or distinctly.
example: At this distance, I can barely distinguish the outline of the tower.
distinctions: The speaker is trying to make out an outline, rather than determine which of two objects is authentic. Barely indicates limited clarity; it does not establish a diagnosis of the speaker’s eyesight.

originalSense.definition: To see someone or something clearly or distinctly.

distinctionTask.prompt: Barely distinguish the tower’s outline concerns being able to _____.
options: see clearly enough to make out its shape
distinctionTask.answer: see clearly enough to make out its shape
distinctionTask.explanation: This sense concerns clear perception.

definition: To make someone, especially oneself, stand out through achievement or merit.
example: She hopes to distinguish herself through careful research.
distinctions: Distinguish herself is reflexive: she hopes to become notable through her achievement. Hopes to describes an intention rather than proving that she has already earned recognition or an award.

originalSense.definition: To make noticeably different or better from others through accomplishments.
originalSense.example: The soldier distinguished himself in combat and received a medal.

distinctionTask.prompt: She hopes to distinguish herself through research seeks _____.
options: a guarantee that an award was already presented
distinctionTask.explanation: The reflexive construction concerns standing out by merit, while hopes to is not completed achievement.

definition: To confer an honour or distinction on someone.
example: The academy will distinguish her with an honorary award.
distinctions: This formal use concerns an honour conferred by another person or institution. It differs from distinguishing oneself through achievement; the future statement does not establish that the award has already been presented.

originalSense.definition: To confer an honor upon.
originalSense.example: The soldier was distinguished with a medal for his bravery.

distinctionTask.prompt: Distinguish her with an award means _____.
options: only recognise her among a crowd
distinctionTask.explanation: The formal honour sense is separate from recognising an identity.

definition: In an obsolete use, to make different or cause to differ.
example: In this obsolete use, distinguish means cause things to differ, rather than recognise a difference that is already present.
distinctions: The historical causative meaning concerns producing a difference. It is separate from the ordinary modern recognition and perception uses.

originalSense.definition: To make to differ.
originalSense.example: For who diſtinguiſheth thee?

definition: To change things so as to create a difference or distinction.
example: We can differentiate the two versions by adding an extra feature to one.
distinctions: Adding the feature creates a difference between the versions. This modifying use differs from simply recognising an existing difference.

originalSense.definition: To modify so as to create a difference or distinction.
originalSense.example: A humble instance of Ablaut may be quoted which took place in the seventeenth century, when the word then was differentiated into the two forms then and than.

distinctionTask.prompt: Differentiate versions by adding an extra feature means _____.
options: create a difference by modifying one version
only notice a difference while changing nothing
distinctionTask.answer: create a difference by modifying one version
distinctionTask.explanation: The added feature produces a distinction.

definition: To be or show the characteristic that makes one thing different from another.
example: The extra handle is what can differentiate this version from the earlier one.
distinctions: Here the handle is the distinguishing feature. The sentence identifies a difference without claiming that the extra feature necessarily makes the product better overall.
usage: Transitive; constituting or showing the difference.

originalSense.definition: To show or be the difference or distinction between things.
originalSense.example: What differentiates an alligator from a crocodile?

distinctionTask.prompt: The extra handle differentiates the versions because it _____.
options: proves every aspect of the new version is better
distinctionTask.explanation: A distinguishing feature identifies a difference without establishing an overall ranking.

definition: To recognise things as different or distinct.
example: Can you differentiate the original from the copy?
distinctions: This sense concerns identifying an existing distinction, much like distinguish. It does not require modifying the original or the copy.

originalSense.definition: To recognize as different or distinct.
originalSense.example: How do you differentiate a fake smile from a genuine one?

distinctionTask.prompt: Differentiate the original from the copy asks the reader to _____.
options: necessarily add a new feature to one of them
distinctionTask.explanation: This recognition use identifies a difference that already exists.

definition: In mathematics, to calculate the derivative of a function.
example: Differentiate f(x) = x² to obtain f′(x) = 2x.
distinctions: For real x, the derivative of x² is 2x. It gives the local rate of change, not the original function’s value; at x = 3 the derivative is 6 while f(3) is 9.

originalSense.definition: To calculate the derivative of a function.

distinctionTask.prompt: For f(x) = x², differentiating with respect to x gives _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The derivative of x² is 2x, rather than the original function.

definition: In multivariable mathematics, to calculate the differential of a function.
example: We differentiate z = x² + y² to obtain dz = 2x dx + 2y dy.
distinctions: For real x and y, dz = 2x dx + 2y dy is the differential. It is not generally the exact finite change in z: a finite increment also includes the squared increments. The differential gives the linear part of the change.
usage: Mathematics; transitive; differential of a multivariable function.

originalSense.definition: To calculate the differential of a function of multiple variables.

distinctionTask.prompt: For z = x² + y², the differential is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The differential uses the partial derivatives 2x and 2y as coefficients of dx and dy.

definition: To perceive or recognise a difference, without a direct object in the construction.
example: Readers need to differentiate between fact and opinion.
distinctions: Between introduces the two categories, so this is an intransitive construction. An opinion can draw on facts; identifying a distinction does not mean every opinion is false or unsupported.

originalSense.definition: To perceive the difference between things; to discriminate.
originalSense.example: he refused to instruct that actual intent to harm or recklessness had to be found before punitive damages could be awarded, or that a verdict for respondent should differentiate between compensatory and punitive damages.

distinctionTask.prompt: Differentiate between fact and opinion means _____.
options: recognise the distinction between those categories
declare that every opinion must be false
distinctionTask.answer: recognise the distinction between those categories
distinctionTask.explanation: An opinion can be supported by facts; distinguishing categories is not a universal truth judgment.

definition: In education, to adapt teaching in different ways to meet differing learning needs.
example: Teachers may differentiate by varying the support and challenge in a lesson.
distinctions: Differentiation can change support, challenge or presentation in response to learning needs. It does not guarantee each learner’s progress or require treating ability as a fixed category.
usage: Education; intransitive construction in the example.

originalSense.definition: To teach a lesson in multiple different ways in order to meet the needs of more or less advanced students.
originalSense.example: Like most teaching, differentiating is a mix of art and science. When it works, "it's like a jazz rhythm," said Carol Tomlinson, an education professor at the University of Virginia and an expert on differentiation.

distinctionTask.prompt: To differentiate by varying support and challenge is to _____.
options: adapt the teaching to differing learning needs
guarantee that every learner has already mastered the lesson
distinctionTask.answer: adapt the teaching to differing learning needs
distinctionTask.explanation: Differentiation adapts instruction; it does not itself demonstrate mastery.

definition: In biology, to develop or cause development into forms or functions that differ.
example: Under suitable conditions, these precursor cells can differentiate into specialised cell types.
distinctions: The biological process concerns development of form or function. Can expresses possibility under suitable conditions; it does not mean a precursor can become every possible cell type or that every cell follows the same pathway.
usage: Biology; transitive or intransitive; intransitive in the example.

originalSense.definition: To (cause to) go through a process of development called differentiation; to make or become different in form or function.
originalSense.example: In Chapter IV we learned that every animal consists of a body, or soma, formed of cells that are differentiated from the germ cells usually at an early stage of development.

distinctionTask.prompt: Cells that can differentiate under suitable conditions _____.
options: may develop specialised forms or functions
must be able to become every possible cell type
distinctionTask.answer: may develop specialised forms or functions
distinctionTask.explanation: Cell differentiation is development, with possibilities depending on the precursor and conditions.

definition: In geology, a material or body that has become differentiated or stratified.
example: In this geological noun use, a differentiate is something produced or distinguished by differentiation or stratification.
distinctions: The noun concerns a geological product or body, rather than the act of recognising a difference or calculating a derivative. Its precise origin and composition depend on the geological context.

originalSense.definition: Something that has been differentiated or stratified.
originalSense.example: There is no discernable tendency, however, for the differentiates to fall into two extremities, as would be expected if they were trending toward distinct eutectics in a residua system.

definition: To establish who someone is or what something is.
example: The witness could identify the driver from a clear photograph.
distinctions: Identify establishes identity; recognize often matches a current perception to a previous encounter. A confident identification can still be mistaken.
usage: Transitive: identify someone or something; identify something as a particular thing.

originalSense.definition: To establish the identity of someone or something.
originalSense.example: It was hard to identify the shoplifter because the CCTV records didn't have a clear image.

distinctionTask.prompt: A witness examines photographs to establish who drove the car. Identify here means _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The task establishes identity. It does not say that the identity is publicly disclosed.

definition: To disclose who someone is.
example: The report will not identify the witness by name.
distinctions: Disclosing an identity is separate from discovering it. A writer may know a person's name and choose not to reveal it.
usage: Transitive; often by name, publicly, or in a negative statement about protecting identity.

originalSense.definition: To disclose the identity of someone.
originalSense.example: The Associated Press will not identify the suspect of the crime because he is a juvenile.

distinctionTask.prompt: The editor knows the witness's name but will not identify her in the report. Identify here concerns _____.
options: finding out her identity for the first time
distinctionTask.explanation: The editor already knows the name. The issue is whether to reveal it.

definition: To determine the taxonomic group to which an organism belongs.
example: The botanist used a field key to identify the plant as a common daisy.
distinctions: Identifying a specimen assigns it to a taxon; it does not necessarily describe a previously unknown species. The available evidence limits the identification.
usage: Biology; identify a specimen as a member of a named taxon.

originalSense.definition: To establish the taxonomic classification of an organism.
originalSense.example: A recent biological inventory uncovered 41 species and 2 subspecies of insects new to science and many species not before identified in the State of Washington.

distinctionTask.prompt: Using a field key, a botanist identifies a specimen as a common daisy. This means _____.
options: placing the specimen in an existing taxonomic group
distinctionTask.answer: placing the specimen in an existing taxonomic group
distinctionTask.explanation: The stated identification uses an existing name. Discovery of a new species requires separate evidence and description.

definition: To equate things or treat them as one; to unite them.
example: In the quotient construction, we identify each pair of opposite boundary points.
distinctions: In this mathematical use, identify means treat specified objects as the same in a construction. The original points need not occupy the same position. Elsewhere it can mean equate or unite things.
usage: Usually identify A with B or identify specified objects; the construction or argument determines what is equated.

originalSense.definition: To equate or make the same; to unite or combine into one.
originalSense.example: Every precaution is taken to identify the interests of the people, and their rulers.

distinctionTask.prompt: A quotient construction identifies two originally distinct points. It _____.
options: treats the two points as one in the resulting construction
merely gives both original points a name
distinctionTask.answer: treats the two points as one in the resulting construction
distinctionTask.explanation: The construction equates the specified points. This is different from naming or locating them.

definition: To feel strongly connected to someone or something, often seeing oneself in them.
example: Maya could identify herself with the novel's homesick narrator.
distinctions: Feeling an affinity does not mean being the same person or sharing every experience. The reflexive form identifies the person whose affinity is described.
usage: Reflexive: identify oneself with someone or something. The non-reflexive identify with is also common.

originalSense.definition: To have a strong affinity with; to feel oneself to be modelled on or connected to.
originalSense.example: Der Traum erhält eine neue Deutung, wenn sie im Traum nicht sich, sondern die Freundin meint, wenn sie sich an die Stelle der Freundin gesetzt oder, wie wir sagen können, sich mit ihr identifiziert hat.

distinctionTask.prompt: A reader identifies herself with a fictional narrator because both miss home. She _____.
options: feels an affinity with the narrator
claims that she literally is the narrator
distinctionTask.answer: feels an affinity with the narrator
distinctionTask.explanation: Identify oneself with expresses a felt connection in this sentence.

definition: To feel associated with a group or believe that one shares its outlook or experiences.
example: Although he lived abroad, Leo continued to identify with his local community.
distinctions: Identify with can express a sense of association without asserting formal membership, identical views, or agreement with every action of the group.
usage: Intransitive with with: identify with someone or a group.

originalSense.definition: To associate oneself with some group; to feel, or believe one feels, the same way.
originalSense.example: Now, the vast majority of us identify with the second group, the one that believes in trusting the wisdom of the people rather than taking power away from them and concentrating it in the other hands.

distinctionTask.prompt: Leo identifies with a community even though he is not a registered member. This describes _____.
options: his felt association with the community
distinctionTask.answer: his felt association with the community
distinctionTask.explanation: A sense of connection need not establish a formal membership status.

definition: To describe oneself using a particular identity or as a member of a group.
example: On the voluntary survey, Priya chose to identify herself as bilingual.
distinctions: Identify as introduces a self-description; identify with expresses connection or affinity. A self-description alone is not an independent assessment of every skill associated with the term.
usage: Identify oneself as or identify as, followed by an identity term.

originalSense.definition: To claim an identity; to describe oneself as a member of a group; to assert the use of a particular term to describe oneself.
originalSense.example: "The main message is that it's the interface between individuals and society that causes students who identify as gay, lesbian, or bisexual the most distress," said study first author Yue Zhao.

distinctionTask.prompt: Priya identifies herself as bilingual in a survey. The phrase reports _____.
options: the identity term she uses for herself
the result of a separately administered language test
distinctionTask.answer: the identity term she uses for herself
distinctionTask.explanation: The sentence gives her self-description, without asserting an independent test result.

definition: A standard British spelling of recognize; for example, to know someone or something from a previous encounter.
example: I recognise that voice from yesterday's interview.
distinctions: Recognise is an established British spelling, not a misspelling. Recognize is standard in American English and also used in Oxford-style British spelling. The voice example illustrates one meaning; the spelling relation applies more broadly.
usage: Both spellings are correct in their established conventions. Use the convention required by your course or publication consistently.

originalSense.definition: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of recognize.
originalSense.example: “[…] That woman is stark mad, Lord Stranleigh. Her own father recognised it when he bereft her of all power in the great business he founded. […]”

distinctionTask.prompt: In British spelling, “I recognise that voice” uses _____.
options: a spelling error that must always be corrected
distinctionTask.explanation: Recognise is standard British spelling. Recognize also occurs in British usage, particularly Oxford-style spelling.

definition: To know someone or something because it matches a memory of an earlier encounter.
example: I recognize that voice from yesterday's interview.
distinctions: Recognize in this sense connects a present perception with memory. Identify can instead establish identity using new evidence, without a previous encounter. Recognition can be mistaken.
usage: Transitive: recognize someone or something; recognize someone from an earlier encounter.

originalSense.definition: To match (something or someone which one currently perceives) to a memory of some previous encounter with the same person or thing.
originalSense.example: I recognized his face immediately, although his voice was different.

distinctionTask.prompt: You hear a voice and remember hearing the same person yesterday. Recognize describes _____.
options: matching the present voice to an earlier encounter
necessarily learning the person's legal name
distinctionTask.answer: matching the present voice to an earlier encounter
distinctionTask.explanation: Recognizing a familiar voice does not require knowing its owner's name.

definition: To acknowledge the existence or legality of something, or treat it as valid or worthy of consideration.
example: The university will recognize this qualification for entry to the course.
distinctions: Recognition of a qualification or right concerns its accepted status in a specified setting. It does not guarantee acceptance everywhere or endorse every related action.
usage: Transitive; state who recognizes what and for which purpose when the scope matters.

originalSense.definition: To acknowledge the existence or legality of; to treat as valid or worthy of consideration.
originalSense.example: The US and a number of EU countries are expected to recognize Kosovo on Monday.

distinctionTask.prompt: A university recognizes a qualification for admission to one course. This establishes _____.
options: its acceptance for that stated purpose
distinctionTask.answer: its acceptance for that stated purpose
distinctionTask.explanation: The institution and purpose limit the stated recognition.

definition: To acknowledge or regard someone or something as having a particular nature, status or quality.
example: The committee recognizes the building as an important local landmark.
distinctions: Recognize as attributes a stated status or quality; recognize that can acknowledge a proposition. The sentence reports a judgment or acknowledgment, not an automatic proof that it is correct.
usage: Recognize A as B; recognize that followed by a clause.

originalSense.definition: To acknowledge or consider (as being a certain thing or having a certain quality or property).
originalSense.example: Slavery is widely recognized as immoral.

distinctionTask.prompt: “We recognize that the timetable is unrealistic” uses recognize to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The that-clause gives the proposition being acknowledged.

definition: To realize or discover the nature or significance of something.
example: The engineer was first to recognize the fault in the design.
distinctions: Recognize here concerns understanding what something is or why it matters. It does not imply repairing the fault, taking the opportunity, or confirming a medical diagnosis.
usage: Transitive; often a problem, pattern, opportunity or significance.

originalSense.definition: To realize or discover the nature of something; apprehend quality in.
originalSense.example: In plants, the ability to recognize self from nonself plays an important role in fertilization, because self-fertilization will result in less diverse offspring than fertilization with pollen from another individual.

distinctionTask.prompt: The engineer recognizes a design fault but has not repaired it. She has _____.
options: realized the nature of the problem
distinctionTask.answer: realized the nature of the problem
distinctionTask.explanation: Recognizing the fault concerns understanding it. Repair is a separate action.

definition: To show formal appreciation of a person or achievement, for example with an award or commendation.
example: The council will recognize the volunteers' work with a public commendation.
distinctions: Formal recognition shows appreciation. It is separate from recognizing a familiar person, and a plan to recognize an achievement does not say the ceremony has already happened.
usage: Recognize someone or their work; recognize someone with an award; recognize someone for a contribution.

originalSense.definition: To show formal appreciation of, as with an award, commendation etc.
originalSense.example: His services were recognized in a testimonial.

distinctionTask.prompt: A council plans to recognize volunteers with a commendation next month. This means _____.
options: it plans to show formal appreciation
the award has already been presented
distinctionTask.answer: it plans to show formal appreciation
distinctionTask.explanation: The formal appreciation is planned for a future occasion.

definition: An obsolete use meaning to review or examine again.
example: In older writing, recognize can describe examining something again. Modern readers should use the context to separate this from remembering or formally acknowledging it.
distinctions: This obsolete meaning concerns another examination, not necessarily a remembered encounter or an award.
usage: Obsolete; reading guidance rather than a model for ordinary modern use.

originalSense.definition: To review; to examine again.
originalSense.example: We do moste humbly submytte it [this treatise] to[…]your maiestie, to be recognised, ouersene, and corrected.

definition: An obsolete use meaning to reconnoitre or survey an area for information.
example: In an older account of an expedition, recognize may mean reconnoitre: inspect an area to gather information about it.
distinctions: This historical scouting use is separate from recognizing a familiar place. Modern reconnoitre or reconnoiter is clearer.
usage: Obsolete; interpret from the historical context.

originalSense.definition: To reconnoiter.
originalSense.example: before the siege was layd to the Towne, of minde to recognize, he fell unawares amongst an Ambushcade

definition: To be able to bind to particular antigens through a specific molecular interaction.
example: In the assay, the antibody can recognize a particular antigen.
distinctions: In immunology, recognize can concern molecular binding. Binding depends on the molecules and conditions and does not by itself establish a complete immune response, perfect specificity, or a clinical diagnosis.
usage: Immunology; commonly an antibody or receptor recognizes an antigen or a particular part of it.

originalSense.definition: To have the property to bind to specific antigens.

distinctionTask.prompt: An assay shows that an antibody recognizes a particular antigen. This finding concerns _____.
options: a complete clinical diagnosis on its own
distinctionTask.explanation: Binding evidence has a limited scope. Diagnosis and downstream immune effects require further context and evidence.

definition: To cognize again: to apprehend or become aware of something anew.
example: The wording “cognize again” concerns another act of apprehension or awareness. It does not by itself assert matching a present perception to a memory.
distinctions: Keep this literal re-cognition meaning separate from the familiar-person or familiar-object sense. The hyphenated re-cognize can make the repeated act clearer.
usage: Read this literal repeated-action wording according to context rather than treating it as the usual everyday meaning.

originalSense.definition: to cognize again
originalSense.usage: British, English, North-American, Oxford, UK, US
originalSense.register: British, English, North-American, Oxford, UK, US

definition: To place things into groups according to stated features or criteria.
example: For this survey, we classify journeys of less than two kilometres as short trips.
distinctions: A classification depends on its criterion. The survey's two-kilometre boundary is a stated working rule, not a universal definition of a short trip. Identifying an item and assigning it to a group are related but distinct tasks.
usage: Classify A as B; classify items by a feature or into groups.

originalSense.definition: to identify by or divide into classes; to categorize
originalSense.example: Should we classify "make up" as an idiom or as a phrasal verb?

distinctionTask.prompt: A survey classifies journeys under 2 km as short. Under that rule, a 1.5 km journey is _____.
options: a trip that fails the stated short-trip criterion
distinctionTask.explanation: 1.5 is less than 2. The answer follows this survey's explicit rule.

definition: To designate information as secret or restricted, especially under a government classification system.
example: The agency decided to classify the report as secret.
distinctions: Classifying a report assigns a secrecy status. It does not itself encrypt the file, grant anyone access, or establish that its claims are true.
usage: Commonly information or documents; classify something as secret or under a named security level.

originalSense.definition: to declare something a secret, especially a government secret
originalSense.example: They decided to classify that information.

distinctionTask.prompt: An agency classifies a report as secret. That action assigns _____.
options: proof that every claim in the report is true
distinctionTask.explanation: A secrecy status concerns handling and disclosure, not the truth of the content.

definition: To make something classy or stylish.
example: In the make-classy meaning, classify concerns giving something a more stylish character. This is separate from sorting items or assigning a secrecy level.
distinctions: This use concerns style or elegance, rather than class membership. Make more stylish is clearer for an ordinary description.
usage: Interpret this uncommon wording from context; it does not mean categorize.

originalSense.definition: To make classy

definition: To notice or watch something, especially carefully and with attention to detail.
example: From the hide, we could observe the birds without approaching their nests.
distinctions: Observation concerns what is noticed or watched. It does not by itself establish why an event happened, and watching need not involve intervening.
usage: Transitive: observe someone, something or an event.

originalSense.definition: To notice or view, especially carefully or with attention to detail.
originalSense.example: From this vantage point we can observe the behavior of the animals in their natural habitat.

distinctionTask.prompt: Researchers observe birds from a hide without handling them. They are _____.
options: necessarily changing the birds' behaviour deliberately
distinctionTask.explanation: The sentence describes observation, without asserting an intervention or a proven causal explanation.

definition: To follow or comply with a rule, custom or practice.
example: Drivers must observe the posted speed limit on this road.
distinctions: Observe a rule means comply with it, rather than merely see that it is displayed. Which rule applies depends on the stated context.
usage: Transitive; observe a rule, requirement, custom or practice.

originalSense.definition: To follow or obey the custom, practice, or rules (especially of a religion).
originalSense.example: Please observe all posted speed limits.

distinctionTask.prompt: A driver observes the posted speed limit. Observe here means _____.
options: only notice the sign while ignoring the limit
distinctionTask.explanation: This use concerns following the rule, not simply perceiving its sign.

definition: To mark or keep a holiday or similar occasion, or follow a time or calendar convention.
example: The family will observe the festival with an evening meal.
distinctions: Observing a holiday concerns keeping or marking the occasion; observing daylight saving time concerns following that time convention. The two constructions do not assert the same activity, and neither implies a universal practice.
usage: Transitive; the object shows whether an occasion or a time convention is meant.

originalSense.definition: To take note of and celebrate (a holiday or similar occurrence), to keep; to follow (a type of time or calendar reckoning).
originalSense.example: Ye shall observe the feast of unleavened bread.

distinctionTask.prompt: A family observes a festival with a special meal. They _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The object festival and the special meal establish the occasion-keeping meaning.

definition: To make a comment or remark about something.
example: As Mina observed, the plan gives no deadline for completion.
distinctions: A person can observe that something is so by saying it. The remark may arise from careful thought, but the verb alone does not prove its accuracy or establish an experiment.
usage: Often observe that followed by a clause, or as someone observed.

originalSense.definition: To comment on something; to make an observation.
originalSense.example: The senator observed that the bill would be detrimental to his constituents.

distinctionTask.prompt: “The plan gives no deadline,” Mina observed. Observed introduces _____.
options: a requirement that she watched an experiment
distinctionTask.explanation: Here observed is a reporting verb for the remark.

definition: An archaic noun meaning an observation, remark, comment or judgment.
example: In older prose, an observe may mean a remark or judgment. Read it as a noun in that construction, rather than as an instruction to watch.
distinctions: This archaic noun is separate from the modern verb observe. Observation or remark is clearer in ordinary modern writing.
usage: Archaic noun; reading guidance rather than a model for ordinary modern use.

originalSense.definition: An observation (remark, comment or judgement).
originalSense.example: “It sticks in my mind that he would take it very ill,” says Alan. “But the little man cried to me to run, and indeed I thought it was a good observe, and ran. The last that I saw they were all in a knot upon the beach, like folk that were not agreeing very well together.”

definition: To interpret or regard someone or something in a particular way.
example: Students may perceive the same feedback as helpful or discouraging.
distinctions: A perception in this sense is an interpretation or judgment. Different people can interpret the same message differently; the verb does not make every interpretation accurate.
usage: Perceive A as B; A is perceived as B.

originalSense.definition: To interpret something in a particular way.
originalSense.example: John was perceived to be a coward by his comrades

distinctionTask.prompt: Two students perceive the same feedback differently. This concerns _____.
options: a guarantee that both interpretations are correct
distinctionTask.explanation: Perceive as describes how the feedback is regarded, without certifying either judgment.

definition: The act or state of noticing or becoming aware of something.
example: The spelling error escaped my notice during the first reading.
distinctions: In escape my notice, notice is an uncountable noun for awareness or attention. It is separate from a printed notice, even though a written announcement may attract attention.
usage: Uncountable noun; often in expressions such as escape notice, take notice and come to someone's notice.

originalSense.definition: The act of observing; perception.
originalSense.example: He took no notice of the changes, and went on as though nothing had happened.

distinctionTask.prompt: An error escapes your notice. You _____.
options: fail to become aware of it
distinctionTask.answer: fail to become aware of it
distinctionTask.explanation: The uncountable noun concerns awareness; escape notice means remain unnoticed.

definition: A written or printed announcement.
example: A notice on the library door said it would close early on Tuesday.
distinctions: A notice in this sense is an announcement in written or printed form. Its content can also perform a formal notifying function; these uses can overlap.
usage: Countable noun: a notice, several notices.

originalSense.definition: A written or printed announcement.
originalSense.example: A series of notices signpost patients to the X-ray department.

distinctionTask.prompt: A notice is pinned to a library door announcing an early closure. The notice is _____.
options: the reader's act of becoming aware
distinctionTask.explanation: The noun names the announcement itself.

definition: A formal notification or warning.
example: The council sent a formal notice stating that the permit would expire on 30 June.
distinctions: This use concerns formal notification. A notice may also be written or printed, so form and notifying function can overlap. The sentence alone does not establish legally effective service in every jurisdiction.
usage: Countable noun; give or serve a notice, or notice of a specified event.

originalSense.definition: A formal notification or warning.
originalSense.example: The sidewalk adjacent to the damaged bridge stonework shall be closed until further notice.

distinctionTask.prompt: The council sends a notice of a permit's expiry. This notice functions as _____.
options: proof that the permit has already expired
distinctionTask.explanation: Notification can concern a future expiry; it does not itself establish that the date has passed.

definition: Advance notification that employment will end, given by an employee or employer.
example: Under her contract, Leah gave four weeks' notice before leaving the job.
distinctions: The four-week period belongs to this example's contract, not to every employment relationship. Giving notice is separate from completing the departure.
usage: Employment; usually uncountable, including give notice and work a notice period. Applicable rules depend on the contract and jurisdiction.

originalSense.definition: Advance notification of termination of employment, given by an employer to an employee or vice versa.
originalSense.example: I gave her her mandatory two weeks' notice and sacked her.

distinctionTask.prompt: Leah's contract requires four weeks' notice. She gives notice today. The sentence establishes _____.
options: a universal four-week rule for every employee
distinctionTask.explanation: The period is expressly tied to her contract, and giving notice does not mean the departure is already complete.

definition: A published critical review, for example of a play.
example: The play received a favourable notice in the local newspaper.
collocations: a newspaper notice of a play
distinctions: A critical notice evaluates the work. It is separate from a simple announcement that a performance will take place, and a review need not be favourable.
usage: Countable noun; often notices in discussion of theatre or other reviewed work.

originalSense.definition: A published critical review of a play or the like.
originalSense.example: The first-night audience, yes. The first-night reviewers, not exactly. The notices have so far been mixed, only The Financial Times having delivered itself of an unequivocal rave.

distinctionTask.prompt: A play receives a favourable notice praising the acting. Notice here is _____.
options: only an announcement of the performance date
distinctionTask.explanation: The praise evaluates the performance, establishing the review sense.

definition: Notification given before an event or change.
example: Please give us advance notice if you need to cancel the booking.
distinctions: Prior notice concerns the timing of notification. Employment termination notice is one specific use, but this broader meaning also applies to bookings, visits and other changes.
usage: Usually uncountable; advance notice, prior notice, at short notice, without notice.

originalSense.definition: Prior notification.
originalSense.example: I don't mind if you want to change the venue; just give me some notice first, OK?

distinctionTask.prompt: You ask for advance notice of a cancellation so that you can rearrange the booking. You want notification _____.
options: only after every consequence is complete
distinctionTask.explanation: Advance notice gives information beforehand.

definition: A dated use meaning attention, respectful treatment or civility.
example: In older writing, notice can refer to respectful attention or civil treatment shown to a person. The context distinguishes this from an announcement or advance warning.
distinctions: This dated attention sense does not concern a formal notification. Its countability varies with the construction.
usage: Dated; reading guidance for older prose.

originalSense.definition: Attention; respectful treatment; civility.

definition: An archaic verb meaning to mention or remark upon something.
example: In an archaic use, to notice a subject may mean to mention it or make a remark about it. This is separate from simply becoming aware of it.
collocations: refer to something in a comment
distinctions: The remark meaning is separate from the ordinary become-aware verb. Mention or remark upon is clearer for ordinary modern use in this sense.
usage: Archaic transitive verb; interpret it from context.

originalSense.definition: To remark upon; to mention.
originalSense.example: Numberless are the arguments […] that men have used morally and physically, to degrade the sex. I must notice a few.

definition: To become aware of someone or something; to observe it.
example: Did you notice the change in the opening paragraph?
distinctions: Notice commonly marks becoming aware of a feature or event. Observe can additionally suggest attentive watching; detect can suggest a search or test. These verbs overlap, and none alone guarantees a correct causal explanation.
usage: Transitive: notice something; notice that followed by a clause; notice someone doing something.

originalSense.definition: To become aware of; to observe.
originalSense.example: Did you notice the flowers in her yard?

distinctionTask.prompt: You notice that a paragraph has changed, but do not know who edited it. You _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Noticing the change does not establish who caused it.

definition: An obsolete verb meaning to give someone abundant attention or treat them favourably.
example: In older prose, notice can describe favouring or paying marked attention to someone. The context must distinguish this social treatment from merely seeing the person.
distinctions: This obsolete favourable-treatment meaning is separate from the ordinary verb notice a person in a room.
usage: Obsolete transitive verb; reading guidance for historical writing.

originalSense.definition: To lavish attention upon; to treat (someone) favourably.
originalSense.example: She would notice her; she would improve her; she would detach her from her bad acquaintance, and introduce her into good society; she would form her opinions and her manners.

definition: To be noticeable or to show.
example: In this intransitive meaning, notice concerns a feature showing or being noticeable, without an object naming what is perceived.
distinctions: This construction differs from transitive notice a mark, in which someone becomes aware of the mark. Be noticeable or show is clearer for an ordinary description.
usage: Intransitive; interpret according to the surrounding grammar.

originalSense.definition: To be noticeable; to show.
originalSense.example: The blackness didn't notice so much when she was born; but it's unmistakeable now.

definition: An antisemitic online use that insinuates Jewish influence or responsibility.
example: In some antisemitic online rhetoric, notice is used as coded language insinuating Jewish influence or blame. Such an insinuation is a prejudicial claim, not evidence of who caused an event.
distinctions: This derogatory online use is separate from the neutral everyday verb become aware. Recognizing the insinuation helps readers distinguish a prejudicial claim from supported evidence.
usage: Derogatory antisemitic online usage; critical reading guidance.

originalSense.definition: To perceive Jewish influence or responsibility.
originalSense.example: Coordinate term: pattern noticer

definition: To discover or become aware of something, especially through a search, examination or test.
example: In this test, the sensor can detect a 0.2°C rise in temperature.
distinctions: Detection concerns finding evidence or noticing a feature. It does not by itself establish its cause, guilt, a diagnosis, or perfect reliability. The temperature change is specific to this example, not every sensor.
usage: Transitive: detect something, often a signal, change, trace or problem.

originalSense.definition: To discover or notice, especially by careful search, examination, or probing.
originalSense.example: The forensic examiners detected tiny traces of the poison on the suspect's gloves.

distinctionTask.prompt: A sensor detects a temperature rise but the source of the heat is unknown. The finding establishes _____.
options: that the rise was detected in that test
a complete explanation of its cause
distinctionTask.answer: that the rise was detected in that test
distinctionTask.explanation: Detection and causal explanation are separate steps.

definition: To work on or solve cases as a detective.
example: In the story, he is paid to detect rather than patrol the streets.
distinctions: In this informal intransitive use, detect describes detective work. Being paid to investigate does not guarantee that every case is solved.
usage: Informal and intransitive; no direct object is required when the detective-work activity is meant.

originalSense.definition: To work or solve cases as a detective.
originalSense.example: Parker would in all likelihood have done so; he was paid to detect and to do nothing else, and neither his natural gifts nor his education (at Barrow-in-Furness Grammar School) prompted him to stray into side-tracks at the beck of an ill-regulated imagination.

distinctionTask.prompt: A fictional investigator says he is paid to detect. This informal use describes _____.
options: a guarantee that every case will be solved
distinctionTask.explanation: The verb names the work; a successful result in every case is not asserted.

definition: An obsolete adjective meaning detected or discovered.
example: In older writing, detect may appear as an adjective meaning detected. The grammatical position distinguishes it from the ordinary verb detect.
distinctions: This obsolete adjective does not introduce a different modern detection process. Detected is clearer in ordinary modern writing.
usage: Obsolete adjective; reading guidance rather than a model for ordinary modern use.

originalSense.definition: Detected.

definition: An obsolete intransitive use meaning to seek for something or after someone.
example: In older prose, explore can mean seek for something or after someone. This obsolete construction is separate from modern explore a place or explore an idea.
distinctions: The source labels this intransitive search meaning obsolete. Seek or look for is clearer in ordinary modern use with this intended meaning.
usage: Obsolete and intransitive; reading guidance for older prose.

originalSense.definition: To seek for something or after someone.

definition: To examine or investigate something systematically.
example: The committee will explore three alternatives before choosing a plan.
distinctions: Explore alternatives means examine them. Exploring a possibility does not commit the committee to it or establish that a plan has already been chosen.
usage: Transitive: explore an idea, option, possibility or topic.

originalSense.definition: To examine or investigate something systematically.
originalSense.example: The committee has been exploring alternative solutions to the problem at hand.

distinctionTask.prompt: A committee explores three alternatives before deciding. It is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Exploring an option is examination, without an assertion that it has been selected.

definition: To travel around a place in search of discovery.
example: They plan to explore the islands by kayak.
distinctions: Exploration can make a place new to the travellers without making them the first people ever to visit it. Plan to explore describes an intention.
usage: Transitive: explore a place or area.

originalSense.definition: To travel somewhere in search of discovery.
originalSense.example: It was around that time that the expedition began exploring the Arctic Circle.

distinctionTask.prompt: Travellers plan to explore islands already inhabited for centuries. The plan concerns _____.
options: travelling around to discover more about the islands
being the first humans ever to visit them
distinctionTask.answer: travelling around to discover more about the islands
distinctionTask.explanation: Discovery in exploration can be personal; the sentence does not erase the inhabitants or earlier visitors.

definition: In medicine, to perform a diagnostic examination.
example: In a clinical account, explore can describe a diagnostic examination. The surrounding account identifies what is examined and how.
distinctions: This specialist intransitive use concerns examination for diagnosis. An examination does not itself guarantee a conclusive finding.
usage: Medical and intransitive; reading guidance for a specialist account.

originalSense.definition: To examine diagnostically.

definition: To seek or gain first-hand experience of something.
example: In her first year at university, Jo wanted to explore life away from home.
distinctions: Explore here concerns first-hand experience. Wanting to try a way of life does not establish that the planned experiences occurred.
usage: Transitive: explore an experience or aspect of life.

originalSense.definition: To (seek) experience first hand.
originalSense.example: It is normal for a boy of this age to be exploring his sexuality.

distinctionTask.prompt: Jo wants to explore life away from home through her own experience. She wants _____.
options: first-hand experience of that way of life
only a second-hand definition of it
distinctionTask.answer: first-hand experience of that way of life
distinctionTask.explanation: The intended exploration is experiential, rather than limited to a description from others.

definition: To be engaged in exploring, with no direct object stated.
example: After lunch, we had two hours to explore.
distinctions: The surroundings supply what is being explored. This intransitive construction can illustrate the broader activity without restricting explore to aimless wandering.
usage: Intransitive; the object or topic is understood from context.

originalSense.definition: To be engaged exploring in any of the above senses.
originalSense.example: He was too busy exploring to notice his son needed his guidance.

distinctionTask.prompt: We had two hours to explore. In this construction, explore _____.
options: must be an obsolete search construction

definition: The visible, interactive part of a computer program presented to its user.
example: The search view contains a text box and a results list.
distinctions: This view concerns the program’s interface. It need not be a database view or the underlying stored data.

originalSense.definition: The part of a computer program which is visible to the user and can be interacted with.

distinctionTask.prompt: A search view contains a text box and a results list. View here refers to _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The controls and results identify a program interface.

definition: A wake.
example: The linked dictionary also gives view the noun meaning a wake, without an example. The surrounding passage is needed to identify the intended wake.
distinctions: This brief gloss needs context. It should not be replaced automatically with the usual sight or opinion meanings.

originalSense.definition: A wake.

definition: To look at or watch something.
example: We viewed the flat on Saturday before deciding whether to rent it.
distinctions: Viewing the flat means looking at it. It does not establish that a rental decision or agreement followed.
usage: Transitive; view an object, place or recording.

originalSense.definition: To look at.
originalSense.example: The video was viewed by millions of people.

distinctionTask.prompt: We viewed the flat before deciding whether to rent it. The sentence establishes _____.
options: that we looked at the flat
that we signed a rental agreement
