distinctionTask.explanation: Looking at a property is separate from agreeing to rent it.

definition: To regard or interpret someone or something in a stated way.
example: They view the delay as a chance to revise the plan.
distinctions: View as introduces an interpretation. It need not describe physical seeing, and another person can interpret the same delay differently.

originalSense.definition: To regard in a stated way.
originalSense.example: I view it as a serious breach of trust.

distinctionTask.prompt: They view the delay as a chance to revise the plan. This tells us _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: View as supplies an assessment rather than a visual property.

definition: The act of seeing or looking at something.
example: Move a little so I can get a clear view of the demonstration.
distinctions: Here view concerns seeing the demonstration. It is not a drawn picture of it or an opinion about its quality.
usage: Physical noun; seeing or looking at something.

originalSense.definition: The act of seeing or looking at something.

distinctionTask.prompt: I move to get a clear view of the demonstration. I want _____.
options: to state a theory about it
distinctionTask.explanation: The physical movement supports seeing rather than an opinion.

definition: The range or field within which something can be seen.
example: The cyclist disappeared from view behind the wall.
distinctions: From view identifies the observer’s range of sight. Disappearing from sight does not establish that the cyclist stopped existing or reached a destination.
usage: Physical noun; the range of vision.

originalSense.definition: The range of vision.

distinctionTask.prompt: The cyclist disappeared from view behind a wall. The cyclist is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The obstruction concerns sight, not the cyclist’s motion.

definition: Something that can be looked at, especially scenery.
example: The room has a view of the river.
distinctions: This view is the visible scene. A painted view of the same river is a separate representation meaning.
usage: Physical noun; scenery or another scene to look at.

originalSense.definition: Something to look at, such as scenery.

distinctionTask.prompt: The room has a view of the river through its window. View refers to _____.
options: a required painting on the wall
distinctionTask.explanation: The window context identifies scenery.

definition: An individual user viewing of a web page, video or similar online content.
example: The report counted three video views from two viewers, including one repeat.
distinctions: Views count viewing events under the report’s counting rules. A repeat can make the view count larger than the number of distinct viewers; the definition does not set every platform’s threshold.
usage: Internet noun; a counted viewing event.

originalSense.definition: An individual viewing of a web page or a video etc. by a user.

distinctionTask.prompt: A report counts three views, one of them a repeat by the same viewer. Three views establish _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The repeat prevents equating event count with unique viewer count.

definition: An obsolete noun meaning appearance, show or aspect.
example: In older prose, view can describe an appearance, show or aspect. This particular meaning is obsolete.
distinctions: The appearance meaning is obsolete. The ordinary scenery and opinion meanings remain current.

originalSense.definition: Appearance; show; aspect.

definition: A mental image or conception of something.
example: The briefing gave us a clearer view of how the parts fit together.
collocations: form a view of the situation
distinctions: This view concerns a mental conception. A clearer conception need not be a literal picture or guarantee complete accuracy.
usage: Mental noun; a mental image or conception.

originalSense.definition: A mental image.

distinctionTask.prompt: A briefing gives us a clearer view of how the parts fit together. It improves _____.
options: our mental conception of the arrangement
distinctionTask.answer: our mental conception of the arrangement
distinctionTask.explanation: The context concerns understanding the arrangement.

definition: A way of understanding something, an opinion or a theory.
example: My view is that the library should stay open later.
distinctions: This is an opinion about desired opening hours. It does not report the library’s current closing time.
usage: Mental noun; an opinion may be expressed with a that-clause.

originalSense.definition: A way of understanding something, an opinion, a theory.

distinctionTask.prompt: My view is that the library should stay open later. This states _____.
options: a judgement about what the hours should be
distinctionTask.answer: a judgement about what the hours should be
distinctionTask.explanation: Should identifies the proposed situation, not a factual timetable.

definition: A point of view or perspective from which something is considered.
example: In the residents’ view, the plan would improve access.
distinctions: The phrase attributes a perspective to the residents. The projected improvement has not necessarily happened.
usage: Mental noun; in someone’s view attributes a perspective.

originalSense.definition: A point of view.

distinctionTask.prompt: In the residents’ view, the plan would improve access. The improvement is presented as _____.
options: their assessment of a proposed plan
distinctionTask.answer: their assessment of a proposed plan
distinctionTask.explanation: The attributed view and would describe an assessment of the proposal.

definition: An intention, aim or prospect.
example: They are saving with a view to buying a home.
collocations: with a view to doing something
distinctions: With a view to introduces the aim of the saving. It does not establish that a purchase has occurred; to is followed by the -ing form here.
usage: Intention noun; with a view to plus an -ing form.

originalSense.definition: An intention or prospect.

distinctionTask.prompt: They save with a view to buying a home. Buying is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The construction introduces an intention.

definition: To send light or other waves back from a surface.
example: A flat mirror reflects incoming light back into the room.
distinctions: In the illustrated ideal flat-mirror case, the incident and reflected rays make equal angles to the normal. Reflection is separate from light passing through or being absorbed.
usage: Transitive: a surface reflects light; the diagram illustrates specular reflection.

originalSense.definition: To bend back (light, etc.) from a surface.
originalSense.example: A mirror reflects the light that shines on it.

distinctionTask.prompt: A flat mirror reflects a beam. The illustrated reflection sends the light _____.
options: only through the mirror without returning
distinctionTask.explanation: Reflection concerns the returning ray; transmission is a different process.

definition: Of light or similar radiation, to be sent back from a surface.
example: The light reflected from the mirror onto the wall.
distinctions: Light is the subject in this intransitive construction. In the mirror reflects light, the surface is the subject and light is its direct object.
usage: Intransitive: light reflects from or off a surface.

originalSense.definition: To be bent back (light, etc.) from a surface.
originalSense.example: The moonlight reflected from the surface of water.

distinctionTask.prompt: The light reflected from the mirror. The grammatical subject is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The intransitive construction makes the returning light the subject.

definition: To show the image of someone or something, as a mirror does.
example: The still water reflected the tree beside the pond.
distinctions: The water shows an image of the tree. The image is separate from a second physical tree, and disturbed water can produce a different appearance.
usage: Transitive: a surface reflects an object or its image.

originalSense.definition: To mirror, or show the image of something.
originalSense.example: The shop window reflected his image as he walked past.

distinctionTask.prompt: Still water reflects a tree. The reflection is _____.
options: a second living tree beneath the water
distinctionTask.explanation: An optical image does not duplicate the physical object.

definition: To appear as a mirrored image in or from a surface.
example: The tree reflected in the still water.
distinctions: The tree is the subject of this intransitive image construction. It is the image that appears in the water; the physical tree need not be in it.
usage: Intransitive; the subject appears as a mirrored image.

originalSense.definition: To be mirrored.
originalSense.example: His image reflected from the shop window as he walked past.

distinctionTask.prompt: The tree reflected in the water. This does not require _____.
options: the physical tree to be under the water
a mirrored image of the tree
distinctionTask.answer: the physical tree to be under the water
distinctionTask.explanation: The sentence concerns the tree’s image.

definition: To agree with or closely follow something.
example: The revised timetable reflects the new train times.
distinctions: The timetable is arranged to correspond to the train times. It is not a literal mirror, and reflecting a pattern need not explain what caused it.

originalSense.definition: To agree with; to closely follow.
originalSense.example: Entries in English dictionaries aim to reflect common usage.

distinctionTask.prompt: A revised timetable reflects new train times. It _____.
options: necessarily caused the trains to change
distinctionTask.explanation: Reflect here means match or closely follow, not cause.

definition: To give evidence of someone’s or something’s character or qualities.
example: Her careful preparation reflects her professionalism.
distinctions: Preparation can be evidence of professionalism. The sentence is an assessment; it does not make any one action conclusive proof of a person’s whole character.
usage: Transitive; reflect a quality. Reflect well on also evaluates how an action presents someone.

originalSense.definition: To give evidence of someone's or something's character etc.
originalSense.example: The team's victory reflects the Captain's abilities.

distinctionTask.prompt: Careful preparation reflects her professionalism. The preparation is presented as _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The context uses reflect figuratively for evidence of a quality.

definition: To think seriously about something or consider it carefully.
example: After the meeting, we reflected on what we could improve.
distinctions: Reflect on describes deliberate consideration. It does not establish that a decision was reached or an improvement completed.
usage: Intransitive; reflect on or upon a topic.

originalSense.definition: To think seriously; to ponder or consider.
originalSense.example: People do that sort of thing every day, without ever stopping to reflect on the consequences.

distinctionTask.prompt: We reflected on what we could improve. We _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Consideration is separate from completed action.

definition: To be certain that something is true or factual.
example: I know that the shop is closed today because I checked its opening hours.
distinctions: Know presents something as known to be true. Think and suppose can express an opinion or an uncertain belief; the speaker’s claim alone is not independent verification.
usage: Transitive; know a fact or know that + clause.

originalSense.definition: To perceive the truth or factuality of; to be certain of; to be certain that.
originalSense.example: Question things. I have the most fun when I'm writing questioning things that people do not question- the assumptions that everybody knows are true.

distinctionTask.prompt: I know that the shop is closed. The speaker presents the closure as _____.
options: something they know to be true
only a guess they have not accepted
distinctionTask.answer: something they know to be true
distinctionTask.explanation: Know presents knowledge, whereas I think it is closed can leave more uncertainty.

definition: To be aware or become aware, without stating a direct object.
example: The route has changed. I did not know until this morning.
distinctions: The information is supplied by the previous sentence. This intransitive use differs grammatically from I know the route, which states an object.
usage: Intransitive; the surrounding context supplies what is known.

originalSense.definition: To be or become aware or cognizant.
originalSense.example: Did you know Michelle and Jack were getting divorced? ― Yes, I knew.

distinctionTask.prompt: The route has changed. I did not know. Here the information is _____.
options: stated as a direct object after know
distinctionTask.explanation: There is no direct object after know in this example.

definition: To be aware of a fact or situation.
example: I know the risks of travelling without insurance.
distinctions: Being aware of risks does not mean approving of them or having personally experienced them. Know the risks states an object; I already know leaves the information implicit.

originalSense.definition: To be aware of; to be cognizant of.
originalSense.example: Did you know Michelle and Jack were getting divorced? ― Yes, I knew.

distinctionTask.prompt: I know the risks of travelling without insurance. I am _____.
options: necessarily willing to accept those risks
distinctionTask.explanation: Awareness alone does not establish acceptance.

definition: An obsolete intransitive use meaning to be acquainted with another person.
example: The preserved source records an obsolete intransitive acquaintance use. For present-day learning, use a direct object in I know her, or say I am acquainted with her.
distinctions: The obsolete label concerns this intransitive record. It does not apply to the everyday transitive I know her.

originalSense.definition: To be acquainted (with another person).
originalSense.example: You, and I haue knowne ſir.

definition: To be acquainted or familiar with a person, place or thing.
example: I know our new neighbour; we met last year.
distinctions: Know a person describes familiarity. Meet describes an encounter; knowing someone does not mean knowing every fact about them.
usage: Transitive; know + person, place or thing.

originalSense.definition: To be acquainted or familiar with; to have encountered.
originalSense.example: I know your mother, but I've never met your father.

distinctionTask.prompt: I know our new neighbour; we met last year. Know expresses _____.
options: only a plan to meet them for the first time
distinctionTask.explanation: The sentence states an existing acquaintance.

definition: To experience a condition, feeling or event.
example: The town has known severe flooding in the past.
distinctions: The town has experienced flooding. This literary or formal use differs from residents merely knowing information about a flood.
usage: Transitive; often with an experience or condition.

originalSense.definition: To experience.
originalSense.example: Their relationship knew ups and downs.

distinctionTask.prompt: The town has known severe flooding. This says the town _____.
options: only holds information about floods elsewhere
distinctionTask.explanation: Know here describes experience.

definition: To understand a subject or know how to do something through study or experience.
example: She knows how to repair a puncture because she has practised.
distinctions: Know how to concerns practical or explanatory knowledge. Know that a tyre is flat states a fact and does not by itself establish repair skill.
usage: Know how to + verb; know how + clause; know a subject.

originalSense.definition: To understand or have a grasp of through experience or study.
originalSense.example: Let me do it. I know how it works.

distinctionTask.prompt: She knows how to repair a puncture. This concerns _____.
options: knowledge of how to carry out the repair
only awareness that a puncture exists
distinctionTask.answer: knowledge of how to carry out the repair
distinctionTask.explanation: Know how to describes procedural knowledge.

definition: To distinguish one thing from another or recognise its nature.
example: She knows right from wrong.
distinctions: Know A from B concerns discrimination between things. Recognising that a familiar person has returned is a separate recognition use.
usage: Transitive; especially know A from B.

originalSense.definition: To be able to distinguish, to discern, particularly by contrast or comparison; to recognize the nature of.
originalSense.example: to know a person's face or figure

distinctionTask.prompt: She knows right from wrong. She can _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The construction know A from B expresses discrimination.

definition: To recognise someone or something encountered before, despite an absence or change.

usage: Transitive; knew is the past tense of know.

originalSense.definition: To recognize as the same (as someone or something previously encountered) after an absence or change.
originalSense.example: At nearer view he thought he knew the dead, / And call'd the wretched man to mind.

met her for the first time

distinctionTask.explanation: The voice prompts renewed recognition.

definition: To possess knowledge or information, without specifying a direct object.
example: Ask the receptionist; she will know.

usage: Intransitive; context supplies the relevant information.

originalSense.definition: To have knowledge; to have information, be informed.
originalSense.example: It is vital that he not know.

distinctionTask.prompt: Ask the receptionist; she will know. She is expected to _____.
options: introduce herself for the first time
distinctionTask.explanation: No direct object is stated; the question supplies the topic.

definition: To be able to play, sing or otherwise perform a piece of music.
example: The pianist knows the opening song and can play it from memory.
distinctions: Here knows concerns ability to perform the piece. Know of a song can mean only having heard that it exists.
usage: Transitive; know a song, tune or piece.

originalSense.example: Do you know "Blueberry Hill"?

distinctionTask.prompt: The pianist knows the song and can play it from memory. Know here concerns _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The explicit ability to play identifies the musical meaning.

definition: Of a database or system, to have indexed information about something.
example: The catalogue knows this title because the record is in its database.

usage: Technical, transitive use; the subject can be a system.

distinctionTask.explanation: Know is a technical personification of indexed information.

definition: In philosophy, to have knowledge according to the account of knowledge being discussed.

distinctions: Justified true belief is one traditional account of knowledge. Gettier-style objections challenge its sufficiency, so it should not be presented as an uncontested definition.
usage: Philosophical sense; the relevant criteria depend on the account under discussion.

originalSense.definition: To maintain (a belief, a position) subject to a given philosophical definition of knowledge; to hold a justified true belief.

definition: A rare noun meaning knowledge or the state of knowing.
example: In the source’s Hamlet quotation, know is a noun for knowledge or awareness of the contents. In ordinary present-day prose, knowledge is the usual independent noun.
distinctions: This rare independent noun differs from the familiar fixed phrase in the know. Its literary attestation does not make ordinary verb know obsolete.
usage: Rare noun; reading guidance for the preserved literary source.

definition: Knowledge of a matter, now used in the fixed phrase in the know.

distinctions: In the know means informed about a matter, often information unavailable to others. It does not mean physically located inside a place.
usage: Noun within the fixed phrase in the know.

originalSense.definition: Knowledge; the state of knowing. (Now confined to the fixed phrase in the know.)

distinctionTask.explanation: The fixed phrase describes access to information.

example: The source gives Make sure you water the plants, know… . The final know draws the listener’s attention; it is not a request to define the word plants.

originalSense.example: Make sure you water the plants, know…

definition: An archaic, Biblical or euphemistic use meaning to have sexual relations with someone.

usage: Archaic, Biblical and euphemistic; reading guidance.

originalSense.definition: To have sexual relations with. This meaning normally specified in modern English as e.g. to 'know someone in the biblical sense' or to 'know biblically'.

definition: In Singlish, a discourse marker equivalent to you know, used to emphasise something.
example: In Singlish conversation, this know works like you know as a discourse marker. It can add emphasis or help manage a turn, rather than assert that the listener knows a particular fact.
collocations: you know as a discourse marker
distinctions: This regional conversational use adds emphasis or helps manage a turn. Ordinary know that instead introduces information presented as known.

originalSense.definition: Synonym of you know (used as a conversational discourse marker, to emphasize something).

definition: To comprehend the meaning of words, statements, signs or other communication.
example: I understand the instructions, so I can explain what they ask us to do.
distinctions: Understanding a message concerns its meaning. Hearing its sounds or reading its words does not by itself establish comprehension or agreement.
usage: Transitive or intransitive; communication is the focus of this source record.

originalSense.definition: To know the meaning of; to parse or have parsed correctly; to comprehend.

distinctionTask.explanation: Comprehension is separate from agreement.

definition: To be familiar enough with a skill, task or profession to carry it out properly.
example: She understands her job and can organise the work without help.
distinctions: This concerns practical familiarity with a task. Knowing a job title alone does not establish competence to do the work.
usage: Transitive; the object is a skill, task or profession.

originalSense.definition: To be thoroughly familiar with; to be able to undertake properly.
originalSense.example: The students understood the assignment.
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: She understands her job and can organise the work. This concerns _____.
options: only recognition of her job title
distinctionTask.explanation: The stated ability identifies familiarity with the task.

definition: To comprehend a fact or principle, or come to regard a belief as one.
example: The pupils understand that water expands when it freezes.

synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: The pupils understand that water expands when it freezes. The clause states _____.
options: the words omitted from an imperative
distinctionTask.explanation: This is conceptual comprehension, not grammatical ellipsis.

definition: To comprehend a person’s motives or character, or the reasons for an event.
example: I understand why she left early: she had to collect her child.

usage: Transitive; people, motives and reasons for events.

originalSense.definition: To know the intent, motives or character of; (of events) to know the causes of or reasons for.
originalSense.example: One day you say you love me, the next you ignore me—I don't understand you!
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: I understand why she left early. This does not necessarily mean I _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: Comprehension of a motive and approval are separate judgements.

definition: To believe or infer something on the basis of information that may be incomplete.
example: I understand that the meeting has moved to Friday, but I have not checked.
distinctions: I understand that can report an inference or received information. Here the speaker explicitly has not checked; this is not independent confirmation of Friday.
usage: Transitive; often a cautious report of one’s present understanding.

originalSense.definition: To believe or infer, to think one grasps sufficiently despite potentially incomplete knowledge.
originalSense.example: I've been given to understand that you have a package for me?

distinctionTask.prompt: I understand the meeting is on Friday, but I have not checked. Friday is _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The explicit qualification leaves the information unverified.

definition: In grammar, to interpret an unexpressed word or element as implicit.
example: In the command Sit down, you is understood as the subject.
distinctions: An understood subject is implicit in the grammatical interpretation. It is not printed in the command, and this technical use does not mean that a listener agrees to obey.
usage: Grammatical sense; often passive, as in the subject is understood.

originalSense.definition: To regard as present when not.
originalSense.example: In the imperative mood, the word “you” is usually understood.
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

distinctionTask.prompt: In Sit down, the subject you is understood. It is _____.
options: a visible word in the command
distinctionTask.explanation: The command has no written you, but the subject is interpreted.

definition: A rare literal use meaning to stand underneath and support, especially in acrobatics.

distinctions: The circus exception belongs to this rare literal record. It does not make the everyday comprehension verb obsolete.
usage: Humorous and rare; obsolete except in circus acrobatics, according to the checked source.

originalSense.definition: To stand underneath, to support.

LAUNE: Ay, and what I do too: look thee, I'll but lean, and my staff understands me.
SPEED: It stands under thee, indeed.
LAUNCE:Why, stand-under and under-stand is all one.
synonyms: pick up what someone is putting down

definition: In Singapore and Malaysia, an interjection acknowledging what another speaker has said.
example: The checked source records understand as a backchannel, comparable to uh-huh or I see. In this use a listener acknowledges a turn in conversation; it is not automatically a command to someone else.
distinctions: This regional interjection is distinct from the imperative Understand! and the question Do you understand? Acknowledgement also need not imply agreement.

originalSense.definition: Uh-huh, I see; a way to acknowledge something said by the other speaker.

definition: To know the meaning of something.
example: Do you understand the meaning of this symbol?
distinctions: Understanding a symbol means interpreting what it signifies. Recognising its shape or colour alone does not show that its meaning is understood.
usage: Transitive; understand the meaning of + noun phrase.

originalSense.definition: To know the meaning of.

distinctionTask.prompt: To understand the meaning of a symbol is to know _____.
options: only the colour of the page
distinctionTask.explanation: Meaning concerns what the symbol signifies.

definition: To take or keep hold of something, especially with the hand.
example: She grasped the handrail firmly as the boat moved.
distinctions: This is physical holding. Grasp an explanation instead concerns understanding, and grasp at something can describe an attempt without a secure hold.

originalSense.definition: To grip; to take hold, particularly with the hand.

wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

distinctionTask.prompt: She grasped the handrail firmly. She _____.
distinctionTask.explanation: The handrail and physical action identify the literal meaning.

definition: To understand an idea, explanation or situation.
example: After seeing the diagram, he grasped how the pump worked.
distinctions: Grasp emphasises getting an intellectual hold of something. Knowing that a pump exists does not establish understanding of how it works.
usage: Verb; grasp an idea or grasp how/that + clause.

originalSense.definition: To understand.
originalSense.example: I have never been able to grasp the concept of infinity.
wordFamily: a drowning man will grasp at a straw
a drowning man will grasp at straws

distinctionTask.prompt: He grasped how the pump worked. This means he _____.
options: held the pump in his hand by definition
distinctionTask.explanation: The how clause identifies intellectual comprehension.

definition: To seize or take advantage of an opportunity.
